abigail-adams-remember-the-ladies.context_blurb: Abigail Adams was the wife of John Adams, future second president of the United States, and one of the most impressive women of the American Revolutionary generation. She grew up without formal schooling but with full access to her father's library in Weymouth, Massachusetts, and taught herself history, political philosophy, and classical literature. During the Revolution she ran the family farm by herself while her husband was away for years at the Continental Congress or on diplomatic missions in Europe. The two of them wrote each other constantly, and their letters, which have been preserved, are one of the best windows anywhere into the political thinking of the founding generation. In March 1776, while her husband was in Philadelphia helping draft the laws of the new nation, she wrote him a famous letter urging the men now making the rules of the new republic to think about the legal position of women, who had no voice in their own government and no meaningful protection against the private authority husbands held over them. Her husband's reply was a joke, but Abigail Adams did not forget the argument. Her life is now treated as the earliest serious American case for the rights of women, pressed from inside the household of a founding father.

abolition-of-the-british-slave-trade-wil.context_blurb: William Wilberforce was a British Member of Parliament and devout evangelical Christian who, from the late 1780s until his death in 1833, led the long campaign in Westminster to end his country's slave trade and then slavery itself. He was a small, sickly man with a beautiful speaking voice, and he worked alongside a tightly knit group of reformers often called the Clapham Sect — former slavers turned preachers, Quakers, lawyers, and women who ran kitchen-table campaigns across the country. Their fight dragged on for nearly fifty years because the trade was enormously profitable: British ships carried hundreds of thousands of Africans across the Atlantic in brutal conditions, and plantation owners in the West Indies and the colonies had powerful friends in Parliament. The abolitionists answered with every weapon a peaceful movement could invent — mass petitions, consumer boycotts, printed images of the ships below decks, firsthand testimony from Africans who had survived the Middle Passage, and detailed court cases that forced the horrors into public view. Wilberforce brought a bill nearly every year, lost nearly every year, and kept going. The slave trade was finally abolished in 1807, and slavery itself across the British Empire a generation later, with Wilberforce dying days after the final vote. The questions ahead tell that story through its most famous images and lines — the campaign medallion, the shock exhibits, a hymn long associated with the movement, and the Royal Navy's later work hunting the trade down at sea. It matters because this was one of the first great modern campaigns in which ordinary people organized across a country to abolish an evil they could still profit from — and won.

abraham-lincoln-the-man-and-leader.context_blurb: Abraham Lincoln was the sixteenth president of the United States, in office from 1861 until his death in April 1865. He was born in a Kentucky log cabin, grew up on the frontier of Indiana and Illinois, and spent most of his adult life as a self-taught country lawyer and politician before being elected to the White House on the eve of civil war. He was famously tall, famously plain-looking, and famously honest — stories about his boyhood honesty, his split rails, his wrestling matches, and his gentle wit traveled with him his entire career. As president he held the Union together through the bloodiest war the country has ever fought, picked and fired generals until he found ones who would win, grieved publicly for his son and for the dead on both sides, and spoke in a prose so plain and musical that short speeches of his are still memorized by schoolchildren. The questions ahead are a tour of the man himself: boyhood stories, nicknames, little moments of character on the frontier and in the White House, a few lines of his most famous speeches, and the Latin words shouted the night he was shot. It matters because Lincoln became the kind of figure Americans measure other leaders against — a politician who kept his word, used power carefully, and took moral responsibility for a bloody war.

adam-smith-and-the-wealth-of-nations.context_blurb: Adam Smith was an 18th-century Scottish moral philosopher who taught, wrote, and thought about how ordinary people manage to live together peacefully. In 1776, the same year America declared independence, he published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, the book now treated as the beginning of modern economics. Smith had already written an earlier book on ethics and conscience called The Theory of Moral Sentiments, and he thought of economics not as a cold science but as a branch of moral philosophy, a study of what makes a society decent as well as prosperous. He saw commerce as something that could civilize people, not just enrich them. Smith never married, lived with his mother for most of his life, and died a bachelor in Edinburgh. Beneath the fame he was shy and famously absent-minded, known for wandering around in his dressing gown and getting so lost in his own thoughts that he once walked miles down the road before anyone noticed he was still in his nightclothes. His books have been quarreled over ever since by people who agree with him, people who hate him, and people who have never actually read him.

adwa-ethiopia-defeats-italy.context_blurb: In the 1890s, during the European Scramble for Africa, the newly united Kingdom of Italy tried to turn the ancient Christian empire of Ethiopia into one of its colonies. The Ethiopian emperor was Menelik II, a shrewd ruler who had been quietly buying modern rifles from France and Russia and knitting the empire's regional lords together under his crown. His queen, Empress Taytu Betul, rode and camped with the army and took a leading role in the diplomacy. The questions ahead cover two moments in that fight — a smaller siege in which the Ethiopians outthought the Italian garrison, and a treaty trick where the Italian and Ethiopian versions of the same document said different things. The showdown came at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, where Menelik's army — larger, well-armed, fighting on home ground — crushed the invading Italian force. Italy was forced to recognize Ethiopia as a fully independent country. It mattered then and still matters now because Ethiopia became the one African kingdom that beat back a European power during the age of imperialism, kept its throne, and remained a symbol of African freedom for generations of pan-Africanists and civil rights leaders afterward.

aesop-s-fables.context_blurb: Aesop was, in the Greek tradition, a slave in the Greek-speaking world of the 6th century BC, remembered as the author of short, pointed moral stories told through talking animals. Whether a single person named Aesop ever actually lived is uncertain; the stories themselves may have been collected and attributed to him by later generations, the way Mother Goose rhymes work. What is certain is that a vast body of these short tales circulated under his name throughout the ancient Mediterranean world, were later gathered and polished by writers like Phaedrus in Latin and La Fontaine in French, and have never gone out of circulation since. The fables are usually just a few lines long, feature a fox or a crow or a lion or a mouse, and end with a sharp proverbial lesson about greed, pride, friendship, laziness, or cleverness. They were used for over two thousand years to teach Greek and Latin to beginners, and generations of European schoolchildren learned to read ancient languages by stumbling through them. The phrases they coined — sour grapes, the lion's share, the boy who cried wolf, slow and steady wins the race — have passed into dozens of languages as everyday idioms.

african-art-benin-bronzes-and-masks.context_blurb: The medieval Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southwestern Nigeria, produced one of the great metalworking traditions of the pre-modern world. For centuries, Benin's royal craftsmen cast beautiful cast-brass and bronze sculptures using the lost-wax method, including portrait heads of past kings (obas), long plaques depicting royal processions and warriors, and ritual objects used in the palace precinct. The sophistication of the castings surprised European observers when the pieces first reached Europe. Across sub-Saharan Africa, from the Yoruba kingdoms to the Dogon of Mali to the ancestor-carvers of the Fang and the great mask-making traditions of the Dan, Mende, and others, African artists developed powerful traditions of ritual wood carving and ceremonial masking that would deeply influence 20th-century European modernists like Picasso, Modigliani, and Matisse. The great African sculpture traditions were produced by professional specialists working for royal patrons or religious societies, and they carried meanings about kingship, ancestry, fertility, and the spirit world that most Western collectors never fully understood. Many of the finest pieces were looted during the colonial period, especially the Benin collections taken in a British punitive expedition in 1897, and are now the subject of long-running disputes about restitution to the African societies that made them.

african-decolonization-ghana-1957.context_blurb: After the Second World War, the European colonial empires in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean began to come apart. Across Africa the process ran from the 1950s through the 1970s. The former British colony of the Gold Coast became independent as Ghana in 1957 under the leadership of Kwame Nkrumah, becoming the first sub-Saharan African country to break free of European colonial rule in the postwar wave. Nkrumah himself had studied in the United States, admired African American civil-rights leaders, and framed Ghanaian independence as the first step in a broader liberation of the entire continent. Over the following two decades nearly every African country gained independence, often peacefully and sometimes through long bitter wars (Algeria from France, Angola and Mozambique from Portugal, Zimbabwe from a settler-ruled Rhodesia). Many of the new states inherited colonial-era borders drawn in Europe without regard to the peoples living inside them, and the resulting ethnic strains helped produce political instability in many places. The independence era produced some of the great African political figures of the 20th century — Nkrumah, Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya, Julius Nyerere of Tanzania, Leopold Senghor of Senegal, and many others — some of whom became liberators, some of whom became dictators, and some of whom became both.

aggression-unchecked-rhineland-ethiopia-.context_blurb: Between 1935 and 1938 Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini carried out a series of territorial moves that broke the peace settlement of 1919, and each time the Western democracies refused to stop them. In October 1935 Mussolini sent the Italian army into Ethiopia, the last independent African empire, to avenge an old defeat forty years earlier; Emperor Haile Selassie fled into exile and later pleaded his case in person before the League of Nations in Geneva. In March 1936 Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, the stretch of German territory along the French border that the Treaty of Versailles had required to stay demilitarized — a bluff his own generals thought dangerous. Two years later, in March 1938, he marched into his native Austria and announced the Anschluss, the union of Austria into a greater Germany, while Austrian Jews were pulled out of their shops and homes in Vienna and subjected to public cruelties no one in power rose to stop. Each step was a test, and each failed test taught Hitler what he needed to know about Britain and France. Winston Churchill, from his back-bench seat in the House of Commons, kept warning anyone who would listen that each unanswered move was making a bigger war harder to prevent, not easier; nobody who mattered listened to him until it was too late.

al-andalus-and-moorish-spain.context_blurb: Al-Andalus was the name Muslim rulers gave to the Spanish peninsula they governed from 711 to 1492, with their peak capital at Cordoba under an Umayyad dynasty that had fled the slaughter of its family in Damascus. For about three centuries Cordoba may have been the greatest city in Europe, with paved streets, running water, and a palace-city called Madinat al-Zahra that one caliph built for his favorite wife. Non-Muslims there lived under the dhimma system, which protected Jews and Christians as 'peoples of the book' but kept them in a lower legal rank with their own obligations to the state. Great minds flourished across all three communities — the Jewish philosopher Maimonides was born in Cordoba, the Muslim philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes) wrote his commentaries on Aristotle there, and the court drew poets, mathematicians, astronomers, and musicians from across the Islamic world and well beyond it. The small Christian kingdoms of the north slowly fought their way south in a long campaign called the Reconquista, finally taking Toledo in 1085, Cordoba in 1236, and Granada in 1492 — the same year Columbus sailed and the same year the triumphant monarchs expelled the Jews from a Spain that had been home to them for well over a thousand years.

albrecht-durer-northern-renaissance-prin.context_blurb: Albrecht Durer was a German painter, printmaker, and theorist who lived in Nuremberg from 1471 to 1528 and is generally considered the greatest artist of the Northern Renaissance. He trained as a goldsmith's apprentice before switching to painting, traveled twice to Italy to study the Renaissance there, and brought back a close knowledge of Italian perspective, proportion, and classical learning that he blended with his native northern precision and symbolic imagination. His large religious and allegorical paintings earned him commissions from Holy Roman Emperors, but it was his printmaking that spread his fame across Europe during his own lifetime, because printed images could be mass-produced and sold across borders at a price ordinary people could afford. He raised engraving and woodcut to a new level of technical and expressive sophistication, producing extraordinary single-sheet images and series of prints on religious themes. He was also one of the first European artists to make a serious practice of self-portraiture across his life, leaving a series of famous paintings and drawings showing himself at different ages. He wrote treatises on perspective, measurement, and the proportions of the human body, trying to put the German Renaissance on a scientific footing comparable to the Italian one. His influence on European art lasted for generations.

alexander-graham-bell-and-the-telephone.context_blurb: Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born inventor and teacher of the deaf who settled first in Canada and then in Boston in the 1870s. His mother and later his wife were both deaf, and his lifelong fascination with how human speech worked drew him into experiments on sending the human voice down an electrical wire. He was not the only person chasing the idea; several American inventors were working the same problem at the same time, and the race to the United States Patent Office in 1876 became one of the most famous legal fights in the history of invention. Bell got there first, by a margin so narrow that courts and historians have been arguing about it ever since. He went on to found the company that would carry his name for over a century and to become a wealthy, bearded sage of science in his later years at his estate in Nova Scotia. The first clear voice sent on his instrument from one room to another passed between Bell and his young assistant, and in the months before it the men had already managed to coax recognisable sounds out of training versions of the device. Bell himself kept inventing to the end of his life, dabbling in flight, in hydrofoil boats, and in breeding sheep, but it is this one summer of 1876 that put his name in every schoolbook.

alexander-hamilton-treasury-national-ban.context_blurb: Alexander Hamilton was born an illegitimate child in the Caribbean, orphaned young, educated by charity, and arrived in New York as a teenager with nothing. He served brilliantly on George Washington's staff during the Revolution, delegate to the Constitutional Convention, co-author of the Federalist Papers, and the first United States Secretary of the Treasury under Washington's new government. In that role he reorganized the finances of the young country from near bankruptcy into a serious credit footing. He pushed through federal assumption of state Revolutionary War debts, founded a national bank, established the United States mint and the Coast Guard, and set up the federal customs system that funded the early government. His economic vision — of a commercial, manufacturing republic underwritten by sound credit — set the long argument against Thomas Jefferson's more agrarian vision that would define the first American political parties. Hamilton was also combative, prolific, and physically small, which was an unfortunate combination given the dueling culture of his age. He was killed in 1804 by Vice President Aaron Burr in a duel across the Hudson River from New York. His face is on the ten-dollar bill today, and a wildly popular Broadway musical about his life has reintroduced him to a huge modern audience.

alexander-the-great-s-conquest-of-the-pe.context_blurb: Alexander the Great was a Macedonian king who in the span of about a decade, between 334 and 323 BC, built the largest empire the ancient world had ever seen and then died suddenly at the age of thirty-two. He had inherited a well-drilled, battle-hardened army from his father Philip II, who was assassinated when Alexander was twenty, and he set out immediately to carry out the Macedonian plan to invade and conquer the Persian Empire. In a series of battles across Asia Minor, the Levant, Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia proper, Central Asia, and finally into northern India, he defeated the Persian king Darius III, destroyed every army sent against him, and marched his tired men farther east than any Western army had ever gone. His soldiers eventually refused to go any farther, and he turned back; he died of fever in Babylon shortly afterward. His empire was partitioned between his generals and did not survive him as a unit, but his conquests spread Greek language, Greek urban design, and Greek habits of thought across an enormous belt of the Old World, launching the long period historians call the Hellenistic Age.

allied-commanders-eisenhower-patton-maca.context_blurb: The Allied victory in the Second World War was planned and executed by a group of senior commanders who became household names. Dwight D. Eisenhower was the American general chosen to serve as Supreme Allied Commander for the European theater, overseeing the invasions of North Africa, Italy, and finally Northwest Europe starting with the D-Day landings in Normandy in June 1944. George S. Patton was the aggressive, famously profane American tank general who led the Third Army's rapid armored breakout across France and later across Germany. Douglas MacArthur was the vain, theatrical American general who commanded Allied forces in the Pacific theater, famously promising to return to the Philippines after the fall of Bataan in 1942 and keeping that promise two years later. Omar Bradley led huge American ground forces in Europe under Eisenhower. On the British side, Bernard Montgomery commanded British forces in North Africa and in Northwest Europe. The commanders quarreled constantly with each other but got the strategic job done. Several of them, especially Eisenhower and MacArthur, had major postwar political careers, and Eisenhower himself was elected the thirty-fourth president of the United States in 1952.

america-enters-world-war-i.context_blurb: The United States watched the Great War from the sidelines for nearly three years. President Woodrow Wilson had been reelected in 1916 on the slogan 'He kept us out of war,' and most Americans wanted to stay out. Two things changed their minds in early 1917: Germany's return to unrestricted submarine warfare, which was sinking passenger and merchant ships without warning, and the public exposure of a secret German telegram offering Mexico an alliance against the United States with the promise that Mexico could get back lost territory if Germany won. British intelligence had quietly intercepted and deciphered that telegram, and when American newspapers printed it the national mood turned. Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war that April, and General John J. Pershing's American Expeditionary Force sailed for France; by the summer of 1918 fresh American troops — the doughboys — were landing in Europe by the hundreds of thousands and fighting at Belleau Wood, Chateau-Thierry, and in the Argonne, where several American soldiers and Marines performed feats that would become legend. The American weight on the Western Front broke the final German spring offensive and tipped the war to its end that November. By the time the shooting stopped, over two million Americans had served in Europe and more than 50,000 had been killed in action.

american-modern-art-hopper-pollock-warho.context_blurb: In the 20th century, American painters pushed to the center of international art for the first time, with a wave of major figures and movements that between them transformed what Western art looked like. Edward Hopper (1882 to 1967) painted lonely, meticulously observed scenes of ordinary American interiors and streets — diners, gas stations, hotel rooms, lighthouses — in which human figures look quietly isolated. Jackson Pollock (1912 to 1956) was the great figure of American Abstract Expressionism, producing enormous paintings by dripping, flinging, and pouring commercial house paint onto canvases laid flat on his studio floor. Mark Rothko's great color-field canvases, Willem de Kooning's slashing figurative paintings, and the work of Lee Krasner, Helen Frankenthaler, and others shared the same mid-century New York scene. In the 1960s, Andy Warhol led the Pop Art movement away from Abstract Expressionism and back toward recognizable imagery drawn from mass-market advertising and celebrity photography, with his silkscreened soup cans, Marilyn Monroes, and Chairman Maos. Over roughly four decades New York took over from Paris as the capital of Western painting. The individual artists are now routinely sold at auction for extraordinary prices, but their work transformed how Americans saw themselves.

american-vocal-traditions-spirituals-fol.context_blurb: American music, especially sung music, grew out of several deep traditions blending together. The African American spiritual tradition, developed by enslaved people in the American South, produced an immense body of religious songs rooted in biblical imagery and the longing for freedom. Many of them later shaped the Civil Rights movement, the folk revival of the 1960s, and the whole American gospel tradition. White Appalachian ballad traditions, carried over from the British Isles by Scottish-Irish and English settlers, preserved old English murder ballads and love songs that nineteenth-century collectors eventually tracked back to their European sources. Shape-note singing in the rural South, Shaker hymnody in New England, and black-face minstrelsy (an uglier element of the record) all contributed. American patriotic song grew up in parallel, with The Star-Spangled Banner, My Country 'Tis of Thee, America the Beautiful, and the Battle Hymn of the Republic becoming part of the national soundtrack. The 20th-century folk revival, led by figures like Woody Guthrie, Leadbelly, Pete Seeger, Odetta, and Joan Baez, consciously drew on all of these older strands. The hybrid tradition that resulted is one of the richest native repertoires of any country.

amerigo-vespucci-naming-of-america.context_blurb: Amerigo Vespucci was an Italian merchant and navigator who made voyages across the Atlantic shortly after Columbus. He wrote lively travel accounts describing what he had seen along the long coastline of South America, and in the age of cheap books those accounts spread quickly across Europe. A young German cartographer named Martin Waldseemuller, working in a small Alsatian scriptorium, decided to honor the Italian traveler on a huge world map he was engraving in 1507. The label he chose stuck, spread north with later mapmakers, and eventually covered two whole continents. Columbus himself, who had made landfall years earlier, interpreted what he had found through the lens of his own old convictions and held to them until the day he died. Vespucci, who sailed the same waters later with fresh eyes, read the coasts differently, and his way of describing them, carried widely in print, played a quiet role in how educated Europeans began to think about the New World. The result is one of history's great geographical ironies: Columbus's name is on no major landmass, while his younger contemporary's name is on two whole continents. Vespucci himself appears to have found the whole business bewildering; he was still alive when Waldseemuller's map began circulating, and seems to have had no idea at the time that his modest writings had been turned into a continent-scale label.

ancestral-puebloans-anasazi-of-the-south.context_blurb: The Ancestral Puebloans — once called the Anasazi, a Navajo name their modern descendants no longer prefer — were a group of farming peoples who lived in the Four Corners region of the American Southwest from roughly the 1st century AD until around AD 1300. They built astonishing settlements out of carefully fitted stone, mud brick, and shaped timbers, including multi-story apartment-like complexes tucked into the alcoves of enormous sandstone cliffs. They dry-farmed corn, beans, and squash on the arid plateau, dug ceremonial underground chambers for religious gatherings, kept turkeys, traded for seashells and parrot feathers from Mesoamerica, and left behind an immense amount of pottery, basketry, and rock art that archaeologists are still studying. Around the 13th century a long and severe drought, probably combined with internal pressures, pushed them to abandon their most spectacular sites and move south and east. Their descendants are the modern Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande valley and the Hopi mesas, who still live in the Southwest and whose own oral traditions describe this long migration. The empty cliff dwellings of the Four Corners remain one of the most hauntingly beautiful ruins in North America.

ancient-china-s-rivers-oracle-bones-shan.context_blurb: The earliest Chinese civilization archaeologists can firmly document grew along a particular river in northern China whose yellow silt gives it its name. The Shang dynasty, which flourished from roughly 1600 to 1046 BC along this river, is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by written evidence. The Shang were skilled bronze-casters who produced some of the most beautiful ritual vessels anywhere in the ancient world, with intricate taotie monster-face designs. They are especially famous for leaving behind thousands of oracle bones — ox shoulder blades and tortoise shells into which Shang diviners carved questions for the royal ancestors, then heated with a hot bronze rod until the bone cracked, with the pattern of cracks read as the ancestors' answer. The questions carved on the bones are the earliest known Chinese writing and recorded everything from war and weather to royal hunting trips. These bones were only recognized as ancient artifacts in 1899 (previously ground up as medicine), and their rediscovery pushed Chinese history back by centuries. The Shang were overthrown by the Zhou in 1046 BC in a battle that set the stage for everything that came later in Chinese imperial history.

angkor-wat-the-khmer-empire.context_blurb: The Khmer Empire, which ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from around AD 802 to the 15th century, built one of the greatest urban complexes of the pre-industrial world at Angkor in what is now northwestern Cambodia. At its height Angkor may have covered over a thousand square kilometers and housed hundreds of thousands of people, which would have made it the largest low-density city on Earth. The Khmer kings built an extraordinary system of canals, reservoirs (called baray), and causeways to control the monsoon water supply and feed vast rice fields. The most famous of their stone temple complexes, originally built as a Hindu temple in the early 12th century under King Suryavarman II and later converted to Buddhist use, is the largest religious monument on Earth by area. Its sandstone bas-reliefs, running for nearly a kilometer along its lower galleries, tell stories from the great Hindu epics along with scenes of Khmer court and war life. The empire declined over the 14th and 15th centuries as Thai expansion, environmental stress on the water system, and shifts in trade routes drained its power. The temples were never fully abandoned but became overgrown; French explorers and archaeologists rediscovered them for the Western world in the 1800s.

anne-frank-and-the-diary.context_blurb: Anne Frank was a Jewish girl born in Frankfurt, Germany, in 1929 whose family fled to Amsterdam when the Nazis took power in Germany. After the Germans occupied the Netherlands in 1940 and began deporting Jews, Anne's father Otto arranged a hiding place in a concealed set of rooms above his business premises on the Prinsengracht canal in central Amsterdam. The Frank family and four others lived in hiding there for just over two years, from July 1942 to August 1944, sustained by a small group of Dutch employees who risked their own lives to bring food and news. Anne, who was thirteen when she went into hiding and fifteen when she was arrested, kept a careful diary throughout, writing with astonishing emotional precision for her age. The group was betrayed by someone whose identity has never been conclusively identified, arrested, and deported to Nazi concentration camps. Anne and her older sister Margot died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen in early 1945, just weeks before the camp was liberated. Only her father Otto survived the war. He published Anne's diary in 1947. It has since been translated into over seventy languages and read by millions of children around the world as one of the most intimate human documents of the Holocaust.

antietam-the-bloodiest-single-day.context_blurb: Antietam was a battle fought on September 17, 1862, in rolling Maryland farmland just outside the little town of Sharpsburg, along a creek called Antietam. It was the first major fight of the American Civil War on Union soil, after the Confederate general Robert E. Lee led his Army of Northern Virginia north in hopes of swinging a wavering Europe toward recognizing the Confederacy and of forcing President Lincoln to the peace table. Opposing him was George B. McClellan, cautious commander of the Union Army of the Potomac, who had just stumbled into an unlikely piece of good fortune on the march up to the battle. The story covers that intelligence windfall, the terrible names soldiers gave to the places where the worst killing happened, the civilian volunteer who became a legend by nursing the wounded under fire, the look of the famous cornfield after the first hour, a creek crossing that became infamous for its stubbornness, and the political door the battle opened for Lincoln. Antietam remains the bloodiest single day in American history — more Americans fell between sunrise and sunset there than on any other date before or since — and the Union's narrow success gave Lincoln the victory he had been waiting for to change what the war was about.

antony-cleopatra-and-the-battle-of-actiu.context_blurb: Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII are one of the great doomed couples of history. Antony was a Roman general, a close companion of Julius Caesar, and after Caesar's assassination he ran the eastern half of the Roman world. Cleopatra was the last pharaoh of Egypt, the clever and well-educated final ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty that had held Egypt since Alexander the Great. Their alliance began as politics and became a love affair, and together they threatened the ambitions of Antony's rival in the west, Caesar's adopted son Octavian. In 31 BC the two sides met in a huge naval battle in Greek waters off the coast of Epirus, and Antony and Cleopatra lost. Within a year both were dead by their own hands, Egypt was absorbed into Rome, and Octavian emerged as the sole master of the Roman world, soon to be rebranded as the emperor Augustus. The story has been retold by Plutarch, Shakespeare, and Hollywood many times over, which is why most people picture Cleopatra with asps and Elizabeth Taylor's eyes rather than as the shrewd Greek-speaking queen she actually was.

apartheid-nelson-mandela.context_blurb: After the Second World War, the white-minority National Party government of South Africa formalized a brutal system of racial separation it called apartheid, meaning literally apartness in Afrikaans. The policy, officially adopted in 1948, legally classified every South African by race, confined non-whites to specific areas of the country, denied them voting rights, forced them to carry pass books that controlled where they could travel, forbade interracial marriage and sexual relationships, and limited their education and work. Mass resistance to apartheid, led by the African National Congress and other groups, produced waves of boycotts, protests, strikes, and (after a certain point) armed sabotage. The young ANC lawyer Nelson Mandela became one of the central figures of the movement. He was arrested in 1962 and spent the next twenty-seven years in prison, mostly on Robben Island off the coast of Cape Town, becoming an international symbol of resistance to apartheid. Decades of internal protest and international pressure, including trade and sports boycotts, finally forced the National Party government to negotiate. Mandela was released from prison in 1990, apartheid was formally dismantled in the early 1990s, and in 1994 Mandela was elected the first president of a democratic post-apartheid South Africa by a huge majority.

apollo-11-and-the-moon-landing.context_blurb: Apollo 11 was the mission that answered President John F. Kennedy's 1961 promise to put American astronauts on the Moon and bring them home safely before the end of the decade. In July 1969 three men — Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins — rode an enormous Saturn V rocket up out of Florida on a trip that lasted eight days. Two of them took a spidery lander down to the lunar surface while the third stayed in orbit alone. The landing itself was tense: computer alarms flashed and the fuel gauge wound down low before they were safely on the ground. On the surface the two moonwalkers planted an American flag, bounced around in one-sixth gravity, read a plaque, scooped up rocks, and left behind footprints, scientific instruments, and a small disc inscribed with messages from world leaders. An enormous worldwide audience watched the broadcast on television or listened on radio, and the mission is still probably the most-watched event in human history. All three men came home as heroes, though Armstrong in particular shunned the fame for the rest of his life. The Apollo program would land ten more men on the Moon over the next three years before the United States stopped going. Many later writers have asked whether what the three men said, saw, or privately did during those few hours in space was properly reported at the time, and little details about the landing have kept turning up in interviews for the rest of their lives.

apollo-11-moon-landing-1969.context_blurb: On July 20, 1969, the American spacecraft Apollo 11 landed two human beings on the surface of the Moon, in a flat lunar plain called the Sea of Tranquility, in a feat that is still the farthest from Earth any human being has ever traveled. The mission was the climax of nearly a decade of American effort launched by President John F. Kennedy's 1961 promise to put a man on the Moon by the end of the decade — a promise made in the aftermath of a series of Soviet space firsts that had embarrassed the United States during the Cold War. Apollo 11 was commanded by Neil Armstrong, who became the first human to step onto the lunar surface. His crewmate Buzz Aldrin followed him down the ladder; the third astronaut, Michael Collins, stayed in orbit around the Moon aboard the command module. The two Moon walkers spent about two and a half hours outside their lander, collected rocks, planted a flag, took photographs, and performed experiments before rejoining Collins for the long return trip home. Six more Apollo missions attempted lunar landings over the following three years, five of which succeeded. The last human beings on the Moon left in December 1972, and nobody has walked there since, which is an increasingly strange historical fact.

appeasement-and-the-munich-agreement.context_blurb: Through the mid-1930s, the British and French governments watched Adolf Hitler's Nazi Germany rearm in open violation of the Treaty of Versailles, remilitarize the Rhineland, annex Austria, and threaten Czechoslovakia, without seriously opposing him. The strategy, which became known as appeasement, was pursued most actively by the British prime minister Neville Chamberlain. At a conference in Munich in September 1938, Chamberlain, French Prime Minister Edouard Daladier, Hitler, and Benito Mussolini agreed to allow Germany to annex the Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia in exchange for Hitler's promise of no further territorial demands. The Czechoslovak government was excluded from its own negotiations. Chamberlain returned to London waving a piece of paper and declared he had secured peace for our time. Within six months Germany had seized the rest of Czechoslovakia, and within a year of the Munich conference Hitler had invaded Poland and set off the Second World War. Appeasement has become a shorthand in English for giving in to an aggressor's demands in the hope of avoiding war. Winston Churchill, who had opposed appeasement throughout the 1930s, replaced Chamberlain as prime minister in May 1940.

appomattox-and-lee-s-surrender.context_blurb: Appomattox Court House was a tiny Virginia village where, on April 9, 1865, Confederate general Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Union general Ulysses S. Grant, effectively ending the American Civil War. By that spring Lee's starving army had been chased west out of its trenches around Petersburg and Richmond, and Grant's columns had finally cut it off. The two generals met in the parlor of a local merchant named Wilmer McLean, a man whose family had already been forced to move once before during the war. Grant, in a muddy private's coat, offered famously generous terms; Lee, in his best dress uniform, accepted them. The questions ahead cover that strange coincidence of McLean's two homes, a small keepsake carried off from his parlor, the specific mercies Grant allowed the surrendering men, a quiet gesture of respect at the formal stacking of arms a few days later, and a later legend of Appomattox that the Union officer in charge dismissed in print. It matters because the way the war ended — mercy from the victor, dignity preserved for the vanquished, and no mass executions — set a tone of reconciliation that both sides would later struggle, and often fail, to live up to.

aqueducts-roads-and-roman-engineering.context_blurb: The Romans were not the first great engineers in the ancient world, but they were the ones who industrialized the practice. For centuries they built, maintained, and extended one of the most impressive public works systems ever assembled: paved roads that bound their empire together, aqueducts that carried fresh water tens of miles into Roman cities, drainage sewers under their streets, harbor jetties into the sea, and public baths and theaters in nearly every provincial town. Their engineers worked with careful survey, with a specific mix of mortar they had figured out, and with a geometric shape that let them span openings many times wider than any previous builders could manage. Roman roads, especially the great road running south from Rome, became the arteries of the empire; some stretches are still in use today. Later ages would stare at Roman ruins and wonder how it had all been done, and the famous question — what have the Romans ever done for us? — was really a half-joking admission that in sheer practical engineering they had rewritten what was possible, and medieval Europe would not fully match them for a thousand years.

aquinas-the-salamanca-school-the-natural.context_blurb: This story traces a line of Christian thinkers across four centuries, from the high Middle Ages to the age of empire, who argued that moral law is not just a king's command but something written into human nature itself and knowable by reason. The chain starts with the greatest teacher of the medieval Church, a quiet friar whose masterwork tried to show that reason and faith lead to the same truth, and whose simple writing method is still taught in philosophy classes today. It picks up centuries later in Spanish universities wrestling with what Europeans were doing to peoples across the ocean, asking out loud whether conquest, slavery, and forced conversion could ever be just, and whether distant pagan peoples really did or did not possess their own lands by nature. And it reaches jurists of the age of exploration trying to tie princes to a law that stands above their palaces, their armies, and their oceans. Their critics called the project dusty or impractical, but each thinker in the chain was willing to be ignored, exiled, or killed to defend the idea that no earthly power can quietly rewrite what is right and what is wrong. Modern talk of human rights still draws on the taproot these thinkers laid down, even when the people who draw on it do not remember the names of the Christian scholars who dug it.

arabic-numerals-and-the-spread-of-zero.context_blurb: The numerals we call 'Arabic' actually traveled thousands of miles before reaching Europe. Muslim scholars adopted the system — digits 0 through 9 and the strange, powerful idea of zero — from older traditions they encountered as the caliphate expanded through Persia and across the Hindu Kush, then refined it in Baghdad's House of Wisdom under caliphs who valued arithmetic for everything from inheritance law to astronomy. The real breakthrough was zero itself: a symbol for nothing, which many earlier European mathematicians had resisted on philosophical grounds about whether a symbol could stand for the absence of number, but which makes long division, place value, and algebra possible at all. From there the new numerals spread west through Islamic Spain and Sicily; by the thirteenth century an Italian merchant's son named Fibonacci was preaching them across Europe as faster and cleaner than Roman numerals for keeping accounts, and his book Liber Abaci showed Italian bankers how much easier they made commercial arithmetic. The old Roman system clung on in formal uses — chapter headings, clock faces, royal titles — but for everyday math the Hindu-Arabic digits took over the Western world within a few generations, and no modern scientist or merchant would try to work without them.

archimedes-eureka-and-the-siege-of-syrac.context_blurb: Archimedes was a Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, and inventor who lived in the 3rd century BC in the Sicilian city of Syracuse, in a Greek colony then being squeezed between Rome and Carthage. He was arguably the greatest mathematician of antiquity. He worked out the ratio of a sphere's volume to a cylinder's, which he was so proud of that he asked for the diagram to be carved on his tomb. He wrote treatises on levers, pulleys, and the behavior of floating bodies. He designed defensive war machines for the city that are said to have hurled stones and grappled Roman ships out of the water during the Roman siege of Syracuse in the Second Punic War. When Syracuse finally fell in 212 BC, a Roman soldier killed Archimedes in his home even though the Roman general had given orders to spare him. The story goes that Archimedes was drawing diagrams in the sand and told the soldier not to disturb his circles. His inventions, his thought experiments on the lever, and his way of thinking about shapes with infinite subdivisions anticipated calculus by nearly two thousand years.

archimedes-of-syracuse.context_blurb: Archimedes was a Greek mathematician and engineer who lived in the city of Syracuse on the island of Sicily in the third century BC. He was the greatest mathematical mind of the ancient world, a friend and relative of the city's kings, and the inventor of enough clever machines that stories about him blurred into legend within a few generations. His pure mathematics is what he himself prized most highly: he found the volumes and areas of curved shapes by careful geometrical argument long before any symbolic equation for such a thing existed. But he could also build. During the long Roman siege of Syracuse in 212 BC, machines he had designed held off the attackers' fleet for an astonishing length of time, and tales of what those machines could do grew taller with each retelling by Greek and Roman historians. When the Romans finally broke in, their general Marcellus had given orders that the old mathematician was to be spared. The soldier who found him did not know who he was, lost his temper over a stubborn old man too absorbed in his work to look up, and killed him. Marcellus was reportedly furious. The grave later fell into neglect; it was the Roman writer Cicero, visiting Sicily as a young official, who hunted the overgrown tomb down by a small carved emblem Archimedes had asked to have placed on it as a monument to what he considered his finest piece of work.

aristotle-as-natural-philosopher.context_blurb: Aristotle was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC who studied under Plato in Athens, tutored the young prince who became Alexander the Great, and later founded his own school in Athens called the Lyceum. For almost two thousand years after his death, in Christian Europe and in the Islamic world alike, he was simply 'the Philosopher,' and medieval scholars quoted him as a near-final authority on nearly every subject a human being could ask about. He wrote on ethics, politics, poetry, logic, metaphysics, and the soul — but he was also a tireless and patient observer of the living world. He spent a long stretch of his life on the island of Lesbos cataloguing marine life, dissecting animals, and interviewing the working people who actually handled them for a living. He grouped living things into a vast ladder of complexity, insisted that every creature had a purpose knit into its shape, and tried to explain the stars, the weather, memory, dreams, and even the beating of a chicken embryo's heart within a single sweeping system. Many of his specific guesses were later overthrown — about the brain, about where small animals come from, about the arrangement of the heavens — but his habit of looking first, naming carefully, and arguing from evidence set the pattern that European natural science would eventually recover and extend. Even Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin, centuries later, spoke of him with respect.

aristotle-the-lyceum-and-tutoring-alexan.context_blurb: Aristotle was a 4th-century BC Greek philosopher born in Stagira in northern Greece. He studied under Plato in Athens for about twenty years before Plato's death, after which he went east, became tutor to a boy named Alexander who would later conquer most of the known world, and finally returned to Athens to found his own school called the Lyceum. His writings cover almost every subject the ancient world considered knowledge: logic, metaphysics, biology, physics, meteorology, ethics, rhetoric, poetry, and politics. He was the first serious biologist in the Western tradition, dissecting animals, cataloguing hundreds of species, and recording observations about marine life around the Greek island of Lesbos that twentieth-century biologists could still verify. His system of logic ruled Western thinking for the next two thousand years, and the medieval Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas eventually baptized his philosophy into the heart of the Catholic intellectual tradition. Aristotle was also simply the first person we know of who tried to give a rational account of nearly everything, which is why he is sometimes called "the master of those who know". He died in exile in 322 BC, shortly after Alexander's death, when Athens turned against anyone associated with the Macedonian royal house.

armenian-genocide.context_blurb: During World War I the ruling Young Turks of the Ottoman Empire set out to destroy the Armenian people, an ancient Christian nation that had lived under Ottoman rule for centuries. In the spring of 1915 the Ottoman government rounded up and killed hundreds of Armenian community leaders in Constantinople, and then across the eastern provinces it drove whole villages out on death marches into the Syrian desert, where most died of thirst, exposure, or massacre along the way. Observers inside Ottoman territory sent horrified reports to the outside world, and American churches and schoolchildren responded with one of the largest humanitarian relief drives of the era, raising enormous sums to feed and shelter the survivors. Perhaps a million and a half Armenians perished before the killing finally stopped. The Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who had read about these events as a boy, would later devote his career to arguing for international laws against the deliberate killing of whole peoples; a group of young Armenian survivors meanwhile hunted down the senior Ottoman officials who had ordered the massacres and shot them, one by one, in European capitals. Modern Turkey still officially denies that what happened was systematic, and Adolf Hitler would notoriously point to how fast the world had forgotten as part of his own argument for mass murder in 1939.

armistice-of-november-11-1918.context_blurb: The Great War ended on November 11, 1918, at a time that newspapers and schoolchildren would memorize for a century afterward. The agreement was signed just before dawn in a railway dining-carriage parked in a forest clearing north of Paris, where the French commander Marshal Ferdinand Foch had set out the terms for a German delegation that had crossed the lines by lamplight. Germany had asked for peace after her armies crumbled in the Hundred Days Offensive of the late summer, and with Austria-Hungary falling apart Kaiser Wilhelm II had already abdicated and fled to the neutral Netherlands. The last hours of the war were strange and tragic: both sides knew the guns were about to stop, but some officers ordered attacks right up to the deadline, and men on both sides died for ground that would mean nothing by lunchtime. The railway carriage where the signing happened would itself become one of the most famous objects of the war, with its own long and bitter sequel to come. The day of the signing has been remembered ever since: Armistice Day in Britain and Commonwealth countries, Veterans Day in the United States, and Jour de l'Armistice in France, with two minutes of silence at the time the guns stopped.

art-and-disillusionment-after-the-war.context_blurb: The industrial slaughter of 1914-1918 shattered the Victorian confidence that reason and technology would steadily improve the world, and the artists who emerged after the war set out to break the inherited rules on purpose. In Zurich and Paris a movement calling itself Dada mocked the whole idea of fine art — the French artist Marcel Duchamp famously signed an ordinary store-bought object and submitted it to a 1917 New York exhibition as sculpture, turning the question of what counted as art into a joke on the judges. The Surrealists who followed, led by the French writer Andre Breton and the Spanish painter Salvador Dali, mined dreams and the unconscious for images that felt both tender and nightmarish; Dali's famous droopy clocks hanging in a bare desert landscape became the most recognizable surrealist painting of all time. Writers followed the same drift: Ernest Hemingway's bone-dry sentences, T.S. Eliot's broken poem 'The Waste Land,' and the German Erich Maria Remarque's novel 'All Quiet on the Western Front' all spoke for a generation that no longer trusted the big words — glory, honor, duty — the recruiting posters had used in 1914. In Weimar Germany, painters like Otto Dix and George Grosz turned out savage caricatures of the postwar order; in New York, the Harlem Renaissance was busy inventing a confident American art of its own on the far side of the same cultural rupture.

articles-of-confederation-their-failures.context_blurb: After the American colonies declared independence in 1776, the Continental Congress needed a formal governing framework for the new union of states while the war was still being fought. The Articles of Confederation, drafted in 1777 and finally ratified by all thirteen states in 1781, provided one. They created a weak central government — essentially a wartime committee — with no power to tax, no power to regulate commerce between the states, no national court system, and no executive branch. The states retained almost all meaningful political power. Once the war ended in 1783, the limitations became obvious. Congress could not pay its soldiers, could not pay interest on the war debt, could not stop interstate trade wars between states slapping tariffs on each other's goods, and could not respond effectively when a small farmer rebellion broke out in western Massachusetts in 1786. By 1787 enough leaders of the generation were convinced that something stronger was needed. A convention met in Philadelphia originally to amend the Articles, concluded within weeks that amendment would not be enough, and quietly set about writing a replacement document that became the United States Constitution. The Articles are usually described as a failure, but they held the country together through the end of the war and through peace negotiations with Britain, which is not nothing.

aryan-migrations-the-vedas.context_blurb: Starting around 1500 BC, groups of Indo-European-speaking pastoralists moved from the Central Asian steppes south through the mountain passes into the northwestern plains of the Indian subcontinent, in what historians and archaeologists usually call the Aryan migrations (though the word Aryan has had an ugly later political history and is used only in its original Sanskrit sense here). These migrants mixed with earlier Indian populations, including the inheritors of the Indus Valley civilization that had already declined, and over several centuries developed the Sanskrit language and the religious hymns called the Vedas. The oldest of these hymn collections, the Rigveda, is composed of over a thousand poems to various gods and natural forces and is one of the oldest religious texts in human history still in continuous use. The Vedic hymns were preserved orally for centuries with astonishing precision through a system of memorization that trained reciters in multiple interlocking patterns of each verse, before they were ever written down. From the Vedic hymns grew the complex Hindu religious tradition, with its rituals, philosophy, caste structure, and later texts like the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita. Modern India's ancient religious literature begins here.

assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinan.context_blurb: On a June morning in 1914, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and his wife Sophie as they rode in an open car through Sarajevo. Princip belonged to a small group of young South-Slav nationalists armed and trained by secret backers inside Serbia, who wanted to break Bosnia away from Habsburg rule and bind it to a greater South-Slav state. The morning went badly for the assassins at first — an earlier attack miscarried, several conspirators lost their nerve, and the Archduke's convoy was supposed to leave the city after the near miss. In the confusion the royal car ended up on the wrong street and had stopped a few steps from Princip, who stepped forward and fired twice at point-blank range. The Habsburg government in Vienna, backed by its German ally, used the murder to deliver an ultimatum to Serbia so harsh that no sovereign state could have accepted it in full, and the whole alliance system of Europe tumbled into war within six weeks. Princip himself was too young to be executed under Austro-Hungarian law and died in prison of tuberculosis in 1918, before the Habsburg state he had struck at even outlived him.

athens-vs-sparta-two-rival-city-states-t.context_blurb: In the classical Greek world of the 5th century BC, the two most powerful city-states were Athens and Sparta, and they lived in a long tense rivalry that eventually broke into open war. Each city-state, or polis, was independent, had its own citizen army, its own laws, and its own peculiar way of life. Athens was coastal, built around a famous harbor, dependent on a seaborne trading empire, run as a direct democracy of its adult male citizens, and the center of Greek philosophy, drama, and art. Sparta was inland, run by a dual kingship and a council of elders, and organized its whole society around producing superb heavy infantry. Spartan citizens spent their lives training for war, supported by a huge underclass of state-owned agricultural laborers called helots, whose brutal treatment Sparta institutionalized. The two cities co-led the Greek defense against the Persian invasions early in the century, then fell out, and in 431 BC they led two rival alliances into a devastating war that lasted a generation and ended with the fall of Athens' empire. The ancient quarrel between the two cities became the archetype of a political rivalry between a democracy and a militarized authoritarian state.

augustus-and-the-founding-of-the-empire.context_blurb: Augustus was the great-nephew and adopted heir of Julius Caesar, and he is the man who turned the dying Roman Republic into the Roman Empire that would run the Mediterranean for the next five centuries. He was born Gaius Octavius in 63 BC, and he was only nineteen when Caesar was assassinated, which left him suddenly in charge of a bloody political fight for Rome. Over the next decade and a half he outmaneuvered every rival, including Mark Antony, and became the undisputed first man in Rome. Instead of making himself a king — a word Romans hated — he gradually gathered all the real powers of government under his own hands while keeping the forms of the old Republic as a polite fiction. He ruled for over forty years, reorganized the army, patronized the great poets of his age including Virgil and Horace, and died peacefully in his bed in AD 14, which almost no Roman emperor after him would manage. His long reign set the pattern for every Roman emperor who followed, and his personal name became a Roman imperial title that was still being used in some form a thousand years later.

auschwitz-and-the-death-camps.context_blurb: Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest of the Nazi death camps, a huge complex of three main camps and dozens of subcamps located in occupied Poland near the Polish town of Oswiecim. Over the course of its operation from 1940 to January 1945, roughly 1.1 million people were killed there, the overwhelming majority of them European Jews deported by train from across Nazi-occupied Europe but also including Polish political prisoners, Soviet prisoners of war, Roma and Sinti, and others. The camp combined a concentration-camp complex, where prisoners were worked to death in forced labor for German industrial contractors, with a dedicated extermination facility where arriving transports were sorted on the railway platform and the great majority of the arrivals were sent directly to gas chambers disguised as shower rooms. The dead were burned in large crematoria. Several other dedicated extermination camps existed in occupied Poland alongside Auschwitz, including Treblinka, Belzec, Sobibor, Chelmno, and Majdanek, each with its own grim scale and specialty. Auschwitz was liberated by the advancing Soviet army on January 27, 1945, which is now the international Holocaust Remembrance Day. The site remains preserved as a memorial and museum visited by over two million people a year.

avicenna-ibn-sina-and-islamic-medicine.context_blurb: Ibn Sina — called Avicenna in Latin — was a Persian polymath born around 980 who may have been the single most important doctor of the Middle Ages. He wrote an enormous medical textbook that systematized Greek medicine with Islamic additions and remained the standard reference in European universities for roughly five hundred years, long after his death. He was also a serious philosopher who, as a teenager, is said to have read Aristotle's hardest book — the Metaphysics — forty times without understanding it, before a short book he came across one day suddenly made it click. His own philosophy tried to combine Aristotle with Islam into a single system that could show, by pure reasoning, why there must be exactly one necessary being behind everything — a project that later put him at the center of the fiercest medieval argument about what reason could and couldn't say about God. His influence runs through both the Islamic and the Christian scholastic traditions, from al-Ghazali and Averroes among the Muslims to Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus among the Christians, which is a rare achievement for any thinker to pull off in his own lifetime, much less for a thousand years afterward.

aztec-mass-human-sacrifice-templo-mayor-.context_blurb: In the year 1487, the Aztec Great Speaker Ahuitzotl held the great dedication ceremony for the enlarged Templo Mayor at the center of the capital city of Tenochtitlan — the twin-shrined pyramid that stood at the ritual heart of the Aztec state. According to the chroniclers who recorded the ceremony afterward, including both Aztec sources and the Spanish friars who collected their testimony, the dedication involved the systematic sacrifice of thousands of captives over four days of ceremonies. Lines of victims were led up the steps of the pyramid, held across a stone altar, and killed in the traditional Aztec rite, with their blood poured onto the shrines and their bodies rolled back down the steps. Modern archaeology, including the recent excavation of walls of stacked skulls at the foot of the Templo Mayor, has confirmed that the practice of mass sacrifice was real and on the scale that early Spanish observers reported, which some modern historians had treated as conquistador propaganda until the physical evidence turned up. The event is one of the clearest examples in the historical record of a sophisticated urban civilization institutionalizing mass human killing as a religious system, and it was one of the practices the Spanish and their Indigenous allies suppressed when the empire fell.

aztec-religion-and-human-sacrifice.context_blurb: The Aztec religion, as practiced in the capital city of Tenochtitlan on the lake in the Valley of Mexico in the 14th through early 16th centuries, included one of the most intensive systematic programs of human sacrifice known in any ancient civilization. The Aztecs believed their chief gods, especially the sun god and the war god, needed a steady flow of human blood and human hearts to keep the universe running. Sacrifices were performed on top of the great twin temple at the center of the capital, usually by priests who tore out the hearts of living victims laid on a stone slab, after which the bodies were rolled down the pyramid's steep steps. Most victims were prisoners of war, captured in a form of ritualized warfare the Aztecs called the Flower Wars, which was explicitly designed to produce captives for the altar. A particular temple dedication in the late 1400s is said to have involved the sacrifice of thousands of people over several days. The practice horrified the Spanish conquerors when they first saw it in 1519, and modern archaeology, including the discovery of walls of skulls near the temple foundations, has confirmed that the surviving written descriptions were not simply conquistador propaganda.

babylon-and-the-hanging-gardens.context_blurb: The ancient city of Babylon, on the Euphrates River in what is now Iraq, was the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire that briefly dominated the ancient Near East in the sixth century BC. Its most famous king, Nebuchadnezzar II, rebuilt the city into one of the most impressive urban centers of its age, with huge mud-brick walls, a magnificent gate dedicated to the goddess Ishtar covered in blue-glazed brick with reliefs of real and mythical animals, and the sacred ziggurat called Etemenanki that may have been the inspiration for the biblical Tower of Babel. The Hanging Gardens, famously included among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World by later Greek writers, were a legendary terraced garden supposedly built by Nebuchadnezzar for a homesick foreign queen who missed the green mountains of her homeland. No archaeological trace of the Hanging Gardens has ever been found at Babylon itself, and some modern scholars think the ancient writers may have confused Babylon with the Assyrian capital of Nineveh, which really did have elaborate terraced royal gardens. Nebuchadnezzar also captured Jerusalem in 587 BC and deported much of its population to Babylon, beginning the period called in Hebrew tradition the Babylonian Exile. The Persian king Cyrus the Great captured Babylon in 539 BC.

bach-baroque-counterpoint.context_blurb: Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750) was a German composer and organist who worked almost his entire career for Lutheran churches and princely courts in central Germany, spending his final decades at a St. Thomas's school and church in Leipzig. He was treated in his own lifetime as a highly respected but somewhat old-fashioned musician, since by his middle age the European music world was moving toward lighter, simpler styles. The music he actually produced during that long career has since come to be regarded as one of the greatest bodies of composition in Western history. He wrote prolifically — organ works, keyboard works, chamber works, orchestral works, concertos, hundreds of church cantatas, two long settings of the Passion story, a huge Mass setting, and the Goldberg Variations for keyboard. His writing is famous for its intricate interweaving of multiple independent melodic voices moving simultaneously (counterpoint) in a way nobody else has quite matched. His music was largely forgotten after his death and was dramatically rediscovered in the 19th century, especially by Felix Mendelssohn, whose 1829 Berlin revival of the St. Matthew Passion launched a Bach renaissance that has never slowed down. He is now at the heart of the classical music canon.

bartolom-de-las-casas.context_blurb: Bartolome de las Casas was a 16th-century Spanish priest who began his career in the New World as an ordinary colonist, holding Indian laborers under the Spanish grant system that treated them almost as property. One Pentecost, reading a passage of scripture about masters who exploit the poor, he underwent a sharp conversion of conscience that would reshape the rest of his life. He spent the next fifty years inside the Spanish Empire writing furious books that documented atrocities village by village, lobbying kings and cardinals in person, and defending the New World peoples before Church and Crown. He also made serious mistakes along the way, including an early proposal that would have shifted the burden onto imported African slaves instead; he later renounced that proposal and spent much of the rest of his life bitterly regretting it. The arguments he hammered out in his books are now considered some of the earliest full-throated statements in European thought that no people and no race stands below any other in the eyes of God or natural law, and the mature position he reached late in life, defended at the Valladolid debate against Juan Gines de Sepulveda, is a founding document of modern human rights thinking.

bartolomeu-dias-rounds-cape-of-good-hope.context_blurb: Bartolomeu Dias was a Portuguese captain who, in 1488, became the first European known to sail around the southern tip of Africa. Portugal had been inching down the African coast for decades, hoping to find a sea route to India that would bypass the Muslim merchants controlling the overland spice routes, and Dias finally proved there was one. He was blown out of sight of land for days by weather he had never trained for, and only realized he had rounded the continent when he turned north again and saw the coast running away to the east. Dias gave the headland one name on the way home; King John II of Portugal, thinking of what the discovery meant for the royal treasury rather than how it had felt from the quarterdeck, promptly chose a sunnier name for charts and merchants, and the sunnier name is the one that stuck. Dias had hoped to press on and reach India himself, but a decade would pass before a different Portuguese captain, Vasco da Gama, actually used his route to complete the journey. Dias himself, years later, sailed again as a captain in a Portuguese expedition bound for India and was lost at sea near the very headland he had first charted.

bastiat-and-the-seen-versus-unseen-the-b.context_blurb: Frédéric Bastiat was a French economist, journalist, and member of the National Assembly who died of tuberculosis in 1850, at just forty-nine years old. In the last two years of his life he poured out a series of short, witty pamphlets attacking what he saw as the great confusions of the economic debates of his day — tariffs, make-work schemes, state subsidies, and the loose idea that destruction or waste could somehow make a country richer. His style is unusual for an economist: he writes in dialogues, parables, and satires that a child can follow. One of his pamphlets imagines candlemakers petitioning the government for protection against a ruthless rival — their complaint, taken seriously, forces you to see that the same logic behind many real tariffs is nonsense. Another is the little essay at the center of this story, which asks what truly happens, economically, when something gets broken and must be replaced. His key move is to ask you to compare what you can see — the busy repair, the glazier paid, the new window — against what you cannot see, the invisible second life the owner's money could have had elsewhere. It matters because 'the seen and the unseen' has become one of the most useful habits of thought in economics; once you have it, you spot the same confusion everywhere, in debates about war spending, disaster relief, subsidies, and jobs programs.

bataan-death-march.context_blurb: In April 1942, after months of defensive fighting on the Bataan Peninsula on the Philippine island of Luzon, roughly 76,000 Filipino and American soldiers surrendered to the Imperial Japanese Army following the Japanese invasion of the Philippines. The Japanese commanders then marched these prisoners of war about 65 miles north under brutal conditions to railheads from which they would be shipped to prison camps. The forced march became one of the worst war-crime atrocities of the Pacific War. The Japanese guards systematically beat, bayoneted, or shot prisoners who fell behind, denied water and food to the exhausted men, and killed on the spot anyone who tried to help a fellow prisoner. Somewhere between seven thousand and ten thousand Filipino and American prisoners died on the march itself. Many thousands more died in the Japanese prison camps that followed. News of the Bataan Death March eventually reached the United States through escaped and liberated American prisoners later in the war and became one of the central American grievances against Imperial Japan. After the war, the Japanese commander most directly responsible for the march, General Masaharu Homma, was tried by an American military tribunal in Manila, convicted of war crimes, and executed by firing squad in 1946.

battle-of-britain.context_blurb: After the fall of France in June 1940, Britain stood essentially alone against Nazi Germany in Western Europe. The German plan for the invasion of Britain required first establishing air superiority over the English Channel and southern England, and from July into October 1940 the German Luftwaffe tried to destroy the Royal Air Force in a sustained air campaign that became known as the Battle of Britain. The outnumbered Royal Air Force, flying Spitfires and Hurricanes, with the help of radar, excellent air-defense coordination, Polish and Czech volunteer pilots, and critical cryptographic intelligence, inflicted heavy losses on the attacking German bombers and fighters. The Germans switched tactics in September 1940 to night-bombing of British cities, especially London, in a campaign that became known as the Blitz. The British population held together despite the pounding. By May 1941 the German air offensive against Britain had ceased, with the German Luftwaffe shifting east for the invasion of the Soviet Union the following month. Winston Churchill, in a famous speech honoring the pilots, said that never had so much been owed by so many to so few. The battle was the first major military setback of the war for Nazi Germany.

battle-of-gaugamela-331-bc-alexander-bea.context_blurb: In 331 BC on a wide dusty plain in what is now northern Iraq, Alexander the Great fought the climactic open-field battle of his conquest of the Persian Empire against the Persian king Darius III. The Persian army was much larger, included cavalry recruited from across central Asia, scythed chariots, and even war elephants, but Alexander had a thoroughly professional and loyal Macedonian army and a knack for finding the one weak place in an enemy line and smashing through it in person at the head of his companion cavalry. The battle went that way. Alexander personally led a charge aimed at the Persian king's command position in the center of the line, and when Darius broke and ran for it, his whole army came apart. Darius escaped the field but was killed by his own officers shortly afterward. Alexander entered the Persian capitals of Babylon, Susa, and Persepolis as the new master of the Persian Empire. The battle is still studied in military academies as the model of a smaller but better-trained army defeating a larger, more diverse one by concentrating force at a decisive point.

battle-of-hastings-the-norman-conquest-1.context_blurb: In the autumn of 1066, a duke from across the English Channel landed on England's south coast with a disputed claim to the throne and set in motion the last successful foreign conquest the island has ever seen. The English king who faced him had been crowned barely a year before, and had already fought one desperate battle at the other end of his kingdom against a rival invader when news reached him that a second claimant was burning the southern coast. The two armies met on a hill outside a small Sussex town. They were roughly equal in size, but they fought in very different ways, one army dug in on the ridge above and the other coming up from below, and the battle swung back and forth all day. By nightfall England had a new king, and the French-speaking lords he brought with him spent the next generation remaking England from the top down, scattering stone castles across the countryside, replacing bishops and sheriffs, and threading French words into the English language. A famous picture-chronicle of the battle, made soon afterwards, is still one of the most familiar images in all of Europe. Nine centuries later, English words and French words are still twisted together in the mouths of English-speakers because of what happened on that single afternoon.

battle-of-iwo-jima.context_blurb: The Battle of Iwo Jima was fought in February and March 1945 for a small volcanic island in the Pacific Ocean about halfway between Japan and the American bomber bases in the Mariana Islands. The island was defended by around twenty thousand well-entrenched Japanese soldiers under General Tadamichi Kuribayashi, who had built an elaborate underground network of tunnels, bunkers, and fortified positions carved deep into the island's volcanic rock. The American assault, mostly by the United States Marine Corps, took five weeks of brutal fighting and cost around seven thousand American dead and nearly twenty thousand wounded, with most of the Japanese defenders fighting to the death. The battle produced one of the most famous photographs of the Second World War: Associated Press photographer Joe Rosenthal's image of five Marines and a Navy corpsman raising the American flag over Mount Suribachi, the volcanic peak at the island's southern tip, on February 23, 1945, several days into the battle. The image won the Pulitzer Prize and was later used as the model for the Marine Corps War Memorial outside Washington, D.C. Iwo Jima gave American bombers an emergency airfield within striking distance of Japan and was a central step toward the Japanese home islands.

battle-of-kursk.context_blurb: The Battle of Kursk, fought in July and August 1943 in a huge salient in the Soviet lines around the city of Kursk in western Russia, was the largest tank battle in human history and the last major German offensive on the Eastern Front. The Germans attempted a double envelopment of the salient from north and south using huge concentrations of their new Panther and Tiger tanks, hoping to destroy the Soviet forces inside the pocket and regain the strategic initiative they had lost after Stalingrad. The Soviets had been warned by their intelligence services of the German plan and had spent weeks preparing an enormous defense in depth, with concentric belts of minefields, antitank ditches, dug-in artillery, and reserve tank armies positioned to counterattack. The German offensive stalled within days of launching. A huge tank-on-tank engagement at the village of Prokhorovka on July 12 saw hundreds of tanks fighting each other at close range in a single afternoon. Hitler called off the offensive after a week, and the Soviets launched their own counteroffensive, which drove the Germans steadily westward for the rest of the summer. Kursk was the point at which strategic initiative on the Eastern Front passed permanently to the Red Army, and the Germans were never able to mount a major strategic offensive against the Soviets again.
