battle-of-marathon-490-bc-and-the-runner.context_blurb: In 490 BC a Persian expeditionary force sent by the Great King Darius I landed on the east coast of Attica in Greece, intending to punish Athens for helping Greek rebels along the Persian-controlled coast of Asia Minor. The Athenian army, badly outnumbered and without reliable Spartan reinforcements, met them on a coastal plain north of the city. The Athenian commander, by weighting his flanks and keeping his center light, managed to envelop and crush the much larger Persian force in a single day of fighting. The surviving Persians fled to their ships and sailed home. The battle secured a generation of Athenian independence and became one of the defining memories of Greek civilization — the story of free citizen-soldiers defending their city against an invading autocratic empire. A famous legend grew up around a runner who was said to have carried the news of victory back to Athens on foot and then died from the exertion. The modern long-distance race takes its name from the battlefield, and the distance between the battlefield and the city is the reason the modern race is roughly twenty-six miles long.

battle-of-midway.context_blurb: The Battle of Midway, fought in June 1942 in the central Pacific near the small American atoll of Midway, is one of the most consequential naval victories in modern history. Six months after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, the Imperial Japanese Navy was planning to extend its Pacific perimeter by capturing Midway and drawing the United States Pacific Fleet into a decisive battle in which the Japanese expected to finish the American carriers. American code-breakers had partially broken the Japanese naval cipher and had warned the United States Navy where and when the Japanese attack would come. The American carrier force under Admiral Chester Nimitz was waiting. Over the course of a single day, June 4, 1942, American carrier aircraft sank four Japanese fleet carriers, destroying most of the aircraft and the trained pilots that had conducted the Pearl Harbor attack. The United States lost one carrier in the same battle. The Battle of Midway broke the back of Japanese carrier power and ended Japan's offensive strategic initiative in the Pacific. From Midway onward, the strategic momentum in the Pacific War shifted gradually but permanently to the Allied side.

battle-of-new-orleans-andrew-jackson.context_blurb: The Battle of New Orleans was fought in January 1815 near the mouth of the Mississippi River between an American force under General Andrew Jackson and a veteran British army that had just arrived from the Napoleonic Wars with the intention of seizing the key port of New Orleans and controlling the lower Mississippi. Jackson had assembled a motley defending force of United States regulars, Tennessee and Kentucky frontier riflemen, local militia including both free Black men and Choctaw warriors, Louisiana French Creoles, and a band of Jean Lafitte's pirates in exchange for a general pardon of their past crimes. He positioned the whole force behind improvised earthworks across the main approach road and shredded the British attack with disciplined volley fire, inflicting enormous casualties while suffering few of his own. The famous twist of the battle was that it was fought several weeks after British and American diplomats had already signed a peace treaty at Ghent in Belgium ending the War of 1812; neither army had yet heard the news. The lopsided American victory nonetheless electrified the young country, catapulted Jackson into national politics, and became one of the founding events of the Democratic political coalition he would eventually lead to the presidency.

battle-of-okinawa.context_blurb: The Battle of Okinawa was fought from April to June 1945 for a mid-sized Japanese island about four hundred miles south of the home islands. The battle was the largest amphibious assault of the Pacific War and the last major battle before the atomic bombings. The United States committed over 180,000 ground troops, mostly Army and Marines; the Japanese defended the island with over 100,000 soldiers deeply entrenched in prepared positions. The fighting lasted eighty-two days of brutal close-quarters combat through cane fields, caves, and hills, with the Japanese fighting to the death and extensive Japanese civilian casualties. Mass civilian suicides on the island, encouraged or coerced by Japanese military propaganda about American brutality, horrified American observers. Japanese kamikaze aircraft attacked the American invasion fleet in enormous numbers off the Okinawa coast and sank or damaged many ships. Overall casualties on both sides, including Okinawan civilians, numbered in the hundreds of thousands. The battle demonstrated what a planned invasion of the Japanese home islands was likely to look like, and the projected casualty estimates for that invasion were one of the key considerations President Truman weighed when he authorized the atomic bombings in August 1945. Okinawa was the last major battle before the atomic bombings.

battle-of-plataea-479-bc-persia-driven-o.context_blurb: In the summer of 479 BC, a year after a Greek naval victory had cost the Persian king his fleet, a huge land battle was fought in central Greece between the combined armies of the Greek city-states, led by Sparta, and the Persian force that had been left behind to conquer Greece by occupation. The Greek army was commanded by a Spartan regent, and most of its heavy infantry were the famously disciplined citizen-hoplites of Sparta and its allies. After days of maneuvering, the two armies collided on a dusty plain, and the Greek heavy infantry crushed the Persian force in close combat. The Persian general was killed in the fighting. On the same day or shortly afterward, a Greek naval force operating off the coast of Asia Minor won a parallel victory that destroyed what was left of Persian naval power in the Aegean. Together, these battles ended the Persian attempt to subdue Greece, and the Greek world moved into the extraordinary flowering of culture, art, and thought that we call the classical age.

battle-of-salamis-480-bc-themistocles-na.context_blurb: In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece at the head of an army far larger than any Greek city could meet in open battle, intending to finish the work his father Darius had started a decade earlier. The Greek allied states, under the leadership of Sparta on land and Athens at sea, abandoned Athens itself to the invader and fell back on a defensive line. The Athenian commander, a shrewd and manipulative politician, convinced the Greek allies to anchor their combined fleet in the narrow straits between the mainland and a small nearby island west of Athens. The Persian fleet, lured in by a false message, crowded into the strait and lost its ability to maneuver, where the Greek triremes, lighter and better handled in close waters, could ram them one at a time. The sea-battle that followed broke the back of the Persian navy. Xerxes, who had been watching from a throne he had set up on the opposite shore to enjoy his victory, hurried back home with most of his army, leaving a smaller land force in Greece that would be defeated the following summer. The sea battle is one of the great small-against-large upset victories of ancient history.

battle-of-stalingrad.context_blurb: The Battle of Stalingrad, fought from August 1942 to February 1943 for an industrial city on the lower Volga River, was the most costly single battle of the Second World War and the clearest turning point in the land war against Nazi Germany. The German Sixth Army under General Friedrich Paulus pushed into the ruins of Stalingrad through the autumn of 1942 and fought a brutal street-by-street urban battle against stubborn Soviet defenders led by General Vasily Chuikov. Winter settled in. In November 1942 the Red Army launched Operation Uranus, a massive encirclement that struck the weaker Romanian and Hungarian forces guarding the German flanks and cut off the entire German Sixth Army inside the city. The surrounded Germans starved and froze through December and January, while a German relief offensive failed. In early February 1943 Paulus surrendered what was left of his army. The Germans lost around three hundred thousand soldiers at Stalingrad. The battle broke the forward momentum of the German army in the east and sent a political signal across occupied Europe that the Soviets would eventually win the war in the east. From Stalingrad onward the war on the Eastern Front moved steadily toward Berlin.

battle-of-the-atlantic-and-u-boats.context_blurb: The Battle of the Atlantic was the longest continuous military campaign of the Second World War, running from the first day of the war in September 1939 to the German surrender in May 1945. It was a seaborne struggle for control of the shipping lanes across the Atlantic Ocean, between German surface raiders and submarines on one side and Allied convoys of merchant ships escorted by warships and aircraft on the other. For most of the first three years of the war, the Germans had the upper hand. German submarines, called U-boats, operating from captured French ports, sank Allied shipping faster than Allied yards could build replacements, and Britain was within sight of being starved into submission. The tide turned in 1943 through a combination of factors — better Allied escort tactics, long-range aircraft that could cover the mid-Atlantic gap, escort carriers, improved radar and sonar, cryptographic breaks of the German naval cipher, and the enormous scale of American shipyard construction. German submarine losses became catastrophic in the second half of 1943. By 1944, Allied control of the Atlantic was secure, and the sealift that supplied the European theater became reliable. Winston Churchill later wrote that the only thing that ever really frightened him during the war was the U-boat threat.

battle-of-the-bulge.context_blurb: In December 1944, in the last major German offensive of the Second World War in the west, Adolf Hitler ordered a surprise armored attack through the forested Ardennes region of Belgium, hoping to split the Allied armies, retake the port of Antwerp, and force a negotiated peace. The attack caught the thinly held Allied line by surprise and drove a large bulge into the American lines, from which the battle takes its popular name. For about six weeks, in brutal winter weather, American units including a surrounded force at the Belgian town of Bastogne held key road junctions against overwhelming odds. The surrounded American commander at Bastogne gave a famously laconic one-word reply when the Germans demanded his surrender. Allied air power finally returned when the weather cleared, Allied armored reinforcements under George Patton swung north to relieve Bastogne, and by late January 1945 the German attack had been beaten back. The battle cost the United States around nineteen thousand killed and many more wounded, the largest American battle of the entire war. For the Germans the offensive consumed irreplaceable armor and infantry reserves that could not be rebuilt, and after it the Western Front collapsed. By early May 1945, Nazi Germany had surrendered.

battle-of-the-coral-sea.context_blurb: The Battle of the Coral Sea, fought in early May 1942 in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Guinea, was the first major engagement of the Pacific War in which the opposing American and Japanese surface fleets never came within sight of each other. All of the fighting was done by carrier-based aircraft striking at each other's ships. The Japanese had been planning an amphibious invasion of Port Moresby on the southern coast of New Guinea, aimed at threatening Australia and cutting the supply lines from the United States. American code-breakers had intercepted enough Japanese signals to anticipate the move, and American and Australian naval forces intercepted the Japanese covering carrier force before the invasion could land. In the resulting four-day engagement the Americans lost one fleet carrier (the Lexington) and had another badly damaged, while the Japanese lost a light carrier and had one of their main fleet carriers damaged. Tactically the two sides had come out roughly even. Strategically it was a Japanese defeat: they turned back the Port Moresby operation. More importantly, the two Japanese fleet carriers damaged or exhausted at Coral Sea were not available a month later at Midway, which contributed significantly to the Japanese disaster there.

battle-of-the-somme.context_blurb: The Battle of the Somme, fought along a chalky stretch of northern France from July to November 1916, was the bloodiest campaign in British military history. The British commander Sir Douglas Haig and the French general Ferdinand Foch planned the joint offensive to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun. The attack opened on July 1 after a week-long artillery bombardment and an advance by huge formations of volunteers raised in 1914 and 1915 by Lord Kitchener; on that first day roughly 20,000 British soldiers were killed and another 40,000 wounded, and whole small towns in the north of England got their telegrams in bunches that broke them for a generation. The attack had been prepared with vast tunneled mines dug for weeks under the German lines by British engineers and set off beneath the enemy trenches at the moment of attack. Months of grinding fighting followed through the summer and into the autumn mud, and when the battle finally petered out the Allies had moved the front only a few miles for roughly a million total casualties on both sides. The Somme is also where the first tanks ever used in combat trundled out in September 1916, a weapon so secret that even its name was a cover story about water-cistern production.

battle-of-tours-charles-martel-732.context_blurb: In the early 8th century, armies of the new Islamic empire had swept across North Africa, crossed into Spain, broken the Visigothic kingdom there within a few years, and begun pushing north over the Pyrenees into the land of the Franks. The Frankish ruler who met them in open battle was not a king but a mayor of the royal palace, the real power behind a line of fading do-nothing Merovingian kings, and he was the grandfather of the most famous emperor the medieval West would ever produce. The clash itself was not large by modern standards, and it took place far from the heartland of either civilization, on a wooded ridge in central Gaul between two towns whose names historians still argue over. But it broke the furthest push of a cavalry empire that had conquered more territory in a single century than Rome had taken in five, and later Christians remembered the Frankish commander as the shield who kept the rest of Europe from going the way of Spain. Modern historians argue over how decisive the fight actually was, pointing out that Muslim raids kept coming for decades afterward. But the memory of the moment the tide seemed to turn, in that one stand on that one ridge, shaped how western Europe told its own story for the next thousand years.

battle-of-verdun.context_blurb: The Battle of Verdun, fought from February to December 1916 along the Meuse river in eastern France, was the longest battle of the war and the symbolic heart of the French war effort. The German chief of staff Erich von Falkenhayn chose Verdun because the ring of old forts there carried enormous meaning for France, and he believed the French would defend them at any cost — which was exactly what he wanted. General Philippe Petain, placed in command of the defense, held the line by rotating fresh units through the salient on a single narrow country road the French called the Sacred Way, which was kept running day and night so that men, shells, and food never stopped reaching the front. Two of the great forts, Douaumont and Vaux, changed hands in dramas that would become legend: Douaumont fell early under circumstances almost farcical, and at Vaux the garrison commander Major Sylvain-Eugene Raynal held out for days under siege and smoke before the last of his men were finally taken. Nearly 700,000 French and German soldiers were killed, wounded, or missing in the fighting, and large stretches of the battlefield remain so poisoned with iron and unexploded shells today that French villages inside the zone are still officially 'destroyed' and unlived in.

beethoven-the-deaf-composer-and-the-nint.context_blurb: Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827) was a German composer who moved as a young man to Vienna and became one of the most consequential figures in the history of Western music. He stood at the hinge between the Classical period of Haydn and Mozart and the full Romantic era that followed, and his personal creative drive, his willingness to expand almost every musical form he worked in, and his sense of the composer as a prophetic figure rather than a hired craftsman defined the next century of European music. He wrote nine symphonies, over thirty piano sonatas, sixteen string quartets, concertos, an opera, chamber music, and a huge Missa Solemnis. Beginning in his late twenties he began losing his hearing, slowly at first and then more profoundly, and he was functionally deaf for the last ten years of his life. He kept composing anyway, writing some of his most radical and personal music during his years of deafness, including his final symphony and his late quartets, which pointed decades into the musical future. He died in Vienna of chronic illness and was buried in a funeral that drew tens of thousands of mourners. His influence on everyone who wrote serious music after him was enormous.

bell-edison-and-the-late-century-inventi.context_blurb: In the last quarter of the nineteenth century a small group of inventors and companies, mostly in the United States, turned the laboratory into a factory for new technologies. Two names tower over the period. Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born teacher of the deaf who, working in Boston, patented a device for sending the human voice down a wire; the first words he transmitted to his assistant were a famously ordinary summons from the next room. Thomas Edison, a largely self-taught Midwesterner, built the first great industrial research lab in New Jersey and used it to pour out patents at a rate no one had ever matched — in sound recording, in motion pictures, in electrical distribution, and above all in the long search for a practical electric light. The questions ahead track both men and the generation around them. It also wades into the ugly feud of the 1880s and 1890s known as the War of the Currents, in which Edison fought George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla over which kind of electrical current should power the country, and in which Edison's team ran a cruel public campaign of staged electrocutions to make his rival's system look deadly. The hardest questions ask you to sort through what Edison himself did and did not do in those episodes. It matters because this is the moment the modern networked world — electric light, recorded sound, long-distance voice, mass electrical power — actually gets built.

benedict-arnold-s-treason.context_blurb: Benedict Arnold was a brilliant American general of the Revolutionary War whose battlefield heroism earned him enormous reputation in the early years of the war, and whose later betrayal of the American cause made his name a permanent English-language synonym for treachery. He fought with distinction in the invasion of Canada, led the daring attack at Fort Ticonderoga, and performed brilliantly at the Battle of Saratoga, where he was severely wounded in the leg leading a charge that helped turn the battle. His personal grievances afterwards — slow promotion, financial troubles, perceived snubs by Congress — festered. By 1780, while commanding the American fort at West Point on the Hudson River, Arnold was secretly in correspondence with British officers and had agreed to turn West Point over to them in exchange for money and a British officer's commission. The plot was uncovered when the British courier, Major John Andre, was intercepted on his way back carrying incriminating documents. Arnold escaped to the British lines; Andre was hanged as a spy. Arnold spent the rest of his life as a British officer and finally died in London in 1801, never fully trusted on either side. His name has been shorthand for a traitor in American English for well over two hundred years.

benedictine-monasticism-monastery-life.context_blurb: In the 6th century, an Italian hermit named Benedict wrote a short, humane rulebook for men who wanted to live together as a community of prayer, and his quiet little recipe went on to shape European life for a thousand years. Benedict's rule divided each day into fixed hours of worship, hours of physical labor in the fields and workshops, and hours of quiet reading. It demanded a vow of restraint in speech, measured portions of food and drink, obedience to the abbot, and hospitality to any stranger who knocked at the gate. Thousands of houses grew up on this plan all across Europe. In those houses, monks copied out the Bible and the ancient classics by hand, kept schools and infirmaries, drained swamps and planted vineyards, invented or improved famous liqueurs and cheeses, took in travelers at every hour, and buried the dead. The monk-scribes often added private little notes in the margins of their books, grumbling about the cold, their eyesight, or their aching backs, and sometimes drawing cats and dragons. The quiet discipline of this life was supposed to make interior room for God, and even modern Europeans who have never been inside a monastery still inherit far more from these communities than they tend to notice.

benjamin-franklin-inventor-diplomat-foun.context_blurb: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the youngest son in a Puritan candlemaker's large family, apprenticed to his older brother's print shop as a boy, and ran away as a teenager to make his own fortune in Philadelphia. He succeeded spectacularly. By middle age he was one of the richest men in the colonies, a famous publisher, a serious experimental scientist whose work on electricity made him famous across Europe, an inventor of useful objects, and the founder of some of the first American civic institutions. In the Revolution he was already an elderly man and became one of its elder statesmen, signing the Declaration of Independence, serving as the American minister to France (where his quiet charm helped bring France into the war on the American side), negotiating the peace treaty with Britain, and finally returning home to sign the Constitution. He is the only person to have signed all four of the founding documents of American independence. In his last years he turned openly against slavery, which he had once tolerated. Franklin is probably the most beloved of the founders because he never stopped being funny about himself and because his life embodied the possibility of self-made success that the new republic was supposed to make available to others.

benjamin-franklin-science-and-the-enligh.context_blurb: Benjamin Franklin was an American printer, writer, inventor, scientist, diplomat, and founding father, born in Boston in 1706 and famous almost everywhere by middle age. He ran away from his older brother's print shop as a teenager and arrived penniless in Philadelphia, where he eventually became one of the richest men in the colonies by writing, publishing, and selling almanacs full of wit and advice. Franklin was the rarest of combinations: a serious experimental scientist whose work on electricity made him famous across Europe, and a shrewd practical man who kept inventing useful objects to solve ordinary problems. In Paris during the American Revolution he was treated like a rock star by French society, fur hat and all, and his quiet charm helped win France over to the American cause. He signed the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution, which no one else can claim. In his last years he turned openly against slavery, which he had once tolerated. Franklin's writings, his inventions, his jokes, and his signature are everywhere in American life, and he is probably the most beloved founder because he never stopped being funny about himself.

berlin-blockade-airlift.context_blurb: After the Second World War, defeated Germany was divided among the four victorious Allied powers — the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union — and the capital city of Berlin, which lay deep inside the Soviet occupation zone of eastern Germany, was itself divided into four occupation sectors. By 1948, relations between the Soviets and the three Western Allies had deteriorated rapidly. When the Western Allies introduced a new currency into their occupation zones and into their sectors of Berlin, the Soviet Union responded by closing all the land and water routes into the Western sectors of Berlin, trying to force the Western Allies to abandon the city. Over two million Berliners inside the Western sectors were suddenly cut off from food and fuel. The Western Allies responded with one of the most impressive logistical operations in history: an air bridge that flew enormous volumes of food, coal, medicine, and essential supplies into Berlin's airports continuously, day and night, for nearly a year, in weather good and bad, with flights landing in some periods every ninety seconds. The Soviet Union finally lifted the blockade in May 1949 without having achieved anything. The Airlift became one of the great early victories of the Western Allies in what was becoming the Cold War.

berlin-wall-tear-down-this-wall.context_blurb: On the night of August 12 to 13, 1961, East German soldiers under Soviet direction began laying barbed wire across the border between East and West Berlin, interrupting one of the main escape routes for East Germans fleeing to the West. The barrier was quickly turned into a long concrete wall, with watchtowers, barbed-wire aprons, a cleared death strip, trained guard dogs, and shoot-to-kill orders for any East German trying to climb across. For the next twenty-eight years, the Berlin Wall became the most visible symbol of the Cold War division of Europe — hundreds of East Germans were killed trying to cross it. In June 1987, standing in front of the Brandenburg Gate on the Western side of the wall, American President Ronald Reagan addressed the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev directly in a famous public speech, challenging him to tear it down if he was serious about reform. The speech was mocked at the time by many Western commentators as empty theater. Two years later, with East Germany collapsing under popular pressure, East German authorities announced on November 9, 1989, that East Germans could cross freely to the West, and jubilant Berliners from both sides climbed the wall and began hacking it down with hammers that very night.

bernini-baroque-sculpture.context_blurb: Gian Lorenzo Bernini (1598 to 1680) was an Italian sculptor, architect, painter, and playwright who dominated Baroque Rome for most of the seventeenth century. He trained under his sculptor father, began receiving major commissions as a teenager, and by his twenties was already working for popes and cardinals on sculptures that pushed the technical and emotional possibilities of marble to levels nobody had quite reached before. He could make marble look like soft flesh being gripped by hard fingers, like damp hair, like clinging fabric, or like a woman gasping in religious ecstasy. He designed the enormous twisted bronze canopy under the great dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, planned the vast curving colonnade in St. Peter's Square, and left a sequence of theatrical religious sculptures in various Roman churches that are still bus-stop pilgrimage destinations for art lovers. Bernini was also a working architect, a serious playwright and theater producer, and the personal confidant of several popes. Modern tourists walking across Rome today can hardly cross a major piazza without seeing a Bernini sculpture, a Bernini fountain, or a Bernini-designed facade, which is a signature of how dominant his style became during the Catholic Reformation reshaping of Rome.

bessemer-process-and-the-age-of-steel.context_blurb: Henry Bessemer was an English inventor who, in the 1850s, worked out a way to make strong steel in huge quantities, quickly and cheaply, by blowing cold air through a pear-shaped vessel full of molten pig iron. Before his process, steel had been a specialty metal — expensive, hard to make in large pieces, and reserved for things like sword blades and fine tools; most 'iron' structures were made of brittle cast iron or softer wrought iron. Bessemer himself was not primarily a metallurgist; he had made his earlier money off dozens of patents in things as varied as gold-colored paint, embossed stamps, and sugarcane crushers, and he turned to steelmaking after watching cannon barrels of his own design burst under test fire. The breakthrough that puzzled visitors to his new works was that cold air coming into the molten iron did not cool the metal down. Instead the furnace glowed white-hot and threw a tower of sparks, as something inside the molten mix fed the fire. The questions ahead ask what the hidden fuel was, and roughly how much cheaper the new method made steel compared with the older refining methods. It matters because the price collapse that followed turned steel from a luxury into the structural metal of the modern age — the rails, the bridges, the ocean liners, the first skyscrapers, and the frames of warships are all children of Bessemer's blast.

betsy-ross-the-first-flag-legend.context_blurb: Betsy Ross was a Philadelphia upholsterer and flag-maker who, according to a family story published nearly a century after the fact by her grandson, was personally visited in 1776 by a committee of the Continental Congress — including George Washington himself — and asked to sew the first flag of the new United States of America. The flag, according to the story, had thirteen red and white stripes and a circle of thirteen five-pointed stars on a blue field. The problem with the story is that no contemporary document records such a commission, no entry appears in Washington's own detailed records, and the first flag law passed by Congress in 1777 doesn't mention Ross. Modern historians are generally skeptical that the specific family story is literally true. Betsy Ross was however a real person, really did work as a flag-maker in Philadelphia during the Revolutionary period, really did sew naval flags for the Pennsylvania state navy, and lived long enough to see her new country survive its early wars. Her shop in Philadelphia is now a historic site visited by millions. The story remains a lovely American founding legend — probably more legend than fact, like the cherry tree, but useful as a reminder of the women whose work supported the Revolution.

bill-of-rights-first-ten-amendments.context_blurb: The Bill of Rights is the collective name for the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution, ratified in December 1791 — just three and a half years after the Constitution itself had taken effect. During the ratification debates of 1787 and 1788, Anti-Federalist opponents of the proposed Constitution had argued loudly that it created a federal government powerful enough to threaten individual liberty, and they demanded explicit written guarantees of specific rights. Federalist supporters, including James Madison, initially argued that no such bill was needed because the federal government had only the limited powers listed in the Constitution. Several states ratified the Constitution only on the condition that a bill of rights would be added as the first order of business of the new Congress. Madison, now a member of the House of Representatives, kept the bargain. He wrote a draft, Congress edited it, and ten of the amendments were ratified by the states. They guarantee specific freedoms (speech, press, assembly, religion), specific protections against government overreach (unreasonable searches, forced self-incrimination, cruel punishments, excessive bail), and the reservation of all remaining power to the states and the people. They are the most-cited part of the Constitution in American law and ordinary political argument today.

birth-of-athenian-democracy-cleisthenes-.context_blurb: The direct democracy of classical Athens was not the oldest in the world — Mesopotamian cities had assemblies, and various Greek cities had experimented with wide citizen participation — but it was the most radical in its own time. It grew in stages. An early 6th-century BC Athenian reformer named Solon cancelled debts, outlawed debt-slavery, and reorganized citizens into property classes. A century later, a reformer named Cleisthenes restructured Athenian political identity around new civic groupings rather than the old tribes, and set up an assembly, a rotating council chosen by lot, and a famous procedure for exiling any citizen who was becoming too powerful. By the time of Pericles in the mid-5th century, every adult male Athenian citizen was expected to vote, serve on juries, hold office at some point by lottery, and speak in the assembly if he wished. Women, foreigners, and the city's many slaves were not citizens and had no political voice. Modern democracy owes less to Athens than high-school textbooks sometimes suggest, but the basic experiment — ordinary citizens, by direct vote, running the affairs of their own city — was first tried seriously in Athens, and the questions it raised are still being asked today.

birth-of-jazz-louis-armstrong-and-new-or.context_blurb: Jazz emerged in the early 20th century in the port city of New Orleans, Louisiana, out of a long braided tradition that included African American blues and spirituals, Caribbean rhythms, European marching-band music, ragtime piano, and the dance music of New Orleans's many ethnic neighborhoods. The city's Afro-Creole musical culture was unusually rich, and when the sanctioned entertainment district of Storyville flourished from 1897 to 1917, dozens of small ensembles played for dancers, drinkers, and churchgoers across the city. The young trumpeter Louis Armstrong (born in New Orleans around 1901) grew up in this musical environment, learned on the city's streets, moved up the Mississippi to Chicago in the early 1920s with his mentor King Oliver, and then over the following two decades transformed jazz from a group ensemble tradition into an improvising soloists' art form. Armstrong's recordings from the late 1920s with his small combos are still studied as the moment when the solo improvised instrumental line, swinging rhythm, and virtuoso trumpet playing came into their own. Jazz spread from New Orleans and Chicago to New York and from there around the world, becoming the first native American musical tradition to conquer the global ear. Armstrong remained its most beloved ambassador until his death in 1971.

boltzmann-entropy-and-the-equation-on-th.context_blurb: Ludwig Boltzmann was a nineteenth-century Austrian physicist who insisted, against powerful opposition, that heat and the behaviour of gases could be explained by imagining them as swarms of tiny invisible atoms bouncing around at random. Many of his most respected colleagues — philosophers of science as well as fellow physicists — thought this was nonsense; atoms had never been seen, and treating physics as a problem in counting made some of his critics dismiss his work as metaphysics dressed up in equations. Boltzmann fought this battle for most of his career in Vienna, Graz, and Munich. He showed that the one-way march of time in the physical world — hot things cooling, ordered things spoiling, the universe sliding toward uniform greyness — could be understood as a simple matter of counting hidden arrangements. He summed that insight up in a single short formula that he wanted carved on his gravestone, and after his death by his own hand in 1906 his friends made sure it was. Within a few years, new work by others finally settled the long battle over whether atoms were real, and his statistical picture of heat became the backbone of modern thermodynamics and the foundation of quantum theory. The vindication came too late for Boltzmann himself, but his equation now stands over his tomb in Vienna's Central Cemetery.

borobudur-srivijaya-maritime-se-asia.context_blurb: In the 8th and 9th centuries AD on the island of Java in what is now Indonesia, a Buddhist dynasty built one of the most spectacular religious monuments in the world: the great stepped stone complex of Borobudur, a massive temple-mountain of nine stacked platforms carved with relief panels telling Buddhist stories, culminating in a central stupa surrounded by smaller stupas and gazing out over the surrounding countryside. Borobudur was built not far from the parallel Hindu temple complex at Prambanan, which rose in the same century. Both were products of a cosmopolitan maritime Southeast Asian world knit together by the Buddhist and Hindu kingdom of Srivijaya, centered on Sumatra, which from the 7th to the 13th centuries controlled the trade through the Strait of Malacca linking the Indian and Chinese worlds. Buddhist pilgrims from China and India stopped at Srivijaya's capital on their way to each other's holy sites. Borobudur was quietly abandoned, probably in the 14th century for a mix of volcanic, political, and religious reasons, and sat forgotten and overgrown in the jungle until British and Dutch antiquarians uncovered it in the 1800s. It is now one of the most visited religious monuments in Southeast Asia and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

boston-massacre-1770.context_blurb: On the snowy evening of March 5, 1770, in the center of Boston, a small group of British soldiers posted to guard the Customs House were surrounded by a growing crowd of Boston townsmen who began shouting, taunting, and throwing snowballs, chunks of ice, and oyster shells at the soldiers. In the confusion of the moment the soldiers fired into the crowd, killing five civilians and wounding several others. The event was immediately exploited by Boston's revolutionary propagandists, especially the engraver Paul Revere, whose famous print of the scene (showing redcoats calmly firing on orderly, well-dressed townsmen) became one of the most effective pieces of political propaganda in American history. The soldiers were put on trial for murder in Boston later that year. In one of the great gestures of the pre-Revolution period, the Boston lawyer John Adams agreed to defend them, over enormous public hostility, on the principle that even accused British soldiers deserved a fair trial. His defense was largely successful; most of the soldiers were acquitted and the two found guilty of manslaughter were spared the gallows. The incident became a founding memory of American resistance to British military presence in the colonies.

boston-tea-party-1773.context_blurb: In 1773 the British Parliament passed the Tea Act, which gave the struggling East India Company a monopoly on tea exports to the American colonies and the right to sell directly through its own agents, bypassing colonial merchants. Patriot organizers in several colonial cities, including Boston, saw this not as a tax reduction (the law also lowered the duty on tea) but as a political trap designed to get Americans to accept Parliament's authority to tax them by seducing them with cheap tea. On the night of December 16, 1773, a group of men from the Boston Sons of Liberty — a hundred or more, loosely disguised, many of them with charcoal darkening their faces and feathers in their hair — boarded three British East India Company ships at Griffin's Wharf in Boston Harbor and dumped the entire tea cargo overboard, hundreds of chests. The British government responded with the so-called Intolerable Acts, which closed the port of Boston, revoked Massachusetts's charter, and quartered troops in private homes, and the escalation led directly to the First Continental Congress and then to open rebellion the following year. The night became one of the founding events of American resistance and gave its name, in time, to a long tradition of American protest movements.

botticelli-birth-of-venus-and-primavera.context_blurb: Sandro Botticelli (around 1445 to 1510) was a Florentine Renaissance painter who worked under the patronage of the Medici family and produced some of the most beloved paintings of the fifteenth century. He trained in Florence, probably in the workshop of Fra Filippo Lippi, and by his thirties was producing mature altarpieces, portraits, and large mythological scenes for Medici patrons. Two of his best-known works, both painted during the 1480s on commission from a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent, show figures from Greek and Roman mythology arranged in a complicated allegorical scene — one of a classical goddess arriving on the shore of a sea, the other of several mythological figures standing in a flowering grove. Both are now in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence and are among the most-visited paintings in Europe. Botticelli's style — graceful curving lines, slightly melancholy faces, delicate fabrics, floating hair — made him immediately recognizable. In his later years he came under the sway of the puritanical Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola, grew more severely religious in his work, and reportedly contributed his own paintings to one of Savonarola's bonfires of the vanities. His style went out of fashion after his death and he was largely forgotten until nineteenth-century English critics rediscovered him.

brunelleschi-s-dome-of-florence.context_blurb: In the early fifteenth century, the Florentine cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore had been under construction for over a hundred years and was still missing its central dome. The planned opening was so large — nearly fifty meters across — that no European architect since the fall of Rome knew how to span it. The problem had been quietly ignored for decades. In 1418 the civic authorities finally held a competition to solve it. The winner was Filippo Brunelleschi, a Florentine goldsmith and clockmaker who had never built a major building, but who had spent years studying the ancient Roman dome of the Pantheon and had worked out a double-shelled construction technique with herringbone brickwork that could support itself as it rose without the enormous wooden centering framework a conventional dome required. The construction took sixteen years, from 1420 to 1436, under Brunelleschi's constant personal supervision; he reportedly refused to share drawings of his method and even sabotaged rival schemes. The completed dome dominated the Florentine skyline, inspired every Renaissance architect who came after, and still stands today as the single most recognizable feature of Florence. The feat marked a turning point in European architectural confidence and helped define the Renaissance itself.

brunelleschi-the-florence-dome.context_blurb: Filippo Brunelleschi was a 15th-century Florentine goldsmith turned architect who solved one of the great engineering puzzles of his age — how to crown the enormous cathedral of Florence with a dome. The cathedral had sat open to the sky for decades because no one knew how to raise such a huge dome without the whole thing collapsing partway up. Brunelleschi had spent years in Rome measuring the ruins of ancient buildings, and when Florence held a public competition for the dome's design in 1418, he astonished the judges with a plan no other mason or sculptor could match. He went on to oversee every step of the long build, inventing new hoists and cranes, bickering constantly with his rival Lorenzo Ghiberti, and making engineering decisions that are still studied today. He also had a famously prickly personality and loved to show off with practical demonstrations when he wanted to make a point to a committee that doubted him. The dome was finished in 1436 and still dominates the Florence skyline, visible from miles outside the city. Brunelleschi lies buried in the cathedral directly below the work he gave his life to, and historians sometimes point to his dome as the single engineering feat that announced the Italian Renaissance to the world.

buddhism-four-noble-truths-eightfold-pat.context_blurb: The religion we now call Buddhism was founded in northern India in the 5th century BC by a man named Siddhartha Gautama, remembered by his followers as the Buddha, which simply means the awakened one. He was born a prince in a small kingdom in what is now the border region between India and Nepal, left his comfortable life behind as a young man after seeing an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering holy man, spent years trying different religious disciplines, and finally reached what he called enlightenment while sitting under a particular fig tree. His core teaching, which he began preaching in a deer park near the holy city of Varanasi, was that all human suffering has an identifiable cause (unquenched desire), that it can be ended, and that a specific disciplined way of life — a path with eight distinct spokes — can lead to the ending of suffering. He gathered a monastic community of followers and taught for over forty years before his death at around age eighty. His disciples carried his teachings across South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, and eventually around the world, and Buddhism is now one of the great religious traditions of humanity, with hundreds of millions of followers across many different schools.

bunker-hill-siege-of-boston.context_blurb: In the opening months of the American Revolution, after the April 1775 clashes at Lexington and Concord, thousands of New England militia poured into Boston and essentially bottled up the British army inside the city. Rebel fortifications ringed Boston on the landward side, and the British could resupply only by sea. The British commanders decided to break the siege by seizing the high ground on the Charlestown Peninsula across the river from Boston. On June 17, 1775, the famous Battle of Bunker Hill was fought there — though most of the actual fighting took place on an adjacent hill called Breed's Hill. American militia had dug in overnight behind improvised earthworks. The British made three frontal assaults up the slope. The famous order to the Americans — hold your fire until you can see the whites of their eyes — came from this battle. The Americans eventually ran out of powder and retreated, and the British took the hill. But the British paid an enormous casualty price for a geographical gain they could not sustain. The siege of Boston ground on for most of the following nine months, until George Washington's new Continental Army dragged captured cannon from Fort Ticonderoga across the winter mountains and used them to force the British to evacuate the city in March 1776.

byzantine-empire-justinian.context_blurb: After the western half of the Roman Empire slowly collapsed in the 5th century, the eastern half kept going for another thousand years from a great city on the Bosphorus, and its people never stopped identifying with the old empire they had inherited from their ancestors. The story centers on a brilliant and ambitious 6th-century emperor who came from humble peasant stock in the Balkans, married a sharp-tongued former actress he adored and trusted completely, and set out to put his half of the empire in order. During his reign a near-disastrous riot broke out in his own capital, inspired by rivalries between the city's chariot-racing fan clubs, that nearly cost him his throne until his wife shamed him into standing his ground. His greatest general reconquered lost provinces in Africa and Italy. His engineers raised a vast domed church whose dedication left him comparing himself to figures from the Bible. And his lawyers pulled a thousand years of Roman legal rulings into one orderly body of law whose influence still runs under most European legal systems today. A sharp-penned court historian who had served him faithfully in public then wrote a scandalous attack on him and his wife in private, and that double-faced record is still argued over today.

byzantine-mosaics-and-icons.context_blurb: Byzantine mosaics are made from millions of tiny glass or stone cubes called tesserae, often backed with gold leaf and tilted ever so slightly as they were set into the plaster. The subjects were almost always sacred — Christ as ruler of all, the Virgin and Child, apostles, biblical scenes — and they were meant to teach as well as to beautify, since few ordinary worshippers could read. Byzantine churches were designed to be seen by candlelight and oil-lamp, which made the gilded walls look very different from the modern photographs you may have seen under electric light. The icon, a smaller portable painting on wood or ivory, carried the same theology as the great mosaic: the honor paid to the image was understood to pass through to the person it depicted, not to stop at the paint. Icons could even become political — a long and bitter struggle broke out in the eighth and ninth centuries over whether making religious images at all was a kind of idol-worship, and only after decades of smashed panels and exiled defenders did the empire finally decide to keep them, a resolution that Orthodox Christians still celebrate every year on the first Sunday of Lent as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

byzantium-as-the-bridge-that-preserved-g.context_blurb: Byzantium — the eastern half of the Roman Empire that outlasted Rome by about a thousand years — never stopped speaking Greek, and never stopped copying the Greek classics. While Western Europe went through the long centuries after Rome's fall with only patchy access to ancient learning, Constantinople's monks and scholars kept the old texts alive in their monastery libraries. When Byzantine scholars began traveling west in the late Middle Ages — some for diplomacy, many fleeing the Turkish advance — they brought those manuscripts with them, and a flood of rediscovered ancient philosophy, mathematics, and literature fed directly into the Italian Renaissance. One elderly scholar stunned the Italians at a church council in 1438 by lecturing on strands of Greek thought the Latin West had almost completely forgotten, inspiring Cosimo de' Medici to found a whole Florentine academy to teach it and setting off a chain of translations that would transform European thought over the next century. Another kind of recovery is also famous: a Byzantine prayer book, written on parchment that monks had scraped clean of its earlier contents, was discovered in modern times to still carry the faint traces of a long-lost ancient work underneath, legible only with special imaging — a quietly fitting symbol of a civilization whose scribes kept writing even when they thought the old words were lost.

cahokia-and-mississippian-culture.context_blurb: Cahokia was the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, a huge Mississippian cultural center that flourished from around AD 1050 to 1350 near the junction of the Mississippi, Missouri, and Illinois rivers across the river from what is now modern St. Louis. At its height Cahokia covered thousands of acres, held tens of thousands of residents, and towered around a vast central plaza anchored by a man-made earthen pyramid taller than most European cathedrals of the same era. Mississippian people built dozens of other such mound centers across the eastern woodlands, grew corn, kept the surrounding countryside as a mix of farms and hunting grounds, and traded in copper, mica, marine shells, and ritual objects over vast distances. Something — most archaeologists think a combination of political strain, environmental damage from overfarming the floodplain, and climatic change — pulled Cahokia apart in the mid-1300s, and the city was abandoned long before any European arrived. When early French explorers came through the area in the late 1600s, the mounds were already an overgrown ruin with no inhabited city attached, and nobody could tell them who had built it.

caravaggio-and-the-baroque-tenebrism.context_blurb: Michelangelo Merisi, known from his hometown as Caravaggio (1571 to 1610), was an Italian painter who changed the course of European painting in roughly a decade of mature work. He arrived in Rome as a young man, got by as a studio assistant, and began producing paintings for Roman cardinals that stunned viewers with their intense realism and their dramatic use of light and dark — figures stepping out of pitch-black backgrounds into fierce illumination, with ordinary dirty feet, muscular backs, and recognizable Roman faces playing biblical scenes. The technique later became known as tenebrism and influenced painters all over Europe. Caravaggio's personal life was violent and chaotic. He fought in Roman streets, was repeatedly arrested, and in 1606 killed a man in a sword fight and fled Rome under a death sentence. He spent his last four years running from city to city on the margins of the papal states and the Mediterranean, producing extraordinary dark religious paintings in Malta, Sicily, and Naples as he went, and he died at the age of thirty-eight on a beach north of Rome, possibly of fever or wounds. His influence on painters like Rubens, Velazquez, Rembrandt, and Vermeer was enormous, and he is now regarded as one of the great figures of Western art.

caravel-compass-astrolabe.context_blurb: The great voyages of the late 15th and early 16th centuries did not happen by magic; they rode on three practical inventions that Portuguese and Spanish sailors slowly perfected. The caravel was a light, shallow ship with a rig that let it tack close to the wind, so a captain could beat his way home against the breeze instead of waiting months for it to swing around. The magnetic compass, borrowed centuries earlier from Chinese inventors, let a navigator hold a steady heading even when fog or weeks of open water hid every landmark. The mariner's astrolabe was a solidly built brass instrument that let a sailor measure the angle of the sun or a bright star above the horizon, and work out from that how far north or south he had traveled. The design of the astrolabe deliberately included several features that made it usable on a lurching deck instead of the astronomer's quiet garden where its ancestors had come from. None of these tools was invented from scratch in 1492; it was the combination, cheap and in every captain's chest, that opened the world. The real breakthrough was not any single device but the slow, cumulative knowledge of how to use them all together on a long voyage out of sight of any familiar shore.

castiglione-the-courtier.context_blurb: Baldassare Castiglione was an early-16th-century Italian diplomat, soldier, and courtier at the small but brilliant court of Urbino. He is remembered today for one book, a long work in dialogue form called The Book of the Courtier, which he polished for years and finally published in 1528. The book pretends to record four evenings of after-dinner conversation at the Duke of Urbino's palace, in which the real men and women of that court — all named, often teasing each other across the room — talk about what the perfect courtier ought to be: how he should fight, how he should speak, how he should carry himself around his prince, how he should dress and dance and love. Castiglione's book became the European handbook of elegant manners for the next two centuries, read and copied at every court from Paris to London, and quietly setting the standard that a Shakespeare or a Sidney would measure a gentleman against. Its ideas about how to carry oneself in public would echo into painting, poetry, and public life well beyond Italy, and in one famous passage the book introduced an Italian word of its own that other European languages have been borrowing ever since.

castles-siege-warfare.context_blurb: A medieval castle was a weapon as much as a house. Over the centuries following the fall of Rome, Christian Europe grew a dense forest of fortified lord's houses, from quick earth-and-timber fortifications that could be thrown up in a few weeks to vast stone concentric fortresses that could take generations and treasuries to raise and almost as long to break. Attackers answered the stone with their own cleverness: battering rams, mobile siege towers, swinging-arm engines that hurled stones across long distances, giant torsion catapults, sapper tunnels dug underneath the walls, bribery, deception, hunger, and above all patience. Defenders answered back with everything from carefully angled arrow slits to vats of unpleasant liquid dropped through clever openings in the floor of the gatehouse onto anyone trying to break down the door below. Castles grew more sophisticated over the centuries, with multiple curtain walls, towers of new shapes that resisted undermining, and gate complexes designed as traps. The story covers both sides of the long and expensive game, from the architects who designed the stone and the engineers who tried to crack it, to the legendary engines, named cannons, and strange stories that grew up around the business of taking or holding a stone house with a hundred people inside.

castro-s-cuba-la-caba-a-the-exiles.context_blurb: After the Cuban Revolution overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista in January 1959, the young revolutionary leader Fidel Castro and his lieutenants, including the Argentine physician Ernesto Che Guevara, consolidated control over the country and began a series of show trials and executions of former Batista officials, suspected political opponents, and anyone deemed a counterrevolutionary. The old Spanish colonial fortress of La Cabana in Havana was turned into a prison and execution ground, and in the first years of the revolution Che Guevara presided over the executions there of hundreds of prisoners. The regime also seized private businesses, confiscated land, closed independent newspapers, and sent thousands of political prisoners to a long network of forced-labor camps. Over the following six decades of Castro-family rule, more than a million Cubans — about one in ten — have fled the island, often at enormous personal risk crossing the Florida Straits on rafts and small boats. Thousands died at sea. The Cuban exile community in Miami became one of the most politically active immigrant communities in American history. The Castro regime is one of the longest-running communist dictatorships in the world, and it has produced the predictable results: political repression, economic failure, mass emigration, and a lasting public argument over what counts as revolution and what counts as tyranny.

casualties-and-scale-of-wwii.context_blurb: The Second World War was the deadliest conflict in human history by a wide margin. Over roughly six years of fighting from 1939 to 1945 (longer in the Pacific, where the Japanese invasion of China had begun in 1937), the war killed somewhere in the range of 70 to 85 million people across the entire planet, including military and civilian deaths from combat, bombing, famine, disease, and genocide. The Soviet Union suffered the largest absolute death toll, with somewhere around twenty-seven million dead, mostly civilians. China's death toll was also enormous, somewhere between fifteen and twenty million. Nazi Germany murdered roughly six million European Jews in the Holocaust along with millions of other victims. Poland lost roughly a sixth of its entire prewar population. Germany itself lost about seven million people. Japan lost between two and three million people, mostly in the war's final year. The United Kingdom lost about 450,000 and the United States about 420,000 — comparatively light losses given the scale of their military commitment. The physical destruction was in proportion: much of continental Europe's great cities were in rubble by 1945, and the costs of rebuilding the continent would take over a decade of focused effort.

causes-of-the-civil-war-and-the-cornerst.context_blurb: In the winter and spring of 1861, after the election of Abraham Lincoln, eleven Southern states broke away from the United States to form the Confederate States of America. They set up a new capital, drafted a constitution, elected Jefferson Davis as their president, and — a few weeks before the shooting began at Fort Sumter — chose the Georgia politician Alexander Stephens as their vice president. On March 21, 1861, in Savannah, Stephens delivered what became known as the Cornerstone Speech, in which he explained what he saw as the Confederacy's animating principle. The questions ahead walk through that speech and the broader question of why the war came. It compares what Southern state secession conventions actually wrote down about their reasons at the time, what Stephens himself said in Savannah, and what he and his defenders later tried to say instead, once the war was lost and the Lost Cause version of history was being constructed. It also includes a scientific authority Stephens cited to lend his argument the air of settled fact. It matters because the Cornerstone Speech is one of the few places where the people starting the Civil War stated their foundational reason in their own words, in public, without the softening of later memory — a kind of unguarded primary source every student of the period eventually meets.

cervantes-don-quixote.context_blurb: Miguel de Cervantes was a Spanish soldier, slave, tax collector, and in his later years a novelist. He lived from 1547 to 1616, in the same decades as Shakespeare, and spent nearly half of a long life in misery: he was wounded fighting as a young soldier, captured by pirates on his way home and held for five years as a slave in Algiers, and later jailed more than once in Spain over his bookkeeping. He wrote his great book in his fifties, after everything else had failed. It is the story of a middle-aged country gentleman who reads too many old romances about chivalry, finally cracks, and sets out across the dry plains of La Mancha believing himself a wandering knight. He gives himself a new knight's name, picks a lady to serve, and goes galloping into one disastrous adventure after another, each time absolutely certain he is doing something glorious. The book was published in Madrid and became an immediate hit across Europe, pirated and translated and quoted everywhere, and Cervantes was both pleased and poor until the end of his life. He is said to have died on the same date as Shakespeare in 1616, and his book has often been called a turning point in the whole history of European literature — the moment the long old tradition of knightly romance was replaced by something recognizably modern.

chaco-canyon-and-pueblo-bonito.context_blurb: Chaco Canyon in the dry high country of what is now northwestern New Mexico was the ceremonial and political center of the Ancestral Puebloan world from roughly AD 850 to 1150. The Chacoans built a cluster of enormous masonry complexes in and around the canyon, the largest of which contained hundreds of rooms rising several stories, with carefully fitted sandstone walls, massive timber roof beams dragged in from distant mountains, and dozens of circular underground ceremonial chambers. A network of ruler-straight roads radiates out from the canyon into surrounding country for many miles, their purpose still debated. Chaco appears to have been more than a place to live — it functioned as a pilgrimage destination, with surrounding villages feeding its ceremonies with pottery, turquoise, maize, and macaw feathers traded up from Mexico. By the mid-1100s, a punishing multi-decade drought on the Colorado Plateau helped break the Chacoan system apart. The people drifted south and east, and the great buildings were quietly abandoned. The ruins have stood in the high desert ever since, and they are now among the most important archaeological sites in North America.

charlemagne-the-carolingian-empire.context_blurb: By about the year 800, a tall Frankish king had conquered most of western and central Europe. On Christmas Day in Rome the Pope dropped a crown onto his head, and he was proclaimed by a title that no western ruler had held since Rome itself fell. He is remembered as the man who stitched a Christian empire back together in the west for the first time in three hundred years, and his court became a magnet for scholars, teachers, and reformers from across Christendom and even from the court of the caliph in Baghdad, who sent famous and surprising gifts his way. Though he could never quite master certain scholarly skills himself, he launched a wide program of educational reform, standardizing church liturgy, correcting the Latin of imported books, founding palace schools, and promoting cleaner methods of handwriting whose influence shaped European books for a long time afterwards. His armies also forced Christianity on neighboring pagan peoples with a hand so heavy that his own successors sometimes shuddered at it. His chief paladin, the horn-blowing warrior who guarded his rear-guard in the Pyrenees and died there, became the hero of the greatest French epic poem of the Middle Ages, and the fate of his sprawling empire after his death became the raw material of a thousand later legends.

charles-lindbergh-and-the-age-of-flight.context_blurb: On May 20, 1927, a 25-year-old American airmail pilot named Charles Lindbergh took off alone from a wet runway on Long Island, flew nonstop across the Atlantic in a single-engine monoplane, and 33 and a half hours later landed outside Paris to a crowd of 150,000 Frenchmen who nearly tore his plane apart to touch him. He was chasing a $25,000 prize that a New York hotel owner had offered for the first nonstop New York-to-Paris flight — a prize several more experienced pilots had already died chasing. Lindbergh's plane had been built to his own strange specifications in San Diego, stripped of weight and loaded with extra fuel, and leaving out several features a long-haul pilot might expect to have. The flight transformed him overnight into the most famous man on Earth and set off an aviation craze that filled American skies through the rest of the 1920s with barnstormers, airline startups, and little boys who wanted to fly. His later life would grow dark — a horrifying 1932 kidnapping and murder of his baby son, and prewar political speeches that would damage his reputation — but the solo Atlantic crossing itself stayed the clean, legendary moment, celebrated in parades, popular songs, and Lindbergh's own best-selling memoir of the flight.

chaucer-s-canterbury-tales.context_blurb: In the late 1300s, an English civil servant and courtier began writing a long story about a group of pilgrims riding together to a famous shrine, each telling a tale along the way to pass the time. He wrote not in the Latin or French his educated readers knew but in the English spoken around him, and the result is the first great masterpiece of English literature, so important that scholars still date the start of modern English partly from his pages. His pilgrims are a cross-section of 14th-century England, from a quiet soldier and a sweet-natured parish priest to a worldly widow who has already outlived five husbands, a crooked miller, and a dubious church fundraiser who hawks suspicious holy souvenirs to the gullible. Chaucer loved and gently mocked all of them. Their tales range from courtly romance to lewd barroom comedy to pious legend, and together they are still one of the funniest and warmest portraits of a whole society ever written in any language. The poem was never finished; Chaucer died before his pilgrims ever reached their shrine. But in his hands the English language came of age, and the sly, affectionate way he looked at ordinary human beings became part of what the English novel would one day be when it finally arrived centuries after him.

chavin-de-huantar-early-andean-culture.context_blurb: Chavin de Huantar was a religious center high in the Andes mountains of what is now central Peru, built from around 1200 BC and most active between about 900 and 200 BC. It is one of the earliest known centers of pan-Andean religious influence, long before the better-known Inca Empire. The site features large stone temple platforms, underground stone galleries whose designs could channel the sound of rushing water and torchlight in theatrical ways for visitors, and striking stone carvings of fanged jaguar-like supernatural beings with staring eyes and flaring nostrils. The Chavin religious cult appears to have spread its distinctive artistic style across much of the central and northern Andes without any evidence of military conquest, suggesting that it worked through pilgrimage, religious specialists, and a shared visual symbolism. The site was built on carefully placed ground where mountain springs could be guided through its galleries, and the whole complex seems designed to induce religious awe in the people brought there. Chavin de Huantar is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is studied as one of the foundations of all later Andean civilization, including the one Pizarro would eventually destroy.

child-labor-and-industrial-working-condi.context_blurb: In the first century of industrial capitalism — roughly the 1780s to the 1840s in Britain and a little later in the United States — large numbers of children worked long shifts in cotton mills, coal mines, chimney flues, brickyards, and match factories. Many were as young as five or six; most worked ten to fourteen hours a day; some were pauper apprentices sent out from workhouses to masters who could legally beat them. The questions ahead walk through specific jobs and the specific cruelties attached to them in chimneys, in deep coal pits, in slate breakers, and on the floors of textile mills. Alongside the horrors it also covers the first reformers who worked to end them — a pamphleteer whose attacks on the factory system shook Parliament, a long-remembered aristocratic campaigner, the royal commissions whose horrifying illustrated reports made the facts impossible to deny, and the earliest effective factory inspectors. Finally it covers an industrial-era medical first — the recognition that a particular workplace exposure could directly cause a cancer. It matters because reformers in this period discovered something new in history: that a free society could choose to limit the labor market to protect the people inside it, and could pay inspectors to make the rules real.

child-sacrifice-in-the-ancient-near-east.context_blurb: The practice of ritually killing young children as sacrifices to specific gods appears in various forms across the ancient Near East and the ancient Mediterranean. Archaeological and textual evidence confirms it most clearly among the Phoenician colonies of the western Mediterranean, especially at the city of Carthage in modern Tunisia and at related Phoenician settlements in Sicily and Sardinia. At these sites, archaeologists have uncovered specific sacred precincts, called in modern scholarship by their biblical-Hebrew name tophet, containing thousands of small burial urns holding the cremated remains of infants and very young children, usually buried under memorial stone markers (stelae) addressed to the deities Baal Hammon and Tanit. Phoenician written sources, Hebrew scripture, and Greek and Roman historians all record the practice, including a dramatic account by the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus of a mass sacrifice during the siege of Carthage. The ancient Hebrews repeatedly condemned the practice as among the worst Canaanite abominations and legally forbade it in their own law. Some modern scholars have tried to argue that the Carthaginian tophet is actually a cemetery for stillbirths and infant deaths, but the current archaeological and textual consensus is that systematic ritual child sacrifice really did happen there.

chinampas-the-aztec-floating-gardens.context_blurb: The Valley of Mexico, in which the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built, was dominated in the 15th century by a huge shallow lake complex rather than the dry basin visible today. The Aztecs and their neighbors fed millions of people out of that water by developing a highly productive form of raised-bed farming called chinampas, often misleadingly described as floating gardens. The chinampas were long, narrow rectangular garden plots built up above the lake surface out of alternating layers of mud, lake vegetation, and reeds, anchored at their edges by willow trees whose roots grew down to the lake bed and held the plot in place. Canals between the plots let farmers travel by canoe between their fields and keep each plot wet all year. The system was extraordinarily productive, producing several crops a year of maize, beans, chilies, tomatoes, amaranth, and squash, and feeding one of the densest urban populations the world had yet seen. Patches of chinampa farming still survive today in the Xochimilco district of modern Mexico City, which is why that neighborhood is a maze of flower-lined canals full of small boats, a last fragment of the pre-conquest water world.

chinese-art-landscape-painting-calligrap.context_blurb: Chinese visual art has one of the longest and richest continuous traditions anywhere on Earth, running from the oracle-bone inscriptions of the Shang dynasty into the present. Three closely connected forms sit at its heart: calligraphy, where brush-written characters are themselves regarded as the highest form of visual expression; monochrome ink landscape painting, which from the Song dynasty onward depicted sweeping mountains, mist, and tiny human figures in a tradition of philosophical rather than photographic representation; and ceramics, in which Chinese potters developed glazes, porcelain itself, and techniques (celadon, blue-and-white, famille rose) that the rest of the world spent centuries trying to copy. Chinese painting was traditionally done on silk or paper scrolls, hung or unrolled rather than framed, and was often inscribed with the painter's own poetry. The great Song-dynasty landscape painters — Fan Kuan, Guo Xi, Mi Fu — are still studied as foundational masters. Later dynasties produced the Yuan, Ming, and Qing great painters and the enormous imperial porcelain industry at Jingdezhen, whose blue-and-white wares reached Islamic, European, and Southeast Asian markets by the shipload. The whole Chinese tradition stayed fairly separate from Western painting until the twentieth century, when the two met and began to influence each other.

chinese-foot-binding.context_blurb: For about a thousand years, from roughly the 10th century AD until it was finally stamped out in the early 20th century, elite Han Chinese parents mutilated the feet of their young daughters through a painful binding process that broke the arches and curled the toes under the sole, producing feet that could be squeezed into shoes just a few inches long. The practice began at Chinese imperial courts and spread downward through the social hierarchy over the following centuries, until most non-rural women across much of China were bound. Bound feet made walking painful and labor nearly impossible, and the practice was closely tied to class marking, marriage markets, and specific aesthetic ideals that treated the resulting small foot as desirable. The practice did real and lifelong physical damage, including broken bones, infections, deformities, and often total loss of independent mobility. It was ended in the first half of the 20th century by a combination of Christian missionary advocacy (especially from British Protestant missionaries who formed anti-footbinding societies in the late 1800s), reform-minded Chinese intellectuals, early feminist movements, and finally government bans under both the Republican and Communist governments. The last women with fully bound feet are now in their nineties and hundreds; the practice is dying out within living memory.

chinese-four-great-inventions.context_blurb: Chinese scholars and craftsmen gave the world a small bundle of inventions so useful that European writers of the Renaissance already singled them out as the technologies that had reshaped civilisation. Francis Bacon, writing around 1620, named three of them as the forces that had, in his own time, changed warfare, learning, and navigation beyond recognition, and later Chinese and Western historians added a fourth to the list. The traditional set of four spans more than a thousand years of invention, roughly from the Han dynasty through the Tang and Song. The oldest of the four was tinkered toward over centuries, with a famous Han court official traditionally credited for making it affordable to produce at scale. The newest grew out of patient experimenting by Daoist alchemists hunting for the elixir of long life and stumbling instead onto something that flashed and roared. Another arose from the mysterious habits of a certain naturally magnetised stone, which Song-dynasty craftsmen learned to float on water or balance on a pin so it would always settle in a particular, predictable orientation. The fourth was the slow working-out of how to reproduce written documents by stamping or impressing them without copying them out by hand, a technology that in the Chinese setting developed in distinctive ways and over several stages.

chinese-revolution-mao-1949.context_blurb: The Chinese Communist Party, under its chairman Mao Zedong, won the Chinese Civil War against the Nationalist government of Chiang Kai-shek in 1949 after decades of intermittent fighting, Japanese invasion, and finally full-scale civil war following the end of the Second World War. Mao proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic of China from the gate at the main square of Beijing in October 1949. Chiang Kai-shek and the surviving Nationalist government fled to the island of Taiwan, which has maintained a separate political existence ever since. Under Mao's rule from 1949 to his death in 1976, China underwent several enormous and catastrophic social campaigns. Mao launched a program of forced rural collectivization, nationalized industry, suppressed religious institutions, and in 1958 launched the Great Leap Forward, a crash industrialization program that caused the largest famine in human history, with somewhere between 15 and 45 million peasants starving to death depending on which modern estimate you accept. In 1966 he launched the Cultural Revolution, a decade of ideological persecution during which teachers, intellectuals, and party moderates were beaten, humiliated, murdered, or driven to suicide across China. Mao's rule left behind one of the great mass-killing records in human history, which the modern Chinese state still refuses to confront honestly.

christian-and-student-resistance-of-cons.context_blurb: A small but genuine German resistance to Nazi rule existed throughout the twelve years of Hitler's dictatorship, and some of its most moving figures came from Christian and student circles. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran pastor and theologian who had broken with the official German Protestant Church when it tried to accommodate Nazi racial doctrine, had joined the dissenting Confessing Church, and later became involved in a conspiracy to assassinate Hitler.
