Erasmus died in 1536, respected by Catholics and Protestants alike and fully trusted by neither — the fate, perhaps, of a man who hoped the Church could reform itself from within without being torn in two.

eratosthenes-measures-the-earth.context_blurb: Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who ran the great library of Alexandria in Egypt in the third century BC, a man so broadly accomplished that his colleagues nicknamed him 'Beta' — second-best at everything, because another specialist always edged him out in each individual field. He wrote on history, poetry, geography, and mathematics; he mapped the known world; he invented a clever sieve for sifting out prime numbers that is still taught today. His most famous feat used nothing but a stick, a shadow, a well, and a bit of geometry. He had heard that on a certain midsummer day the Sun shone straight down to the bottom of a deep well in the southern Egyptian town of Syene — now Aswan — leaving no shadow at all. On the same day in Alexandria, far to the north, a vertical pole did cast a small shadow. Eratosthenes carefully measured the angle of that shadow, learned the distance between the two cities from royal surveyors, and did the sum. His answer came out astonishingly close to what we would get today — within a few percent, depending on which ancient unit of distance you trust him to have been using. More importantly, he had shown that a lone librarian armed with careful measurement and a confident grasp of geometry could reach a precise answer about the whole Earth from the shadow of a single stick.

eratosthenes-measures-the-earth-s-circum.context_blurb: Eratosthenes was a 3rd-century BC Greek mathematician, geographer, and chief librarian at the great Library of Alexandria in Egypt. He noticed a fact in an old travel report that nobody else had done anything useful with: at noon on the longest day of the year, the Sun shone straight down to the bottom of a certain well in southern Egypt and cast no shadow. In Alexandria at the same moment, the Sun did cast a shadow. From that difference, together with the distance between the two cities (which professional pacers had measured), Eratosthenes worked out the size of the whole Earth using nothing but geometry. His answer, converted to modern units, is remarkably close to the real circumference — within a few percent, which is extraordinary given his equipment. The experiment is still routinely repeated in school classrooms around the world because it is one of the most elegant demonstrations of how much a careful ancient geometer could deduce from very simple observations. It also quietly dynamites the modern folk-myth that medieval people thought the Earth was flat; the Greeks had worked out it was round and roughly how big more than two thousand years ago.

euclid-and-the-elements-geometry.context_blurb: Euclid was a Greek mathematician working in Alexandria around 300 BC, during the generation after Alexander the Great. Very little is known about his personal life, but his great mathematical textbook, titled the Elements, became one of the most influential books ever written. In thirteen compact volumes, Euclid gathered up almost everything Greek mathematicians had worked out about plane geometry, solid geometry, and number theory, and he arranged it all into a strictly logical system beginning from a short list of definitions, postulates, and common notions. From those seeds he deduced every theorem, each one building on the ones before it, in a long chain that readers could check for themselves. The Elements was used as a standard geometry textbook in schools around the world for over two thousand years, and most of it is still taught today, often without students realizing where the material comes from. Just as importantly, Euclid's method — define your terms, state your assumptions, prove your results in order from your assumptions — became the model for how to think rigorously about anything, which is why philosophers from Spinoza to Newton tried to imitate the Elements in their own books on completely different subjects.

european-resistance-movements.context_blurb: In every country occupied by Nazi Germany during the Second World War, some fraction of the civilian population organized resistance against the occupiers. The resistance took different forms in different countries. The French Resistance operated in the Vichy and later fully occupied zones, running underground newspapers, hiding downed Allied aircrews, sabotaging German military transport, and gathering intelligence for Allied planners. The Polish Home Army, loyal to the Polish government-in-exile in London, was one of the largest resistance movements of the war. The Yugoslav Partisans under Josip Broz Tito ran a serious guerrilla war against German and Italian occupation forces across the mountains of the Balkans. Dutch, Norwegian, Danish, Belgian, Greek, Czech, Italian, and other resistance movements worked at various scales. Many resistance members were tortured and executed by the Gestapo. The resistance movements saved Jewish lives in large numbers, especially in Denmark, where almost the entire Jewish population was smuggled to Sweden in October 1943, and in the French and Italian countrysides, where networks of ordinary civilians hid Jewish families throughout the occupation. The resistance played a significant role in the final Allied liberation of Western Europe in 1944 and 1945.

european-union-the-euro.context_blurb: After the Second World War, Western European leaders including Robert Schuman of France, Konrad Adenauer of West Germany, Alcide De Gasperi of Italy, and Jean Monnet began planning closer economic and political cooperation among their countries, partly to make another European war impossible by binding former enemies together economically. The initial 1951 European Coal and Steel Community grew through a series of treaties into the European Economic Community of 1957 and the European Union of 1993. The EU gradually added members from six founding countries up to twenty-seven by the mid-2010s, with the United Kingdom famously withdrawing in 2020 after a 2016 referendum. The EU standardized trade, agriculture, environmental, and labor policy across its member states, allowed free movement of workers between them, and in 1999 launched a common currency (the Euro) that replaced the national currencies of most but not all member states. The project has produced extraordinary results in some respects — a long peace among its member states, major economic integration — and has produced its own serious political strains in others, including financial crises in the weaker member economies and ongoing debates about democratic legitimacy, immigration, and national sovereignty.

everest-hillary-and-tenzing.context_blurb: Mount Everest is the highest point on Earth, straddling the border of Nepal and Tibet in the Himalayas. For over thirty years teams of climbers from several countries died trying to reach its summit — most famously the British mountaineer George Mallory, who vanished high on its slopes in 1924. In the spring of 1953 a large British-led expedition under Colonel John Hunt pushed camps up the mountain in a careful, methodical siege. On 29 May 1953 two men from that expedition finally stood on the top: Edmund Hillary, a lanky beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa guide from a mountain village on the Nepal–Tibet frontier who had already been up the mountain farther than almost anyone alive. Tenzing had tried for the summit on several previous expeditions and knew Everest's upper slopes as well as any human being. The two men spent only about fifteen minutes on the summit — just long enough for Hillary to photograph Tenzing holding up the flags of their partner nations, for Tenzing to leave a small Buddhist offering in the snow, and for both of them to take in a view no one had ever seen before. News of the climb reached London just in time for the coronation of the young Queen Elizabeth II, and Hillary was promptly knighted; Tenzing received the George Medal. Both men stayed close friends for the rest of their lives.

ezana-of-aksum-ethiopian-christianity.context_blurb: In the 4th century AD, the kingdom of Aksum in highland Ethiopia became one of the first countries in the world to adopt Christianity as a state religion. The king who made the decision was named Ezana. He was converted as a young man by a Syrian Christian named Frumentius, who had been shipwrecked in his father's court and raised in the royal household. Ezana later minted coins carrying the Christian cross, and over the following centuries his kingdom built an extensive and strikingly original Christian culture that developed in close contact with the Coptic Church of Egypt and in semi-isolation from the Mediterranean world. Ethiopian Christianity has unbroken continuity from Ezana's conversion to the present day, which is why it is one of the oldest living Christian traditions anywhere. It has its own church music, its own liturgical language (Ge'ez), its own calendar, and its own rich manuscript and iconographic tradition. The modern Ethiopian Orthodox Church still holds that one of its early kings housed the original Ark of the Covenant brought from Jerusalem by the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and it is said to be guarded today in a specific sanctuary in Ethiopia whose contents nobody but its appointed keeper is allowed to see.

fall-of-berlin-and-hitler-s-death.context_blurb: By April 1945, after years of steady Soviet advance from the east and nearly a year of Western Allied advance from the west, the German capital of Berlin was surrounded by the Red Army. Adolf Hitler, by then isolated in his underground bunker beneath the Reich Chancellery, refused to leave the city. The Soviet assault on Berlin, running from mid-April into early May 1945, was one of the bloodiest urban battles of the war, with Soviet forces pushing in street by street against the last remnants of the German Wehrmacht, SS units, Hitler Youth boys, and elderly conscripts of the Volkssturm. On April 30, Hitler committed suicide in his bunker along with his newly married wife Eva Braun. The German commander in Berlin surrendered the city two days later. The formal unconditional surrender of all German forces was signed in a schoolhouse at Reims, France, on May 7 and ratified in Berlin on May 8, 1945. The war in Europe was over after nearly six years. The ruins of the Reich Chancellery and the bunker where Hitler died were later dynamited by the Soviets, and the site today is a parking lot behind an ordinary Berlin apartment building, deliberately kept inconspicuous.

fall-of-constantinople-1453.context_blurb: The siege and fall of Constantinople in 1453 ended a Christian empire that had called itself Roman for over a thousand years. The young Ottoman sultan Mehmed II — just twenty-one — had been planning the attack since his boyhood, and he brought an army of about eighty thousand men against a defending force of perhaps seven thousand. The city's famously layered land walls, built nearly a thousand years earlier, had never been breached by a direct assault, but Mehmed hired a Hungarian cannon-maker named Orban to build him monstrous bronze guns capable of hurling stone cannonballs so heavy they shook the ground. The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, refused every offer of surrender and died when the walls finally gave way after fifty-three days of bombardment and failed sorties by sea. In the aftermath, Greek scholars fled west and helped feed the Italian Renaissance, Mehmed moved the Ottoman capital to the conquered city and set about rebuilding it as the imperial seat of a new Muslim empire that would stand another four and a half centuries, legends grew up among the Greeks that one day their emperor would return, and the fall of the city became the symbolic end of the Middle Ages for most of Europe — the moment, in many textbooks, when the modern age truly begins.

fall-of-constantinople-1453-2.context_blurb: In the spring of 1453, after more than a thousand years of standing against every army and every faith that had been thrown at it, the great Christian city on the Bosphorus finally fell to a young Ottoman sultan who was still in his early twenties. The city's walls had turned back everyone from the Avars to the Vikings to earlier Muslim armies, and the last Roman emperor made a desperate stand on them even as his empire shrank around him down to little more than the city itself. The sultan brought a vast new weapon, a monster gun bigger than anything that had ever been fired at a city wall before, and he pulled off a strange naval trick that let his ships appear in a part of the harbor they should not have been able to reach. His soldiers streamed over the broken walls at dawn and spent three days plundering the city. The fall of this city sent its scholars and their precious ancient Greek books running west into Italy, where their arrival helped feed a cultural movement that was already beginning to reshape the arts, the churches, and the universities of western Europe. For Orthodox Christians the day the city fell is still a date remembered with a kind of national grief seven centuries later.

fall-of-france-1940.context_blurb: In May 1940, Nazi Germany launched a sudden armored and air offensive against France and the Low Countries, bypassing the heavily fortified French defensive line along the German border by sweeping through the forests of the Ardennes in Belgium and Luxembourg. German armored columns reached the English Channel coast within two weeks, cutting off and surrounding the main French field armies and the British Expeditionary Force. The British evacuated over three hundred thousand of their soldiers from the beaches of Dunkirk at the end of May and the beginning of June, in a famous ad-hoc fleet of warships and civilian small craft. The French government, overwhelmed and demoralized, signed an armistice with Germany in mid-June 1940 in the same railway carriage in which Germany had signed its own armistice ending World War I. France was partitioned into a German-occupied northern and western zone and a nominally independent southern collaborationist Vichy regime. A small Free French force under the exile general Charles de Gaulle continued the fight from London. The collapse of France in six weeks shocked the world and left Britain alone in Western Europe against Nazi Germany for the next year. France would not be liberated until the summer of 1944.

fall-of-the-romanovs-and-rasputin.context_blurb: Tsar Nicholas II and the German-born Empress Alexandra had four daughters and one son, Tsarevich Alexei, who had hemophilia — his blood would not clot, and even a childhood bruise could threaten his life. Desperate to save him, Alexandra turned to Grigori Rasputin, a long-haired Siberian wanderer who had appeared at the Russian court and seemed, when nothing else worked, to be able to calm the boy and stop the bleeding. The Empress's reliance on Rasputin, and the rumors around his drinking and his women, scandalized the court, especially after World War I began and the Tsar left to command his armies, leaving Alexandra and Rasputin an alarming influence over wartime appointments. In December 1916 a group of Russian nobles led by Prince Felix Yusupov murdered Rasputin in a Petrograd basement in a famously drawn-out killing that generations of writers would later rework into fiction and film. Within three months the Romanov dynasty itself collapsed in the February Revolution, and in July 1918 Bolshevik gunmen shot the entire imperial family, down to the four princesses and their young brother, in the cellar of a merchant's house in Yekaterinburg — a killing whose full horror the world only pieced together decades later when the bones were finally found and identified.

fall-of-the-western-roman-empire-476.context_blurb: In the late 400s, the western half of the Roman Empire had been shrinking and sickening for a long time, propped up by barbarian generals who ruled behind puppet emperors in the shrunken capital at Ravenna. In 476, the last of those boy emperors was quietly pushed off the throne by a German commander in Italy. He was not killed. He was pensioned off to live out the rest of his life in a comfortable retirement, and nobody in the west bothered to put another emperor in his place, because by then no one really needed one. The eastern empire kept going; the real end in the west was less a crash than a slow handover, as Germanic kingdoms took over Rome's old provinces and settled into them, keeping Rome's roads, its law, its Latin, and most of its daily life. The children of those kingdoms would one day grow into the nations and languages of modern Europe. For Romans alive at the time, the fall barely registered as a single event. For Christian intellectuals writing a generation later, it demanded explanation: why, after a thousand years, had the eternal city stopped being eternal? Their answers shaped how the West has told the story ever since.

families-of-instruments-and-the-orchestr.context_blurb: The modern Western symphony orchestra is organized into four families of musical instruments: strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion. The strings include the violin, viola, cello, and double bass; the woodwinds include the flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, and their relatives; the brass includes the trumpet, French horn, trombone, and tuba; the percussion family covers everything from the timpani and the snare drum to the triangle and the gong. The orchestra as a specific institution — a large standardized ensemble performing in a concert hall — grew into its current shape over the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries alongside the development of symphonic music by composers like Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Brahms, Mahler, and others. Earlier Baroque ensembles were smaller and more varied. The size of an orchestra expanded over time as composers wrote for ever-larger forces, with Mahler's turn-of-the-20th-century symphonies requiring over a hundred players and a chorus. The classification of instruments into families is a Western convention; many other musical cultures classify their instruments differently. But in modern Western music education, the four-family model is the standard introduction to how an orchestra is organized, and it is still the way a visitor hears the instruments in a modern concert hall today.

faraday-maxwell-and-the-conquest-of-elec.context_blurb: Michael Faraday was an English experimenter born in 1791, the son of a blacksmith, who had almost no formal schooling. He worked as a tradesman's apprentice as a young man, educated himself in the evenings, and later became the greatest experimenter of his age — the man who worked out the central link between electricity and magnetism and showed how to turn one into the other. He was devout, humble, famously plainspoken, and gave the Royal Institution's beloved Christmas Lectures for children for decades. A generation after him, the Scottish mathematical physicist James Clerk Maxwell took Faraday's intuitive, field-based picture of electric and magnetic forces and wrote it down as a tight set of mathematical equations, which turned out to describe something astonishing about the natural world. The questions ahead cover Faraday's unlikely rise, his style of plain curiosity, a famous Christmas-lecture demonstration, the key experiment that first showed a changing magnetic field could push a current through a nearby wire, and Maxwell's breakthrough — the hidden identity his equations revealed, and a world-changing technology that followed from it. It matters because almost every piece of electrical technology you use is built on this chain of work — from power stations and electric motors to broadcasting, mobile phones, and GPS.

fdr-and-the-new-deal.context_blurb: Franklin Delano Roosevelt took the oath of office in March 1933 at the darkest moment of the Great Depression — a quarter of American workers were out of a job, banks were failing by the thousand, and the economy had shrunk by about a third. In his first hundred days he pushed through more federal legislation than any president before him, including emergency banking measures and the Civilian Conservation Corps, which put nearly three million young men into tent camps across the national forests to plant trees, fight fires, and build parks. Later came the Works Progress Administration, which hired idle Americans of many kinds for public projects; the Rural Electrification Administration, which extended federally subsidized infrastructure into isolated farm country for the first time; and the Social Security Act, which guaranteed pensions for the elderly. Not everyone was convinced the New Deal was constitutional: the Supreme Court kept striking down New Deal statutes, and when Roosevelt tried to pack the Court with new justices his own party balked, only for the Court itself to suddenly shift its votes in a change that quickly became known by a famous nickname. Critics on the right warned that this growing federal power would, over time, threaten political liberty, a line of argument the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek developed in a short book published in 1944.

fdr-s-wartime-leadership.context_blurb: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was the thirty-second president of the United States, elected to an unprecedented four terms. He led the United States through two of the greatest crises in American history — the Great Depression of the 1930s and the Second World War — and his twelve-year presidency, from 1933 to his death in April 1945, reshaped the role of the American federal government and the position of the United States in the world. During the war, Roosevelt worked closely with Winston Churchill (and more warily with Joseph Stalin) in the leadership of the anti-Axis alliance. He directed enormous American industrial mobilization — the production of ships, aircraft, tanks, and munitions on a scale no one had previously imagined possible — which was arguably the single greatest contribution the United States made to the Allied victory. He launched the top-secret Manhattan Project to develop atomic weapons. He also made serious mistakes, including the mass internment of Japanese Americans on the West Coast in 1942 and acquiescence to Stalin's growing control of Eastern Europe at the 1945 Yalta Conference. Roosevelt died of a cerebral hemorrhage in April 1945, less than a month before the German surrender, leaving his vice president Harry S. Truman to finish the war.

federalist-papers-hamilton-madison-jay.context_blurb: The Federalist Papers are a series of eighty-five essays published in New York newspapers under the pen name Publius between October 1787 and August 1788, during the ratification debates over the proposed United States Constitution. They were written by three authors: Alexander Hamilton, who wrote the majority; James Madison, who wrote some of the most important ones; and John Jay, who contributed a smaller number before illness interrupted his work. The essays laid out, from the inside, a detailed defense and interpretation of the Constitution: why its particular structure of separated powers, checks and balances, and limited enumerated federal authority was supposed to work, what dangers it was designed to prevent, and why the Anti-Federalist objections (which were serious) could be answered. Taken together, the Federalist Papers are probably the single greatest work of political philosophy ever produced in the United States, and the United States Supreme Court still quotes them regularly when interpreting the Constitution, which gives them a continuing legal weight few other founding-era writings possess. They were collected and published as a book during the ratification period and have never gone out of print. The names of the real authors became publicly known within a few years, though the authorship of a few essays is still debated.

feudalism-lords-vassals-fiefs.context_blurb: After the Carolingian empire broke apart in the 9th century, Europe reorganized itself not around a central state but around a web of personal promises between warrior-landholders. A lesser man would kneel in front of a greater one, place his hands between the greater man's hands, swear a solemn oath, and in return receive a grant of land that would feed him and his household. The land came with duties, especially the duty to bring armed men when summoned for war and to serve a fixed number of days on campaign each year, and the whole system ran on sworn trust rather than on paperwork or a civil service. Peasants worked the land underneath this pyramid. Above the ordinary knights stood counts, dukes, and finally kings. Over time this system developed careful customs about how long a vassal had to serve, what he owed instead if he wanted to buy his way out of fighting, what counted as breaking the oath, and how disputes between vassals were to be settled. The story covers the loyalties, the symbols, and the loopholes of this strange arrangement, and the moment in English history when the whole chain of promises, from the lowest knight to the highest earl, was quietly turned to point in the end at a single royal name.

fijian-ritual-cannibalism-its-end-at-chr.context_blurb: Across the islands of Fiji in the central South Pacific, ritualized cannibalism — the eating of defeated enemies as part of specific ceremonies after battle — was a well-documented part of pre-contact Fijian culture well into the 19th century. The practice was not casual; it was wrapped in strict ritual, performed by specific chiefs, and tied to warrior honor, revenge, and spiritual belief. Early Western visitors, including Methodist and Wesleyan missionaries who arrived from the 1830s onward, encountered the practice directly and recorded many firsthand accounts of specific cannibal feasts. European and American sailors wrecked in Fijian waters sometimes ended up at those feasts as the main course. In 1854, a powerful Fijian chief named Cakobau, who had controlled much of eastern Fiji, formally converted to Christianity and ordered his people to abandon the practice; other Fijian chiefdoms followed over the next generation. The last confirmed ritual cannibal killing in Fiji was in 1867, when the Reverend Thomas Baker and seven of his companions were killed and eaten after offending a chief by touching his head. In 2003, a modern descendant of the village involved held a public ceremony of apology to the descendants of the dead missionary. The transformation of Fijian society from the one to the other was accomplished largely by Christian conversion within a single generation.

first-political-parties-federalists-vs-d.context_blurb: The men who founded the United States were suspicious of political parties, which they called factions, and which they associated with civil strife in classical and English history. George Washington in his Farewell Address warned the country sternly against them. The first political parties in American history nonetheless developed anyway, inside Washington's own administration, out of a sharp disagreement over domestic economic policy and over how closely the new country should align with Britain or with revolutionary France. Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton favored a national bank, federal assumption of state debts, protective tariffs, and friendlier relations with Britain. Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and his close ally Representative James Madison opposed all of these. The Hamilton faction grew into the Federalist Party; the Jefferson-Madison faction grew into the Democratic-Republican Party. By the mid-1790s each had organized newspapers, state networks, and local committees. The Federalists elected Adams in 1796 and lost the presidency to Jefferson in 1800. The Federalist Party faded over the following two decades and died in the 1820s, leaving the Democratic-Republicans briefly as the only national party before they too fragmented. The two-party pattern they founded, however, has survived every subsequent realignment in American politics.

fleming-and-the-discovery-of-penicillin.context_blurb: Alexander Fleming was a Scottish bacteriologist working at St Mary's Hospital in London in the late 1920s. He had served as a battlefield doctor in the First World War, where he had watched men die of infected wounds that no medicine of the day could touch, and he spent the rest of his career hunting for substances that would stop bacteria without poisoning the patient. He was also, by many accounts, a famously untidy laboratory housekeeper. In September 1928, after returning from a holiday, he began sorting through a stack of forgotten culture plates on his bench and noticed something unexpected on one of them: a stray spot of blue-green mould had settled onto a dish of staph bacteria, with an unusual effect on the dish nearby that caught his attention. Fleming published his observation and worked on the substance for a while, but he could not purify enough of it to prove it would work in human beings, and the whole thing was nearly forgotten. More than a decade later, a team of researchers at Oxford picked up his old paper and turned his curious discovery into a real drug in time for the Second World War. By the end of the war penicillin was saving tens of thousands of Allied soldiers a month. The 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine was shared between Fleming and the two Oxford men chiefly responsible for the drug. Fleming himself always insisted the discovery had been pure luck noticed by a prepared mind.

florence-nightingale-and-modern-nursing.context_blurb: Florence Nightingale was an upper-class Englishwoman born in 1820 who, against her wealthy family's wishes, trained as a nurse and in 1854 led a small corps of nurses to a British military hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War. She found a place where more soldiers were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery than of their actual battle wounds — the wards were filthy, the sewers backed up, and the hospital was in effect killing the men brought into it. Over the following year she drove through a transformation of sanitation, record-keeping, and ward discipline that drastically cut the death rate. Back home in Britain she became a national hero, and spent the next fifty years, often from her sickbed, writing, calculating, and pushing reform of hospitals, army medicine, and nurse training. The questions ahead cover the romantic image soldiers brought home of her moving through the wards, and the pioneering way she chose to present her hard statistical findings to a hurried, mostly innumerate Parliament. It matters because Nightingale is one of the founders of modern nursing as a profession, one of the founders of modern hospital hygiene, and one of the first people in Britain to use statistical graphics seriously to drive policy.

foreign-allies-lafayette-von-steuben-fra.context_blurb: The American Revolution was not won by Americans alone. Foreign allies — some arriving as volunteers, some as formally allied national armies — were critical to American victory, and three in particular deserve special mention. The Marquis de Lafayette was a very young French aristocrat who arrived in America in 1777 on his own initiative, served as a general in Washington's Continental Army, became a close personal friend and almost adopted son to Washington, fought with distinction in several key campaigns, and spent the rest of his long life as the great transatlantic symbol of French-American friendship. Baron Friedrich von Steuben was a professional Prussian officer who arrived at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777 to 1778 and, over the following months, drilled the ragged Continental Army into a disciplined fighting force along European lines. France itself formally allied with the United States in 1778 after the American victory at Saratoga suggested the rebellion might succeed, and the French navy, French money, and French soldiers were central to the final victory at Yorktown in 1781. Spain and the Dutch Republic also joined the war against Britain, which stretched British resources thin globally. The Revolution was in the end a world war in which the Americans had better allies than their enemies did.

fort-sumter-and-the-outbreak-of-the-civi.context_blurb: Fort Sumter was a brick federal fort built on an artificial island at the mouth of Charleston Harbor, South Carolina. When South Carolina and six other Deep South states seceded in the winter of 1860-1861, Major Robert Anderson, the U.S. Army officer in command of the harbor's defenses, quietly moved his small garrison out to Sumter because he judged it the most defensible of the federal positions. Across the harbor, Confederate authorities under General P. G. T. Beauregard demanded he surrender. On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns opened fire. For about thirty-four hours they battered the fort while a growing crowd of Charlestonians watched from rooftops; Anderson's men held out, running low on food and powder, until he surrendered honorably and marched his garrison out under a salute. The questions ahead cover the specialized ammunition the Confederate batteries used to set the fort's wooden interiors on fire, the single Union soldier killed in the whole engagement under notably bitter circumstances, and the striking way Anderson's personal story reached its public bookend four years later. It matters because the bombardment of Sumter was the opening shot of the American Civil War — a war that would decide whether the United States survived as one country and whether slavery survived in it.

founding-of-tenochtitlan-eagle-on-the-ca.context_blurb: According to the Aztecs' own origin story, their ancestors wandered south out of a mythical northern homeland called Aztlan under the guidance of their patron war god, who promised them that they would know the place to settle when they saw a particular sign. The sign came in the early 14th century on a small marshy island in the great shallow lake in the Valley of Mexico, where they saw a particular bird perched on a cactus devouring a serpent. The Aztecs took the sign at its word, waded ashore, and founded the city of Tenochtitlan on that island in 1325. Over the next two centuries they expanded their city outward across the lake on artificial causeways, drained and built up more land, and turned Tenochtitlan into the capital of a tributary empire that controlled most of central Mexico by the time the Spanish arrived. The founding scene is still the central image on the modern Mexican flag today, where the same bird on the same cactus devouring the same snake is spelled out in detail, which is one of the clearest examples of a modern nation telling its old pre-conquest story about itself as a founding memory.

founding-of-the-united-nations-1945.context_blurb: The United Nations is an international political organization founded in October 1945, in the aftermath of the Second World War, to try to prevent future wars of the kind that had just killed roughly sixty million people and devastated three continents. Its founding treaty was negotiated by representatives of fifty allied governments at a conference in San Francisco during the final months of the war. The organization was designed to replace the earlier failed League of Nations that had been set up after World War I and had collapsed during the 1930s. The UN was structured with a General Assembly in which all member states have one vote and a Security Council on which five permanent members (the United States, the Soviet Union/Russia, Britain, France, and China) hold vetoes. The permanent-member veto has often paralyzed the Council on major disputes, which is both the UN's deepest structural weakness and the compromise that made the great powers willing to join at all. The UN headquarters is in New York, on land donated by John D. Rockefeller Jr. Its original fifty-one member states have grown to nearly two hundred. Its record over eighty years is mixed, with real humanitarian and peacekeeping achievements and some conspicuous failures to prevent genocide.

four-great-inventions-paper-printing-com.context_blurb: Chinese civilization produced a set of foundational inventions during the medieval and early modern periods that are often referred to in short as the Four Great Inventions. All of them reached Europe only centuries after they had become routine in China, and all of them substantially reshaped the world after they did. The oldest was a cheap writing material made from pulped plant fibers suspended in water, patented in modified form by a court eunuch during the Han dynasty in AD 105; it slowly displaced papyrus, parchment, and bamboo strips across Eurasia. The next was block printing of texts, developed under the Tang dynasty well before the year 1000 and used to mass-produce Buddhist sutras, calendars, and almanacs centuries before Gutenberg; movable-type printing was later invented in Song China in the 11th century. The third was the use of magnetized needles for direction-finding, developed in China by the 11th century and in use for Chinese shipping before it reached European sailors. The fourth was a mixture of saltpeter, charcoal, and sulfur originally developed by Daoist alchemists hunting for an elixir of immortality and then weaponized as flaming projectiles and rockets by the 10th century, long before Europe had seen anything like it. The four together quietly reshaped the medieval and early modern world.

franco-prussian-war-and-the-capture-at-s.context_blurb: The Franco-Prussian War, fought from the summer of 1870 into the spring of 1871, pitted the French Second Empire of Napoleon III against the growing north-German coalition led by Prussia and its chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Bismarck wanted a war that would weld the remaining southern German states into a single German Empire under the Prussian king, and he carefully arranged a diplomatic quarrel designed to let France declare war first. The French army of the day was still thought to be the finest in Europe; it was not. Prussian railroads, Prussian artillery, and the Prussian general staff mobilized faster and more effectively, and within a few weeks the French field armies were trapped and shattered. The decisive encirclement came at a small Belgian-border town called Sedan at the beginning of September. The questions ahead cover what happened at Sedan — a battlefield event unprecedented in modern European history — and then the astonishing setting Bismarck chose a few months later for the ceremony founding the new German Empire. It matters because that short war ended one European political order and launched another: it killed the Second French Empire, launched the French Third Republic, created a united Germany, and planted the resentments that would haunt Europe through the First World War.

frederick-douglass-and-the-abolitionists.context_blurb: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery on a Maryland plantation around 1818 and became, by his death in 1895, the most famous Black American of the nineteenth century. He taught himself to read as a boy, escaped from slavery as a young man and made his way north, married his fiancee the week he reached freedom, and launched a public life as an abolitionist speaker, newspaper editor, memoirist, and advisor to presidents. He toured the United States and Britain lecturing against slavery; wrote three autobiographies that are still read; recruited Black soldiers for the Union during the Civil War; argued face-to-face with Abraham Lincoln about the rights of those soldiers; and spent his later decades fighting for Black voting rights, for women's suffrage, and against the terror of the post-Reconstruction South. The questions ahead walk through moments from his life — his birthday, the ingenious ways he learned to read, the little books and poems that shaped him, the risky method of his escape, the fight that he said turned him from a crushed boy into a man, his insistence on being photographed with a defiant face, and his famous Fourth of July speech. It also covers his lasting answer to the question of whether Americans should turn away from their founding documents or press those documents to live up to their words. It matters because Douglass became the clearest American voice arguing that the country's promises were worth keeping — and that keeping them meant abolition and full equal citizenship.

galileo-and-the-telescope.context_blurb: Galileo Galilei was a 17th-century Italian mathematician and professor who, in the autumn of 1609, heard about a new Dutch invention called a spyglass and quickly built a much better one of his own. He turned it toward the night sky and became the first human being to see things in the heavens that nobody had ever seen before. What he saw forced him to argue publicly that the Earth really does go around the Sun, which the Catholic Church of his day considered a dangerous theological claim. He eventually fell afoul of the Inquisition, was tried in Rome in 1633, and spent the rest of his life under house arrest at his villa outside Florence. During those final years, going blind, he quietly wrote the book that founded modern physics. Galileo could be brilliant, funny, vain, and sharp-tongued all at once; he made enemies as easily as he made breakthroughs. He died in 1642, the year Newton was born. His story became the enduring symbol of a lonely scientist against the authorities, which is true as far as it goes but hides how much his trial was also about his personality and the politics of his age.

galileo-the-telescope.context_blurb: Galileo Galilei was a 17th-century Italian mathematician who became one of the first serious users of a new Dutch invention: a tube with lenses in it that made far-away things look near. In 1609 he built his own version, improved it dramatically, and spent the following months pointing it up at the night sky. What he saw there overturned the astronomy that European universities had taught for nineteen hundred years. He published his first observations in a short book that caused an immediate sensation across Europe, and he spent the next twenty years defending the picture of the heavens he had seen through his lenses. His great trouble began when he published a longer book in 1632 presenting his astronomy as a lively conversation between three characters, one of whom was a slow-witted supporter of the old system. The Church turned sharply against him. The Roman Inquisition tried him, forced him to recant some of what he had taught, and placed him under house arrest for the rest of his life. He kept quietly working, nearly blind by the end, and died in 1642. The Church would eventually acknowledge that he had been right, long after everyone else had already come around.

gallipoli-campaign.context_blurb: The Gallipoli campaign, launched in April 1915, was a bold attempt by Britain and France to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war by forcing a naval route through the Dardanelles strait to Constantinople. When British warships failed to break through the Turkish mines and shore guns, the Allies landed troops on the rocky peninsula instead — British, Irish, French, and above all Australian and New Zealand soldiers (the Anzacs) scrambled ashore under withering fire and dug into cliffs they could not get off. The Ottoman defense was commanded on the ground by a young colonel named Mustafa Kemal, who would later become Ataturk, the founder of modern Turkey, and whose decisive leadership in the first terrible hours of the invasion made him a national hero. For nine terrible months the two sides stalemated in trenches on the hillsides until the Allies finally gave up and pulled their men off the peninsula at night, in a quietly brilliant evacuation that the Turks across the way did not detect until it was over. Gallipoli became a founding story for Australia and New Zealand, where April 25, Anzac Day, is still a national day of remembrance, and for Turkey, where it is remembered as the birthplace of the modern nation.

gandhi-and-indian-independence-movement.context_blurb: Mohandas K. Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915 and over the next thirty years built the most important nonviolent political movement of modern history. Trained as a British lawyer, he had already developed in South Africa a method of mass civil disobedience he called by a Sanskrit name he coined himself, and in India he turned the method against the British Raj. His great early campaign came in 1930, when he led a long march to the Indian seacoast to challenge a British monopoly tax that affected every Indian household. The British jailed tens of thousands and later beat Indian protesters bloody at Dharasana, where an American reporter named Webb Miller cabled home scenes of unresisting Indians being clubbed to the ground, scenes that helped turn world opinion against the Raj. Gandhi was assassinated in 1948 by a Hindu nationalist, a few months after India finally won her independence, but his method would travel: Martin Luther King Jr. would carry it to the American South, and Nelson Mandela would carry it back to the country Gandhi had first learned it in. The Partition that accompanied Indian independence split British India into India and Pakistan and triggered one of the largest and most violent population movements in modern history, something Gandhi himself spent his last months walking from village to village trying to calm.

gandhi-nonviolent-independence.context_blurb: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869 to 1948) was an Indian lawyer who trained in London, worked for years as a civil-rights lawyer for Indian immigrants in South Africa, and returned to India in 1915 to become the central moral and political leader of the Indian independence movement against British colonial rule. Gandhi developed and taught a philosophy of mass nonviolent resistance that he called satyagraha, meaning the force of truth, drawing on Hindu, Jain, and Christian ethical sources along with modern Western influences like Henry David Thoreau. Over three decades of campaigning he led huge nonviolent protests against British taxation, salt monopolies, and discriminatory laws, was repeatedly jailed, fasted dramatically in protest, and became an international symbol of principled resistance. His moral authority, together with British exhaustion after the Second World War, helped bring an end to British rule in India in 1947. He was not able to prevent the catastrophic partition of the subcontinent along religious lines, which he had bitterly opposed, and his campaigns against communal violence between Hindus and Muslims after independence put his own life in danger. He was assassinated in Delhi in January 1948 by a Hindu nationalist. His influence on 20th-century movements for civil rights, decolonization, and peace reached far beyond India.

genghis-khan-the-mongol-empire.context_blurb: Genghis Khan — originally named Temujin — was a 13th-century Mongolian chieftain who unified the fractured tribes of the Mongolian steppe through a combination of personal charisma, political skill, and ruthless violence, and then launched his unified Mongol army on the most devastating sequence of military conquests in human history. Over roughly two decades of personal campaigning from 1206 to his death in 1227, he brought northern China, Central Asia, and much of Persia under Mongol control. His sons and grandsons continued the work, conquering the rest of China, the Islamic Middle East, Russia, and parts of Eastern Europe over the following half century, building the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled. The campaigns killed many millions of people — exact numbers are impossible, but estimates range into the tens of millions in direct killings and famines — and often depopulated entire regions. The Mongols also opened up Eurasia to long-distance trade and travel in a period called the Pax Mongolica, during which goods and ideas (and probably the Black Death) flowed on a scale not seen before. Genghis Khan's direct genetic descendants include a significant fraction of modern Central Asian men, which is one of the few truly measurable long-term biological consequences of a single historical individual.

george-washington-general-and-first-pres.context_blurb: George Washington was a Virginia planter, surveyor, French and Indian War veteran, Virginia legislator, Continental Army commander, convention delegate, and first president of the United States. He was already an experienced colonial military officer when the Revolution broke out in 1775, and the Continental Congress chose him unanimously to command the new Continental Army, mostly because he was a Virginian and the Congress needed a southern general to lead what had so far been a New England rebellion. He commanded that army for the next eight years, losing most of his battles, but keeping the army in the field long enough for allies and circumstance to make an American victory possible. After the war he set a critical precedent by voluntarily surrendering his military commission to Congress — the Cincinnatus model — and retiring to his farm. In 1787 he was called back to preside over the Constitutional Convention, and in 1789 he was elected the first president of the new United States without opposition. He served two terms, deliberately refused a third, and set almost every precedent the office has carried since. He died in 1799 at Mount Vernon. He is the one founder nobody of any faction in American politics has ever really tried to tear down.

german-unification-bismarck-and-blood-an.context_blurb: Otto von Bismarck was the formidable Prussian prime minister and later chancellor who, between 1862 and 1871, forged the many separate German states into a single empire under the Prussian king. He is one of the great practitioners of what later writers called Realpolitik — a politics without sentiment, in which the question is never 'is this just?' but 'does this work?' Where his liberal opponents in the Prussian parliament hoped German unity would be achieved by speeches and constitutions, Bismarck believed it would be achieved by armies, railroads, and well-chosen wars. The questions ahead cover that famous phrase of his about speeches versus armies, the sequence of short wars he engineered to isolate and defeat the rivals who stood in Prussia's way, a key piece of military technology that gave Prussian infantry a decisive edge in those wars, the diplomatic trick that finally opened the war Bismarck wanted, and the mingled triumph and bitterness of the ceremony in which the new German Empire was proclaimed on captured French soil. It matters because the Germany Bismarck built reshaped Europe — industrially, militarily, and politically — and the kingdom-centered, army-centered way he built it set up tensions that would help drag the whole continent into world war fifty years later.

gettysburg-and-pickett-s-charge.context_blurb: Gettysburg was a three-day battle fought from July 1 through July 3, 1863, in rolling Pennsylvania farmland around a small market town of the same name. It came in the middle of a second Confederate invasion of the North, when Robert E. Lee led the Army of Northern Virginia across the Potomac hoping to force a decisive battle on Union soil, break Northern will, and perhaps gain European recognition for the Confederacy. The Union Army of the Potomac, now under George Meade, met him there almost by accident, and the fighting swelled day by day as more troops arrived on both sides. On the second day Union forces barely held a chain of hills south of the town — Little Round Top, Cemetery Ridge, Culp's Hill — through desperate close fighting; on the third, Lee gambled everything on a direct infantry assault across open ground against the center of the Union line, an attack usually called Pickett's Charge. It failed, Lee's army limped back to Virginia, and the Confederacy never again mounted a serious invasion of the North. The questions ahead walk through the ground, the generals, a famous act of regimental sacrifice, shouted orders, individual acts of courage by officers on both sides, and a bitter postwar quip. It matters because Gettysburg became both the costliest battle ever fought in the Western Hemisphere and the symbolic turning point of the Civil War.

giordano-bruno-burned-at-the-stake-1600.context_blurb: Giordano Bruno was a 16th-century Italian ex-Dominican friar, teacher, poet, and reckless speculator about the nature of the universe. He had entered the Dominican order as a young man in Naples but repeatedly ran into trouble with his superiors over his readings in forbidden philosophy, and he eventually fled his monastery and spent most of the rest of his life wandering across Europe. He taught in Paris, in Oxford, in Wittenberg, in Prague, and sometimes made bitter enemies in each city before moving on. He wrote strange, dense books in Italian and Latin arguing, among other things, that the stars were other suns and that the universe might go on without end — views that connected him in his readers' minds to the quiet Polish canon Copernicus, who had died fifty years before. In 1591 Bruno made the mistake of accepting a wealthy Venetian's invitation to teach him privately. The man denounced Bruno to the Venetian Inquisition, which handed him over to Rome, where he was held and interrogated for seven years. The sentence came down in February 1600 in a Roman piazza called the Campo de' Fiori, and Bruno was burned there publicly in the final days of that winter. He is often remembered as a martyr of science, though his actual trial covered many more matters than only his astronomy.

globalization-the-internet-age.context_blurb: In the final decades of the 20th century and the opening decades of the 21st, several linked trends radically accelerated the integration of the world economy and the world's communication systems. The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of the Cold War opened large parts of the planet to Western-style trade and investment. The expansion of containerized shipping, the deregulation of international finance, and the opening of previously closed economies (China under Deng Xiaoping, India under its 1991 reforms, Eastern Europe after communism) drove an enormous expansion of international trade. In parallel, the development of the Internet (originally a Pentagon research project in the 1960s), the invention of the World Wide Web by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989, and the subsequent commercial internet boom of the 1990s and the smartphone era of the 2000s put most of the world's population within a few years of each other into instant free-of-charge communication for the first time in human history. The gains have been enormous — the biggest reduction in extreme poverty in all of history has happened over this period — but globalization has also produced significant backlash in the developed world, including industrial decline in formerly manufacturing regions, cultural strains over immigration, and political realignments that are still shaking Western democracies.

gothic-cathedrals-chartres-notre-dame.context_blurb: In the 12th century, French master-masons began building churches that broke with everything older than themselves. They stacked their stones so cleverly that the walls could grow thin enough to pour sunlight through colored glass, and they used engineering tricks on the outside of the building to hold up the vast ceilings on the inside, so that the whole thing could stand up without the dark, heavy walls that older churches had needed. Towns gave decades of labor and small fortunes to raise them, and the great building sites were open workshops of carvers, glaziers, blacksmiths, and theologians, all working on a single enormous prayer in stone. The two most famous of these churches, in a cathedral town southwest of Paris and on an island in the river at the heart of Paris itself, became hubs of pilgrimage, learning, and civic pride. Their stained glass, their saints, their holy relics, their stone beasts, and the sheer height of their vaults were a Bible for people who could not read. Modern visitors can still read the glass and the sculpture and work out the stories a medieval worshipper would have known at a glance, and the buildings still have the power to stop a person at the door and make them look up.

gothic-cathedrals-chartres-notre-dame-2.context_blurb: The Gothic cathedral was the signature architectural achievement of medieval Europe, and the great wave of cathedral-building ran from the mid-12th century into the 14th across northern France, England, Germany, Spain, and much of the rest of Catholic Europe. The style was invented, in effect, by the French abbot Suger of Saint-Denis in the 1140s, with features whose combination had not been seen before: pointed arches that could handle thrust more flexibly than Romanesque round arches, ribbed stone vaults that let the roof weight fall on a few concentrated points, and external masonry supports that carried the thrust safely outward and down to the ground, letting the walls between become mostly glass. The result was interiors flooded with colored light from huge stained-glass windows, with soaring vertical lines pointing the eye and the soul upward. Cathedrals like Chartres, Reims, Amiens, Notre-Dame of Paris, Cologne, and Salisbury took generations to build. Each was a town's main public building, financial engine, and spiritual center at once. Many of them have survived, often with careful restoration after wars and fires. A fire in 2019 devastated Notre-Dame of Paris, and a public restoration campaign has reopened the building to visitors. The style eventually gave way to the Renaissance's return to classical forms.

goya-the-third-of-may-1808.context_blurb: Francisco de Goya y Lucientes (1746 to 1828) was a Spanish painter and printmaker who began his career as a successful court painter to the Spanish royal family under King Carlos III and Carlos IV, and ended it producing some of the darkest, most unflinching images of human violence ever committed to canvas or copper plate. In 1808 Napoleon's armies invaded Spain, and Goya lived through the subsequent six-year guerrilla war, in which the French occupation and Spanish civilian resistance produced appalling atrocities on both sides. After the war Goya produced a pair of enormous paintings commemorating a particular Madrid uprising on May 2, 1808, and the French reprisals on May 3; the second painting shows a line of French soldiers shooting Spanish civilians at point-blank range in a quarry at night, lit by a square lantern, with the central figure throwing his arms wide in a Christ-like pose. He also produced a devastating print series called The Disasters of War, which he kept privately and did not publish in his lifetime. Later in his life, going deaf and increasingly isolated, Goya covered the walls of a small farmhouse outside Madrid with a series of nightmarish paintings now called the Black Paintings. He was far ahead of his time, and the 20th century finally caught up to him.

grand-canal-of-china.context_blurb: The Grand Canal of China is the oldest and longest artificial waterway on Earth, a vast man-made river system that stretches over a thousand miles from the vicinity of Beijing in the north to Hangzhou in the south, linking several of China's great natural rivers running east into the sea. It was built in stages over many centuries, with the first segments cut during the Spring and Autumn period, dramatic early expansions under the Sui dynasty in the 7th century AD using huge forced-labor levies, and later connections and improvements under the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties. The Grand Canal transformed Chinese economic geography by letting the rice-growing south ship grain, textiles, and other goods north to supply the capital and the northern frontier armies on an industrial scale. The scale of the Sui-era construction effort was enormous — millions of laborers worked on it, with significant death rates — and it broke the Sui dynasty politically even as it built one of the most consequential pieces of infrastructure in human history. Large sections of the canal are still in commercial use today. In 2014 it was named a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the surviving stretches of ancient stone-lined canal and old locks and towpaths continue to draw visitors.

great-famine-in-ireland-and-the-age-of-m.context_blurb: The Great Famine of Ireland, which the Irish often simply call An Gorta Mor — the Great Hunger — struck between 1845 and 1852. Ireland was then part of the United Kingdom, ruled from London, and a very large share of its rural poor lived on tiny rented plots and ate little but potatoes. In 1845 a new disease of the potato arrived in Europe and spread rapidly, turning crops rotten in the field and in storage, and it returned year after year. During the famine years roughly a million people died — of hunger, of fevers that stalked the hungry, of exposure after being evicted from their cottages — and roughly another million emigrated, most of them to the United States and Canada. The questions ahead cover the biological cause of the blight, what happened to the people who left, a terrible year that passed into memory under its own grim name, nicknames the hungry gave the strange foreign relief foods they were offered, the ships that carried the emigrants, a famous eye-witness description from an English visitor, the moral debate historians still have about British policy, and a surprising act of solidarity from a Native American nation that had itself been forced along a trail of tears a decade earlier. It matters because the Famine permanently reshaped Ireland, launched one of the great migrations of modern history, and still colors Irish and British politics today.

great-mosque-of-cordoba.context_blurb: The Great Mosque of Cordoba, in the south of modern Spain, was built in stages beginning in the late 8th century AD on a site that had previously held a Visigothic Christian basilica. For over four hundred years, under the Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus and its successors, it was one of the largest and most important mosques in the Islamic world — a vast hall of prayer whose roof was supported by a forest of hundreds of columns and horseshoe-shaped double arches striped in red and white, giving the interior a strange rhythmic forest-like quality. The mihrab (prayer niche) in the back wall was decorated with golden Byzantine mosaic work sent as a diplomatic gift from the Christian emperor in Constantinople. After the Christian reconquest of Cordoba in 1236, the mosque was formally converted into a cathedral, but most of the Islamic structure was carefully kept, and the two religious traditions still coexist within the same walls today, where visitors move between the Islamic prayer hall and the Christian high altar inserted into the middle of it in the sixteenth century. The building is one of the clearest surviving monuments of the long centuries when Christians, Muslims, and Jews lived together on the Iberian peninsula, often uneasily but sometimes productively, in what is sometimes called the convivencia.

great-zimbabwe.context_blurb: Great Zimbabwe was a huge medieval African city in the high country of what is now the modern country that takes its name from the ruins, in southeastern Africa. The city flourished from roughly the 11th to the 15th centuries AD and may have housed as many as 20,000 people at its peak. Its builders were ancestors of the modern Shona people, and the site includes the largest ancient stone-walled complex in sub-Saharan Africa — curving walls of dry-fitted granite blocks up to five meters thick and ten meters tall, with a conical tower rising inside one of them. The city sat at the center of a long-distance trade in gold, ivory, cattle, iron, and copper, with networks reaching to the Swahili coast and from there by sea to Arabia, Persia, India, and China. Archaeologists have found Chinese Ming porcelain, Persian beads, and East African coral in the ruins. The city declined in the 15th century, probably because of exhausted local resources and shifting trade routes, and other Shona cities took its place farther north. European colonizers of the 1800s refused to believe Africans had built it, and spent decades inventing racist alternative theories; modern archaeology has long since confirmed its indigenous origin. The country of Zimbabwe is named for it, and so is the Great Enclosure's famous soapstone bird, which is the national emblem.

greek-alphabet-and-the-gift-of-vowels.context_blurb: The Greeks did not invent writing — the Phoenicians, their close trading partners across the eastern Mediterranean, had been using an alphabet of consonants for several centuries before the Greeks adopted and modified it, probably in the 8th century BC. But the Greeks made one small change that turned out to be a huge improvement. The Phoenician script had no letters for vowels; a reader had to supply them from context, which worked well enough for Semitic languages but was awkward for Greek. The Greeks took several Phoenician letters whose sounds Greek did not need and reassigned them to represent vowel sounds. The result was the world's first alphabet that could unambiguously spell out any spoken word, consonants and vowels alike, and it is the common ancestor of every alphabet now in use across Europe and the Americas, including Latin, Cyrillic, and English. The ancestry runs the names of the letters: alpha, beta, gamma — our alphabet. It is one of those small ancient inventions that quietly reshaped the whole future, because an easy-to-learn phonetic alphabet made literacy spread much farther and faster than it had ever spread in older civilizations.

greek-architecture-doric-ionic-corinthia.context_blurb: The classical Greek temple is one of the most-copied building forms in human history, and the specific vocabulary of columns, capitals, and friezes that Greek architects worked out between the 7th and 5th centuries BC is still being used by builders today. The Greeks developed three main architectural orders, each with its own column proportions, its own capital design at the top, and its own moldings. The oldest and plainest was favored in mainland Greece and in Sicily, with sturdy fluted columns and a severely simple capital. A more slender and graceful variant arose in the Greek cities of Asia Minor, with a famous spiral curl at the top of the column. The newest and most elaborate variant was developed in the classical period, with a capital carved to look like a basket wreathed in curling leaves. All three orders were taken over by the Romans, who then used them on nearly every public building they erected across their empire. Through the Romans, the orders entered the Renaissance, the Neoclassical movement, and the modern Western public-building tradition, which is why banks, courthouses, museums, and legislatures all over the world still look vaguely like Greek temples two and a half thousand years later.

greek-fire.context_blurb: The Byzantines had a sticky, flammable liquid — a kind of ancient napalm — that clung to whatever it touched and kept burning even on water, which made it devastating in naval battles when it was sprayed from siphons mounted on the prows of their warships. Its invention is credited to a Syrian architect-engineer named Kallinikos who defected to the empire with the formula around 672, and the Byzantine fleet rapidly adopted it as the terrifying centerpiece of their naval tactics. The emperors guarded the recipe so fiercely — on pain of death to any sailor or engineer who revealed it — that it was never written down in a complete form, and the exact mixture is still argued over by historians today. Twice, in 677 and 717, this weapon saved Constantinople from huge Arab fleets that would almost certainly have taken the city otherwise, and the memory of their burning ships became a lasting warning against attacking the Queen of Cities from the sea. The surviving descriptions suggest something like a mixture of naphtha, quicklime, and sulfur under pressure, but no modern chemist has fully reconstructed it from the fragments that come down to us — a rare case of an ancient technology genuinely lost rather than merely improved on.

greek-mythology-the-twelve-olympians.context_blurb: Greek religion did not have a single sacred book, a single founding prophet, or a central religious authority, but it did have a rich shared body of stories about a family of gods who were imagined to live on top of a particular mountain in northern Greece. The gods were pictured as a quarrelsome extended family under the king of the gods, with his queen; his brothers who ruled the sea and the underworld; his sons and daughters who patronized war, wisdom, hunting, art, poetry, metalwork, love, messaging, and travel; and various other divine siblings and cousins. Each god had his or her favorite shrine, local titles, festivals, and myths. The Greek stories about these gods were retold by the great poets Homer and Hesiod and dramatized by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, which is why their names and their stories survived long after the religion itself had been quietly replaced by Christianity. The Romans later identified their own gods with the Greek ones under Latin names, and the whole combined collection has provided more raw material for Western poetry, drama, painting, and sculpture than any other religious tradition except Christianity.

greek-myths-and-heroes-heracles-theseus-.context_blurb: In Greek mythology, in the generations between the gods and the Trojan War, the Greek world was told to have been full of heroes — half-divine men born to gods and mortal women — who went on long adventures, killed monsters, founded cities, and generally kept the earlier chaos of the world at bay. A hero known for enormous strength was sent out by a rival king to perform a famous list of impossible labors, including slaying a giant lion, cleaning filthy stables, capturing a hound of the underworld, and fetching golden apples from the ends of the earth. Another hero, the king of Athens in legend, slew a monstrous half-man half-bull creature on the island of Crete in a labyrinth built by a famous craftsman. A third hero flew home from the same island on wings his father had built out of feathers and wax, and died when he climbed too close to the Sun. Another, with the help of various divine gifts, killed a snake-haired monster whose gaze turned men to stone. These stories were old and well-worn by the time the Greek poets fixed them in writing, and most of them have been retold constantly ever since.

greek-natural-philosophy-the-first-searc.context_blurb: Starting in the 6th century BC in the Greek-speaking cities along the coast of what is now western Turkey, a handful of thinkers took a step that nobody in the ancient Near East had quite taken before. They began to try to explain the natural world not by telling stories about gods, but by looking for ordinary natural causes and reasoning about them with arguments. One of the first, a man of Miletus, proposed that everything is ultimately made of water. His successors argued for other candidates, or for underlying forces instead of substances. One imagined a mind directing nature; another suggested that reality is really made of tiny indivisible particles — atoms — moving through empty space, which turned out, two and a half thousand years later, to be strikingly close to the truth. These Presocratic philosophers, as they are now called, got many of the details wrong but established something more important than any particular theory: the idea that the natural world is one connected rational order that reasoning humans can hope to understand. Every later Greek philosopher, from Socrates onward, was reacting to them, and the Scientific Revolution of the 1600s picked up the project the Milesians had started.

greek-theater-tragedy-and-comedy-sophocl.context_blurb: Classical Greek theater grew out of religious festivals held in the city of Athens in honor of the god of wine and ecstasy. In the 5th century BC, during the great period of Athenian democracy and empire, Athenian playwrights wrote and staged tragedies and comedies that are still being performed today, two and a half thousand years later. The theaters were huge stone or packed-earth open-air amphitheaters built into the sides of hills, holding thousands of spectators who could hear a single actor speaking at normal volume from the center of the stone circle. The great tragic playwrights wrote plays about myth — about kings who gouge out their own eyes when they discover what they have done, or about queens who murder their husbands and are murdered in turn by their children. The comic playwrights wrote plays about politicians, intellectuals, foreign ambassadors, and the quarrels of daily Athenian life, often with the raunch and politically pointed cruelty of a modern late-night comedy show. Taken together, these plays founded Western drama, and the words tragedy and comedy both come to us directly out of this moment in classical Athens.

greek-war-of-independence.context_blurb: The Greek War of Independence was a long, bloody revolt that broke out in 1821 and ended, after nearly a decade of fighting, massacres on both sides, and great-power intervention, with the recognition of an independent Greek state in 1832. The Greek-speaking Orthodox Christian population of the eastern Mediterranean had lived under Ottoman rule for roughly four centuries, and in the age of nationalism they rose to try to reclaim a political home of their own. Across Europe their cause caught fire among educated Westerners who had grown up reading Homer and Thucydides — a movement called Philhellenism — and private volunteers, writers, and donors streamed to the Greek side, including the English poet Lord Byron, who died of a fever in a besieged Greek town. The questions ahead cover that famous Western casualty and the strange chance beginning of a decisive sea battle in which an allied fleet of British, French, and Russian warships came to the Greeks' aid and shattered the Ottoman navy. It matters because this was the first successful national independence movement in nineteenth-century Europe, the first time the great powers intervened to carve out a new country in the name of nationality, and the opening of what historians call the long collapse of the Ottoman Empire.

gregorian-chant-and-medieval-sacred-musi.context_blurb: Gregorian chant, the single-line unaccompanied Latin chant sung in medieval Western Christian liturgy, is the oldest body of Western music that has come down to us in a continuously-performed tradition. It is named after Pope Gregory the Great, who ruled from 590 to 604 and was legendarily credited (probably by later generations) with codifying the chant tradition, though most of the actual compilation seems to have been done over the following three centuries. By the Carolingian period of Charlemagne, Gregorian chant had become the standard liturgical music of the Western Church, slowly replacing or displacing earlier regional traditions. Monks and nuns in monasteries across Western Europe sang the full daily cycle of the Divine Office — eight services at specific hours of day and night — for over a thousand years, which means that for many centuries somewhere in Europe at every hour of every day someone was singing some portion of this body of music. Early musical notation evolved precisely to help singers learn and preserve these chants. From Gregorian chant grew medieval polyphony, Renaissance choral music, and most of the Western classical tradition. Modern revival movements, especially in the late 20th century, brought monastic chant back onto popular recordings, and the Benedictine monks of Santo Domingo de Silos surprised everyone with a chart-topping chant album in 1994.

guadalcanal-campaign.context_blurb: The Guadalcanal Campaign was the first major American offensive operation of the Pacific War. It ran from August 1942 to February 1943 on and around a jungle island in the southern Solomon Islands, which the Japanese had begun to use as a base to threaten Australian supply lines. The United States Marines landed on Guadalcanal in August 1942 and seized a half-built Japanese airfield, which they completed and used as a base for American aircraft. The following six months of fighting was ferocious. The Japanese and Americans fought a series of brutal land battles for the airfield, several large and costly night-naval battles for control of the surrounding sea lanes (the stretch of water nicknamed Ironbottom Sound for the number of ships sunk in it), and almost continuous air combat. The jungle, malaria, dysentery, and extreme supply difficulties killed and wounded almost as many Americans as combat did. The Americans eventually prevailed, holding the airfield and starving out the Japanese ground forces, and the Japanese quietly evacuated their surviving troops in February 1943. Guadalcanal demonstrated that American ground forces could beat Japanese infantry in sustained combat and set the pattern for the long slog of the Pacific War.

gunpowder-empires-concept.context_blurb: Historians use the phrase 'gunpowder empires' for a cluster of giant states that rose across Eurasia in the 1400s and 1500s because rulers now had a weapon powerful enough to change the political math of the medieval world. The decisive moment came at the Ottoman siege of Constantinople in 1453, when Sultan Mehmed II hired a Hungarian engineer named Orban to build siege weapons that were huge even by modern standards. Walls that had stood for a thousand years cracked in weeks. Once a monarch could do that to any local lord's fortress, the balance of power inside a kingdom tilted sharply, and over the next century rulers from Istanbul to Isfahan to Delhi to Paris reshaped the political order of their realms around that new fact. The same technology that cracked the ancient walls of Constantinople helped the Ottomans, the Safavids of Persia, and the Mughals of India stitch together enormous multi-ethnic states, and it reshaped Europe's monarchies in parallel. It is one of the clearest cases in history of a single technology rearranging the political map. For about two centuries these new centralized states dwarfed anything that had existed in Europe or the Islamic world before, and their legal, military, and bureaucratic habits shaped the countries that eventually grew out of them.

gupta-empire-india-s-golden-age.context_blurb: The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern India from roughly AD 320 to 550 and is traditionally called the Golden Age of classical Indian civilization. Founded by Chandragupta I (not to be confused with the earlier Mauryan Chandragupta), the Gupta state unified much of the Indo-Gangetic plain under a well-run administration with a stable gold coinage, patronized Hindu religion while remaining tolerant of Buddhism and Jainism, and oversaw an extraordinary flowering of culture. Classical Sanskrit literature reached heights it never again matched: the playwright and poet Kalidasa, often compared to Shakespeare in the Indian tradition, lived during this era.
