Indian astronomers like Aryabhata developed a sophisticated solar-centered picture of the planets, calculated pi to several decimal places, and worked out the daily rotation of the Earth. Indian mathematicians created a working decimal number system including the critical innovation of a symbol for zero, both of which would travel west centuries later through the Islamic world and reach Europe as the so-called Arabic numerals we still use. Gupta temple art set the enduring iconographic patterns for Hindu religious sculpture. The empire fragmented under invasion pressure from the White Huns in the 6th century, but its cultural achievements became the classical reference point for all later Indian civilization.

gutenberg-s-printing-press.context_blurb: Johannes Gutenberg was a goldsmith in the German city of Mainz who, in the 1440s and 50s, put together a cluster of older ideas — a wine-press, a soft metal alloy for casting type, oil-based ink, cheap rag paper — into one working system that could print pages far faster than any scribe could copy them. His great run of the mid-1450s was a two-volume Latin edition of a famous and expensive book, printed on fine materials to show the new craft at its most impressive. A single hand-copied version of that same book had taken a monk a year or more and cost a small fortune; Gutenberg's edition was still expensive, but it existed in bulk, and the price of books in general began to fall year by year after that. Gutenberg himself went broke in a lawsuit with his main investor, lost control of most of his equipment and finished product, and died in modest obscurity. Within fifty years of his breakthrough, printing shops had sprung up in every major European city, millions of books were in circulation, and the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and the Age of Exploration all leaned on the pamphlets, maps, and manuals that his invention made cheap.

gutenberg-s-printing-press-and-the-print.context_blurb: Around 1450, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg in the Rhineland city of Mainz combined several existing technologies — movable metal type, oil-based ink, a modified wine press — into a single invention that could produce identical pages of text much faster than any scribe. His workshop produced the famous Gutenberg Bible, a two-volume Latin Vulgate printed in several copies starting in 1455 that was the first substantial European book printed with movable type. The commercial venture itself went poorly, and Gutenberg lost his equipment to his financial backer in a lawsuit, dying poor in 1468. His invention, however, spread with astonishing speed. Within fifty years, printing presses were running in cities all across Europe, from Venice to London. The effects were enormous. The Bible, once a rare book copied by hand over months by monks, could now be printed in hundreds of copies at a time, and ordinary people could own one. Scientific findings traveled from laboratory to laboratory within weeks instead of generations. Pamphlets could set off reformations and revolutions. Martin Luther's protest against the Catholic Church would almost certainly have been crushed as a local disturbance in 1517 if the printing press had not scattered his words across Germany first.

gutenberg-s-printing-press-c-1450.context_blurb: In the mid-15th century, a German craftsman figured out how to combine three ideas, movable metal letters cast from a special alloy, a thick workable ink that would stick to those letters, and a press borrowed from an older trade, into a machine that could print identical pages faster than any team of scribes. His first great project was a lavish printing of the Bible in Latin, and it was so beautiful that early readers often mistook it for careful handwork. Within a generation the press had spread from his German hometown across Europe. Books that had cost a village's worth of harvest to copy became cheap enough for merchants and tradesmen, and ideas that one monk might have read in a lifetime could now reach a thousand minds in a season. The man himself ended up tangled in lawsuits with his business partner, lost control of his most valuable equipment to the courts, and died with little to show for his invention. But the machine he built lit the fuse under the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and almost every argument that followed. Today we know very little about him personally; the main hard evidence we have for his life is the paperwork of a dispute, not a signed book or any portrait made from the life.

gutenberg-the-printing-press.context_blurb: Johannes Gutenberg was a 15th-century German inventor whose printing press would hold its shape, with only small changes, for the next four hundred years. He was born in the city of Mainz around 1400, trained in a precise craft, and spent decades quietly experimenting with the technology of mass-produced books. European scribes had been copying every book by hand for a thousand years, which meant that even an ordinary volume was expensive and a long one was a treasure; Gutenberg wanted to break that. The famous book he produced on his new press in the 1450s is now one of the most valuable books in the world, and surviving copies are counted and tracked individually by scholars. Gutenberg himself, strangely, did badly out of the invention. His partner and financier, Johann Fust, sued him over an unpaid loan and won. The lawsuit was a serious blow, and Gutenberg died quietly in his home city in 1468. By then his technology was already escaping across the Alps and down the Rhine, and within a generation printing shops were producing books, pamphlets, and other paperwork in every major city of Europe — a revolution that would in short order make Luther's reformation unstoppable, change the shape of science, and remake the way ordinary people in the West read, argued, and prayed.

hadrian-s-wall-and-the-edges-of-empire.context_blurb: The emperor Hadrian ruled Rome from AD 117 to 138 and is remembered as the restless, cultured, and sharp-tempered emperor who travelled every province of the empire personally rather than ruling from Rome. On a visit to the far northern frontier in Britannia around AD 122 he ordered the construction of a stone wall across the whole width of northern England, from the North Sea to the Irish Sea, to mark the edge of Roman territory and police who could cross it. Garrisoned by Roman auxiliaries drawn from all over the empire, Hadrian's Wall ran for about eighty Roman miles, with forts, milecastles, and watchtowers along its length. Letters home from soldiers posted there — some of them discovered on wooden tablets at a fort called Vindolanda — give us one of our most human windows into Roman army life, with men complaining about the cold, asking for warm clothes from relatives, and comparing the local Britons unfavorably with civilized Mediterranean folk. The wall is one of the best-preserved frontier works of the ancient world and is still a tourist pilgrimage, striding across the moors of northern England.

hagia-sophia.context_blurb: Hagia Sophia was the greatest church in Christendom for close to a thousand years. The emperor Justinian built it in just under six years, between 532 and 537, after the previous church on the same site had burned in the Nika riots that nearly cost him his throne. The structure was engineered on an unprecedented scale, with a vast central dome made possible by curved triangular panels that let a round dome sit on a square base; the dome partly collapsed in an earthquake twenty years later and was rebuilt in a slightly different shape, but the building has stood through every disaster to strike Constantinople for the fifteen centuries since. After the Ottomans took the city in 1453, Hagia Sophia was converted to a mosque with minarets added at its corners; Ataturk's republic took it out of religious use in the 1930s, and in 2020 the Turkish government made it a working mosque once again. Visitors today can still find a Viking's name scratched into the marble balustrade in the gallery, left by a Scandinavian guardsman serving in the emperor's elite Varangian regiment many centuries ago — a reminder of how far the empire's reach stretched, and of how deeply Hagia Sophia impressed every traveler who ever stood under its dome, from Russian ambassadors to Western pilgrims to the Prophet's own distant successors.

haitian-revolution-and-toussaint-louvert.context_blurb: Saint-Domingue, the western third of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola, was in the late 1700s the richest colony in the world — a brutal sugar and coffee factory worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans under a smaller French planter class. In August 1791, inspired in part by the ideas of the French Revolution across the ocean, the enslaved population rose in a massive, coordinated revolt. Out of that first explosion a remarkable leader emerged — a formerly enslaved coachman named Toussaint Louverture, in his late forties, self-taught, literate, deeply Catholic, and a reader of Enlightenment classics. Over the next decade he outmaneuvered Spanish, British, and French armies, abolished slavery across the island, held colonial society together, and governed as an uneasy semi-independent lieutenant under the French flag. In 1802 Napoleon Bonaparte sent a huge army under his brother-in-law to re-impose slavery; Toussaint was tricked, arrested, shipped to a cold French prison in the Alps, and died there. His lieutenants fought on, defeated the French, and in 1804 proclaimed the independent Black republic of Haiti. The questions ahead cover the flag the revolutionaries made from France's own tricolor, the meaning of Toussaint's chosen surname, the books he read, his defiant words to his captors, and two striking downstream consequences of the Haitian victory — one that reshaped the map of North America, and a diplomatic condition France later imposed as the price of recognizing Haiti. It matters because the Haitian Revolution is the only successful slave revolution in history to found a nation, and because Western powers punished it for being that for the next two centuries.

hammurabi-s-code.context_blurb: Hammurabi was a Babylonian king who ruled from around 1792 to 1750 BC and who expanded his small kingdom into an empire that briefly dominated most of Mesopotamia. He is best remembered today for the law code inscribed on a tall stone pillar during his reign and discovered by French archaeologists at the Iranian site of Susa in 1901. The pillar is now in the Louvre in Paris. The code is not the earliest known legal document from the ancient Near East (earlier Sumerian codes exist), but it is the most complete and the most dramatically preserved. At the top of the pillar a relief shows Hammurabi standing before the Babylonian sun god Shamash, receiving the royal authority to administer justice. Below runs a long inscription in cuneiform setting out roughly 280 specific laws covering theft, assault, marriage, divorce, inheritance, agricultural wages, medical malpractice, construction standards, slavery, and much else. The famous eye-for-an-eye principle in several of its clauses is often summarized as the lex talionis, which Hebrew law later softened with the principle of equivalent compensation. Hammurabi's Code is one of the earliest surviving pieces of systematic written law and a foundational document in the ancient history of justice.

han-dynasty-the-silk-road-origins.context_blurb: The Han dynasty ruled a unified China from 202 BC to AD 220, in two long stretches separated by a brief usurpation, and is one of the formative periods in Chinese history — Han is still the name the ethnic Chinese majority uses for themselves today. Under the long and vigorous reign of the Emperor Wu in the 2nd and early 1st centuries BC, the Han state expanded dramatically in every direction: south into what is now Vietnam, northeast into what is now Korea, and especially west into the oasis city-states of Central Asia. The Han emperor sent a diplomat named Zhang Qian west on a mission of exploration into the Central Asian valleys in search of allies against the nomadic Xiongnu confederation on China's northern frontier, and Zhang Qian returned years later with the first systematic Chinese knowledge of the lands west of the Pamirs. Han silk began reaching the Mediterranean world through the resulting network of oasis routes within a few decades, and the long-distance Eurasian trade later nicknamed by 19th-century historians the Silk Road was essentially open for business. Chinese silk reached Rome; Roman and Persian goods reached China; Buddhism began traveling east along the same roads over the following few centuries.

han-tang-china-astronomers-chang-an-prin.context_blurb: The Han dynasty of 2nd-century BC through 2nd-century AD China and the Tang dynasty of the 7th through 10th centuries AD are generally considered the two great golden ages of imperial Chinese civilization, with a period of division and foreign rule in between. During the Han, Chinese astronomers kept careful records of eclipses and comets that modern astronomers still use, Chinese ironmongers invented cast iron more than a thousand years before Europe, and Chinese bureaucrats worked out a sophisticated examination system to select officials. The Tang capital of Chang'an grew into the largest city in the world of its day, with over a million people, foreign quarters for Persians, Jews, Nestorian Christians, Arabs, and Central Asians, and a riotous street life full of music, poetry, and horse-riding noblewomen. The Chinese printed books from carved woodblocks for the first time during the Tang and probably invented block printing centuries before Gutenberg. The precursors of gunpowder, developed by Daoist alchemists hunting for an elixir of immortality, show up in Chinese writing by the end of the Tang and would be weaponized under the following Song dynasty. Chinese inventions set the standard the rest of the Eurasian world had to catch up with until well into the Renaissance.

handel-messiah-and-the-hallelujah-chorus.context_blurb: George Frideric Handel (1685 to 1759) was a German composer, born the same year as Bach, who spent most of his working life in London and became the dominant composer of Georgian Britain. He wrote operas, oratorios, concertos, organ works, and ceremonial music for royal occasions including the famous Water Music and the Music for the Royal Fireworks. His greatest and most enduringly popular work is Messiah, an oratorio with libretto drawn from biblical texts about the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, which he composed in a legendary white-heat burst of about twenty-four days in the summer of 1741. It premiered in Dublin in 1742 and in London the following year. The oratorio contains a particular massive choral number toward the end of its middle section whose opening word has become one of the most instantly recognizable moments in all of Western music. Audience members have been standing up for this particular chorus since at least the London performances of the 1740s, following, according to tradition, the lead of King George II himself. Handel became a British subject in 1727, died a wealthy and honored man, and is buried in Westminster Abbey. Messiah is still performed somewhere in the English-speaking world almost every day of the year, especially around Christmas and Easter.

harriet-tubman-and-the-underground-railr.context_blurb: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery on Maryland's Eastern Shore around 1822, escaped to freedom in Philadelphia in 1849, and then — astonishingly — went back into the slave states again and again to lead others out. During the 1850s she worked as a conductor on the loose network of safe houses, free Black and white helpers, hidden routes, and clever disguises that abolitionists later called the Underground Railroad. Short, scarred from a childhood head injury inflicted by an overseer, suffering from spells she experienced as prophetic visions, armed with a pistol and a deep Christian faith, she was one of the single most effective rescuers in American history, and she was proud that she lost no one on her rescue missions. During the Civil War she worked as a scout, a spy, and a nurse for the Union army, and took part in a daring Union raid along the South Carolina coast that freed hundreds of enslaved people in a single night. The questions ahead cover her chosen biblical nickname, the name she was born with, the injury that marked her for life, her famous boast about her record, her rules for the people she led, the coded spirituals used on the road, how escapees quieted a crying infant, her military rank among the soldiers who knew her, her Civil War raid, a tool she carried for a late-life surgery done without anesthesia, a letter from Frederick Douglass about her, and the rough scale of her rescue work. It matters because Tubman's life became the standard American example of what one determined, poor, hunted person can do for others.

harun-al-rashid-and-the-1001-nights.context_blurb: Harun al-Rashid was the fifth Abbasid caliph, ruling in Baghdad from 786 to 809, during what later generations would remember as the golden age of the Islamic world. His court was legendary even in his own lifetime for its wealth, its scholars, and its diplomacy — he exchanged gifts with the Frankish emperor Charlemagne, including a remarkable animal that Charlemagne's court chronicler recorded with wonder, and his engineers built mechanical automata for his palace clock that fascinated visiting envoys. Later Arab storytellers made him the romantic hero of hundreds of tales in which the caliph wanders the streets of Baghdad in disguise to hear what his people are really saying, and those stories were eventually gathered — along with much older Persian and Indian material — into the great cycle called 'The Thousand and One Nights.' Not all of the Nights' most famous stories, though, come from the original Arabic — Aladdin and Ali Baba were added only after Antoine Galland translated the collection into French in the early 1700s, and they have no known earlier Arabic source. The real Harun was a serious ruler, more fierce than the storybook caliph in his own tales, but the legend has outlived the history and probably always will.

hatshepsut-the-female-pharaoh.context_blurb: Hatshepsut was a fifteenth-century BC Egyptian pharaoh who ruled during the Eighteenth Dynasty of the New Kingdom, in the period of Egypt's maximum imperial expansion. She was the daughter of Pharaoh Thutmose I, married her half-brother Thutmose II, and after his death served as regent for her stepson Thutmose III, who was still a child. Within a few years she took the full royal titulary for herself, had herself crowned as pharaoh in her own right, and ruled Egypt for about two decades as its ruling monarch, not merely a regent. She is depicted in Egyptian royal reliefs with the traditional male royal regalia — a false pharaoh's beard, a male royal kilt — in the standard Egyptian convention for pharaonic representation, which has caused some confusion over the centuries. Her reign was peaceful and prosperous, and she built a magnificent mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri on the west bank of the Nile across from Thebes that is still one of the architectural marvels of ancient Egypt. After her death her stepson Thutmose III, who had been shunted aside during her reign, attempted to erase her memory by chiseling her name and image off her monuments. Modern archaeology has largely restored her to history.

heian-japan-the-tale-of-genji.context_blurb: The Heian period of Japanese history, running from the end of the 8th century AD to roughly 1185, was named after the imperial capital at Heian-kyo (modern Kyoto). It was a quiet, cultured, Chinese-influenced age in which the Japanese imperial court developed one of the most refined literary and aesthetic civilizations in world history, mostly indoors and mostly on paper. Chinese writing had been imported from the mainland centuries earlier, but during the Heian period a parallel native syllabic script called kana developed, and women of the imperial court, who were not supposed to learn classical Chinese, used kana to write Japanese prose at a level of sophistication nobody in the world was then equaling. One Heian court lady, remembered as Murasaki Shikibu, wrote a long novel about the romantic and political adventures of a fictional Japanese prince named Genji, following his life, his lovers, his heirs, and the subtle emotional weather of his court across many hundreds of pages. It is one of the first great novels in world literature, written around AD 1000, roughly five hundred years before the European novel really existed. The Heian period ended in a civil war between rival military clans that ushered in the age of the samurai, but its literature survived.

henry-ford-and-the-assembly-line.context_blurb: Henry Ford was a Michigan farm boy who was gripped by the automobile from the moment he first saw one steaming past on a country road, and who, in middle age, set out to build a car cheap enough and tough enough for ordinary farmers and factory workers to own. His Model T, introduced in 1908, was that car. To make it affordable he kept redesigning not just the vehicle but the factory around it, borrowing ideas from meatpacking plants and from the overhead rails of flour mills, and bringing them together at his huge Highland Park plant outside Detroit. By 1913 he had the entire car moving past the men instead of the men moving around the car — a continuously flowing assembly line that cut the labour time per vehicle down by an order of magnitude. He also made headlines in 1914 by sharply raising the pay of his workers, roughly doubling the typical factory wage of the day, in a move that was partly idealism, partly a hard-nosed attempt to stop his workers from quitting out of boredom, and partly a plan to make them affluent enough to buy the cars they were building. He kept the Model T in production for nineteen years, selling more than fifteen million of them. In his later life he was also an angry crank, a notorious antisemite, and a reactionary paternalist who used his own private welfare office to pry into his employees' home lives. The modern consumer economy still bears his fingerprints.

henry-hudson-later-north-american-explor.context_blurb: After Columbus, dozens of European captains tried to find a way around or over the Americas to Asia, convinced the continent must have a short northern passage somewhere. Henry Hudson, an English captain sailing for the Dutch, pushed up a wide river on what became Manhattan Island and later into an enormous Canadian bay that bears his name. A later Arctic winter trapped his ship in ice, his men lost patience with him in a famous mutiny on the ice-shelf, and he was never seen alive again after they had their way. Francisco Vazquez de Coronado had led a huge Spanish expedition north from Mexico decades earlier, chasing rumors of fabulous cities, and found instead a long march through dry country whose actual inhabitants lived in a style that was striking in its own right but completely unlike what the storytellers had promised. Martin Frobisher dug up tons of what he thought was precious ore from Baffin Island and shipped it home to England, where metallurgists eventually broke the news that was waiting there. None of them found the shortcut to China, but between them they put most of the northern coast of North America on the map, and their failures became as famous in English and Spanish memory as any of the successful voyages further south.

henry-viii-the-english-reformation.context_blurb: Henry VIII was King of England from 1509 to 1547 and the royal center of the English Reformation. He came to the throne at eighteen, handsome, athletic, well-read, and devout, and early in his reign he wrote a book attacking Martin Luther, and his piety won him a special honorific from the pope that English monarchs still carry on their coins today. The great trouble of his reign began when his first wife, Catherine of Aragon, failed to produce a living son and Henry decided he needed to be rid of her. The pope refused to grant the annulment Henry demanded, so Henry simply broke with Rome, declared himself head of the Church in England, and married his pregnant mistress. He married six times over the course of his reign in all, and the fates of those six wives are so famous that English schoolchildren still memorize them as a short rhyme. The English Reformation he began was less about theology than about his marriage, but it reshaped England permanently. He dissolved the monasteries, seized their lands and their immense wealth, and executed any high official — including his old friend Thomas More and his once-trusted minister Thomas Cromwell — who would not fall in line. By the time he died in 1547, obese and infirm, he had left his young son Edward a Protestant church, a drained treasury, and an iron precedent that the king could rewrite religion by statute.

herodotus-the-father-of-history.context_blurb: Herodotus was a 5th-century BC Greek writer from the city of Halicarnassus on the coast of what is now southwestern Turkey. He wrote a long book, in nine volumes, called in English the Histories, telling the story of the great wars between the Greek city-states and the Persian Empire a generation before his own time. He is called the Father of History because he is the first writer we have who treats the task of history as something more than a chronicle or a myth — he gathers evidence, interviews people who had been alive during the events, visits distant countries, and tries to figure out why things happened the way they did. He also tells great stories, repeats legends he finds charming, and happily records information he says he does not believe but thinks is worth preserving. Later writers mocked him for including such material and sometimes called him the Father of Lies, but modern archaeology has quietly vindicated a great deal of what he wrote. His book is one of the most entertaining things to survive from the whole ancient world, with vivid portraits of Persian kings, Egyptian priests, Scythian horsemen, and ordinary Greek soldiers.

hieroglyphics.context_blurb: Hieroglyphics (the word is Greek for sacred carved letters) was the formal ceremonial writing system of ancient Egypt, used for roughly three thousand years from the late fourth millennium BC until the Christianization of Egypt in the Roman period. The system combined hundreds of pictorial signs, some of which stood for whole words, some for sound combinations, and some that served as determinatives clarifying which word was meant. It was used primarily on temple walls, royal monuments, religious texts, and tomb inscriptions. For everyday administrative use the Egyptians developed simpler cursive scripts — hieratic, used throughout dynastic history on papyrus, and later demotic, which replaced hieratic for everyday business. The knowledge of how to read hieroglyphics was lost when Egyptian paganism finally died out under Christianization in the fifth century AD, and for the next fourteen hundred years European and Arab scholars could stare at hieroglyphic inscriptions without understanding them. The script was finally deciphered by the French scholar Jean-Francois Champollion in 1822, working from the trilingual Rosetta Stone that French soldiers had discovered in Egypt in 1799. The decipherment opened up ancient Egyptian religion, royal history, literature, and daily life to systematic study for the first time in modern history.

hildegard-of-bingen-medieval-music.context_blurb: In 12th-century Germany, a brilliant and strong-willed abbess spent her long life writing music, theology, natural history, medicine, and letters to popes and emperors telling them what she thought they should do. She founded her own monastery for her nuns after years of pushing against a male superior who did not want to let them leave, and she composed a vast cycle of sung chant unlike anything else in medieval Europe, built around her striking visions of a living creation. She also wrote one of the earliest surviving musical plays, in which a soul in trouble contends with the virtues and with a tempter, and the choices she made about how to write that play tell us a great deal about how she thought about creation and about sin. She catalogued the healing uses of plants and stones. She invented her own private alphabet and vocabulary for her nuns to use. And she had visions she said came from a living, blinding light that spoke to her in words. The modern revival of her music has made her one of the most popular medieval composers alive, and her writings on medicine and on the natural world are still studied today.

hindu-arabic-numerals-and-zero.context_blurb: Modern Western arithmetic rests on a quiet revolution carried out, over centuries, by Indian mathematicians working in Sanskrit and then by Persian and Arab scholars who learned the system from them and passed it on to medieval Europe. The core idea is that any number, however large, can be written using only ten symbols by letting the position of each digit tell you what it is worth — units, tens, hundreds, and so on — with a special symbol holding an empty place when it would otherwise be ambiguous. That special placeholder, which Indian mathematicians fully developed by the seventh century AD, is the thing most Europeans had been missing. Roman numerals have no such placeholder and no column structure, which is why multiplying or dividing with them is a nightmare. The ninth-century Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote a book explaining how to calculate in the Indian way; it was translated into Latin and copied by hand across Europe for several hundred years before Fibonacci of Pisa, in a famous book of 1202, pushed it into general use among European merchants. Church authorities and city councils occasionally tried to ban the new numerals, worrying that the strange placeholder symbol made it too easy to forge accounts, but the system was simply too good at arithmetic to be stopped. Two common English words still carry fossil traces of this long cultural journey from Sanskrit through Arabic into Latin.

hinduism-brahma-vishnu-shiva-core-belief.context_blurb: Hinduism is a vast family of related religious traditions that developed on the Indian subcontinent over roughly four thousand years, blending older Vedic ritual, the philosophical speculations of the Upanishads, the devotional cults of the great gods, and much more. It is one of the three or four largest religious traditions in the world today, with over a billion adherents, mostly in India and Nepal. It does not have a single founder, a single creed, or a single sacred book; its scriptures include the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and many Puranas, all layered on top of each other across centuries. Modern Hinduism recognizes a vast pantheon of gods, often understood as different aspects or manifestations of a single ultimate divine reality called Brahman. Three major gods are usually singled out: a creator figure, a preserving figure, and a transforming or destroying figure, often grouped as a triad though many Hindu traditions emphasize one or another of these far more than the others. Core beliefs usually include karma (the moral weight of actions), rebirth into new lives, dharma (one's proper duty), and liberation from the cycle of rebirth as a long-term religious goal.

hippocrates-and-the-hippocratic-oath.context_blurb: Hippocrates was a Greek physician who lived in the 5th and early 4th centuries BC, on the island of Cos off the coast of Asia Minor. He is remembered as the founder of medicine as a rational discipline, in which illness is understood as the result of natural causes acting on the body rather than as supernatural punishment, and in which the physician's job is careful observation, honest record-keeping, and sober treatment that at a minimum does not make things worse. A large body of ancient medical writing was collected under his name — some of it almost certainly by him, much of it by his students and successors, the whole set now called the Hippocratic Corpus — and it provides the earliest serious systematic literature of Western medicine. The most famous document attached to his name is an oath young physicians were asked to swear, promising to do their best for patients, to keep their secrets, and not to cause deliberate harm. Modern medical schools still have graduates swear a version of it. The exact words have been updated many times, but the central idea — a doctor is bound by a code of honor independent of any legal rule — came out of this island school 2400 years ago.

hiroshima-and-nagasaki.context_blurb: In early August 1945, in the closing days of the Pacific War, the United States used two of the atomic weapons it had just developed under the Manhattan Project against two Japanese cities. The first weapon was detonated over the industrial city of Hiroshima on the island of Honshu on August 6, 1945, killing somewhere around 80,000 people immediately and many more in the following months and years from injuries and radiation sickness. The second was detonated over the port city of Nagasaki on the island of Kyushu three days later, killing somewhere around 40,000 people immediately and many more over the following months and years. The two attacks, together with the Soviet declaration of war on Japan on the same day as the Nagasaki bombing, convinced the Japanese emperor to intervene over the objections of his military leadership and surrender. Japan's formal surrender in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945, ended the Second World War. The decision to use the atomic bombs has been argued over by historians, moralists, and veterans for the eight decades since, with some holding that it saved more lives than it cost by preventing an invasion and others considering it a moral catastrophe. No country has used nuclear weapons in war since.

hitler-s-rise-to-power.context_blurb: Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born corporal in the German army during World War I who entered politics in the chaos that followed Germany's 1918 defeat. In November 1923 he and the First World War general Erich Ludendorff tried to overthrow the Bavarian state government in Munich in what came to be called the Beer Hall Putsch; the coup failed, Hitler was shot in the shoulder, and he was arrested and tried for high treason. He turned the trial itself into a national stage and used his light prison sentence afterward to dictate a long autobiography-and-manifesto that laid out his anti-Semitism and his dreams of eastward conquest for anyone willing to read it. After leaving prison he rebuilt the Nazi Party on a new strategy for seizing power. The Great Depression devastated Germany, and Nazi vote totals rose spectacularly from a small share in 1928 to a huge share by 1932; President Paul von Hindenburg was persuaded by conservative politicians who had reasons of their own for wanting Hitler in government to appoint him chancellor on January 30, 1933. Within weeks a Reichstag fire — blamed on a suspect caught near the burning building that night — gave Hitler the pretext to arrest thousands of political opponents, and a cowed parliament handed him emergency legislative powers. The Weimar Republic was dead inside a hundred days.

homer-and-the-trojan-war-iliad-and-odyss.context_blurb: The Iliad and the Odyssey are two enormous Greek poems traditionally attributed to a blind poet named Homer, written down perhaps around the 8th century BC after generations of oral performance by poets working in a tradition going back to the Mycenaean age. They tell stories from the end of a legendary war in which a coalition of Greek-speaking kings laid siege for ten years to a city on the northwest coast of what is now Turkey. The Iliad covers only a few weeks near the end of that siege and focuses on the rage of a Greek champion who refuses to fight after a quarrel with his commander. The Odyssey tells the long ten-year journey home of a different Greek hero after the city has fallen, and his struggles against monsters, enchantresses, and suitors who have invaded his household in his absence. The two poems were the central school texts of the Greek world — Greek children learned to read by memorizing them — and they shaped Greek religion, Greek art, and Greek identity for over a thousand years. They are the oldest major works of Western literature and remain two of the greatest.

homer-s-epics-iliad-and-odyssey.context_blurb: The Iliad and the Odyssey are two enormous Greek poems traditionally attributed to a blind poet named Homer, written down perhaps around the 8th century BC after generations of oral performance by poets working in a tradition going back to the Mycenaean age. They tell stories from the end of a legendary war in which a coalition of Greek-speaking kings laid siege for ten years to a city on the northwest coast of what is now Turkey. The Iliad covers only a few weeks near the end of that siege and focuses on the rage of a Greek champion who refuses to fight after a quarrel with his commander. The Odyssey tells the long ten-year journey home of a different Greek hero after the city has fallen, and his struggles against monsters, enchantresses, and suitors who have invaded his household in his absence. The two poems were the central school texts of the Greek world; Greek children learned to read by memorizing them. They shaped Greek religion, Greek art, and Greek identity for over a thousand years. Virgil's Aeneid in Latin modeled itself on them. Dante, Milton, Joyce, and modern poets have all drawn on them. The two poems are the oldest major works of Western literature and remain two of the greatest.

hungarian-revolution-1956.context_blurb: In October 1956, students, workers, and former Communist moderates in Soviet-controlled Hungary rose up spontaneously against the brutal Stalinist regime that had been imposed on their country since the Soviet occupation of 1945. The revolt began with a peaceful student protest in Budapest and swelled within days into a nationwide uprising that toppled the hated local Communist leadership, released thousands of political prisoners, and installed the reform-minded Communist Imre Nagy as prime minister. Nagy declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Soviet-dominated Warsaw Pact and announced free multiparty elections. The Soviet Union, which had briefly tolerated the first days of the revolt, decided it could not allow a Warsaw Pact member to leave and sent columns of Soviet tanks and troops back into Budapest in early November 1956. The Soviet forces crushed the revolt in heavy street fighting that killed thousands of Hungarians. Nagy was arrested after being lured out of the Yugoslav embassy under a safe-conduct promise, held in secret for two years, tried in secret, and shot in 1958 — a fact his family only confirmed years later. About two hundred thousand Hungarians fled to the West. The Western powers, who had publicly called for liberation of the captive nations, did nothing to help. The Hungarian Revolution became one of the defining moral failures of Western Cold War policy.

ibn-battuta-s-travels.context_blurb: Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan Berber judge and scholar who in 1325 — at twenty-one — set out from Tangier to make the hajj to Mecca and simply did not stop. Over the next thirty years he traveled further than any medieval person we know of, reaching as far east as China and as far south as the East African coast and the Mali empire south of the Sahara. When he finally came home, the Marinid sultan of Morocco set a court secretary to listen to his memories and shape them into a book usually just called the Rihla, 'the journey.' Ibn Battuta's distances dwarf those of Marco Polo, whom he never mentioned and may not have known about, and his account is one of the richest windows we have on the fourteenth-century Islamic world. He ate at countless sultans' tables, served as a traveling legal scholar wherever a ruler could use one, married and parted along the way, visited the mosques of Delhi and the courts of the great African mansas, and left us an eyewitness picture of a vast, interconnected Muslim civilization — bound together by Arabic, by the hajj, and by a shared body of law — that few modern readers suspect existed in his century.

ibn-battuta-the-great-muslim-traveler.context_blurb: Ibn Battuta was a 14th-century Moroccan legal scholar and traveler who spent nearly thirty years wandering across the Muslim world and beyond, and who ended his life having probably covered more miles than any other individual human being before the modern age. Born in Tangier in 1304, he set out at the age of twenty-one with the modest goal of making the pilgrimage to Mecca and could not seem to stop traveling afterward. He went to Mecca several times, lived for years in Delhi as a judge under the Muslim Sultanate of India, visited the Maldives, Sri Lanka, probably China, and the great West African Empire of Mali, where he was received at the court of the Mansa. He covered somewhere around seventy-five thousand miles over the course of his career, by camel, horse, foot, and ship. On his final return to Morocco he dictated his memoirs to a court scribe, producing a long travel narrative known in English as the Rihla, which is one of the most important sources for the geography, politics, religion, and daily life of the 14th-century Muslim world. Ibn Battuta is one of those historical figures whose actual achievements have never been equaled by anyone later.

ignatius-loyola-the-jesuits.context_blurb: Ignatius Loyola was a 16th-century Spanish nobleman and soldier who, after being badly wounded in battle in 1521, underwent a long and painful recovery, began to read religious books while bedridden, and came out of it a changed man. He gave up his career in arms, left his old life behind at a mountain shrine of the Virgin, and spent the next years as a pilgrim and would-be preacher. He went as far as Jerusalem, came back, started his education over again from the beginning in his thirties, and ended up at the University of Paris, where he gathered around him a small circle of serious young students. In 1540 the pope formally approved their new religious order, the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits took vows of obedience to the pope and threw themselves into the century's two great Catholic missions: education at home — the Jesuits became the schoolmasters of Catholic Europe — and missionary work overseas. Jesuits like Loyola's close friend Francis Xavier sailed to India, Japan, and the coast of China; others followed to the Americas. Loyola himself stayed in Rome in his later years, writing a little devotional book he had been shaping for decades and governing his order with the quiet focus of a general. He died in 1556.

illuminated-manuscripts-book-of-kells.context_blurb: For centuries after Rome fell, monks in Ireland, Britain, and later across Europe spent their lives copying out the Bible and other sacred books by hand, decorating the pages with painted letters, borders of knotted beasts, and whole opening spreads so densely wrought that a careful reader could stare at them for an hour and still miss things. The most famous of all these books, made by Irish monks around the year 800 and now kept in Dublin, is so delicate and so densely illustrated that medieval visitors tried to describe its beauty in sweeping similes, insisting that no ordinary human hand could possibly have produced it. If you look closely at its pages you will find cats, mice, hidden creatures, and quiet jokes hidden in the knotwork. Illuminated manuscripts of this kind carried not only the words of the gospels but the memory of ancient art, since the monks' pigments and their methods preserved recipes going back to the Mediterranean world. These books also preserved the texts of the Latin classics, the writings of the Church fathers, and the hymns and prayers of the whole early Church. They are the picture-Bible of a world that mostly could not read, and the most careful survivors of them are among the most valuable objects in any museum today.

illuminated-manuscripts-book-of-kells-li.context_blurb: In the centuries after the fall of the western Roman Empire, Christian monasteries in the British Isles, Ireland, and continental Europe produced some of the most extraordinary illustrated books in the history of the world. These illuminated manuscripts were handwritten on treated animal skin called vellum, in elegant medieval scripts, and decorated with brilliantly colored designs around the text — enormous ornamented letters at the opening of each book of scripture, geometric and interlace patterns in red and gold and lapis blue, and whole full-page images of saints, evangelists, and symbolic creatures. Two of the greatest surviving examples come from the Insular tradition of Ireland and northern England around AD 700 to 800. The Book of Kells, now kept at Trinity College in Dublin, is a lavishly decorated gospel book whose carpet pages and ornamented initials are among the most intricate images ever produced in Western art. The Lindisfarne Gospels, now in the British Library in London, is a comparable gospel book produced on a holy island off the Northumbrian coast. These books were objects of serious devotional labor — monks produced them over years as acts of worship — and they are the greatest art of early medieval Christianity, preserved by chance through many centuries of wars, fires, and viking raids.

impressionism-monet-and-the-movement.context_blurb: Impressionism was a loose group of French painters who in the 1860s and 1870s broke with the official French academic painting establishment and began producing a radically new kind of modern painting. The core figures included Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Alfred Sisley, Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt (an American working in Paris), and others. They painted outdoors directly from the scene when they could, used short loose brushstrokes to catch the shifting conditions of light and air, employed brilliant unmixed colors straight from the recently invented portable tubes of oil paint, and preferred ordinary modern subjects — train stations, boulevards, suburban gardens, bathers, ballet dancers, haystacks in different lights — over the historical and mythological subjects favored by the academic salon. Monet in particular spent decades on obsessive series of paintings showing the same subject in different light conditions. The group's first joint exhibition in 1874 was ridiculed by critics, and the name Impressionism was coined as a mocking review of one of Monet's paintings and then taken over by the group as a badge. By the end of the century their art had conquered the European art world, and today their paintings are among the most-reproduced and most-valuable works in the Western canon.

inca-road-network-machu-picchu.context_blurb: The Inca ran an empire that stretched for thousands of miles along the spine of the Andes mountains, from modern Colombia down into Chile, and they ran it without the wheel, without draft animals strong enough to pull a wagon, and without any writing system Europeans could read. Instead they built a legendary paved road network crossing deserts, jungles, and some of the highest passes on Earth, strung together by rope suspension bridges hand-woven from the natural fibers available in the high country and replaced every year by the villages beneath them. Royal messages flew along those roads over hundreds of miles in a single day, through a disciplined relay system that is still studied by military historians. Their recordkeepers managed imperial accounts and census data on an ingenious cord-based device whose exact grammar scholars are still arguing about. High in a saddle between two Andean peaks they built Machu Picchu, a royal estate so cleverly tucked into the mountains that Spanish conquerors never found it and it slept there, forgotten by the outside world, until an American explorer stumbled on it in 1911. Modern engineers who study the site are still startled by how well its drainage, terracing, and stonework have survived centuries of earthquakes in a place where modern buildings would struggle.

inca-stonework-and-sacsayhuaman.context_blurb: The Inca were extraordinary stonemasons, and the walls they built in their capital of Cusco and at Sacsayhuaman just above it on the hill are one of the signature achievements of pre-Columbian engineering. The Inca worked without wheels, without draft animals large enough to pull heavy loads, and without iron tools, yet they shaped enormous stone blocks — some weighing many tons — so precisely that the joints between neighboring blocks hold even today without any mortar at all, and have survived five centuries of earthquakes that destroyed Spanish buildings built on top of them. The massive zigzag walls of the great hilltop fortress above Cusco are built of boulders so large that it is still unclear how they were moved into place. Modern experiments suggest a combination of carefully graded earthen ramps, rolling on logs, lots of coordinated labor, and painstaking shaping of each block to fit its neighbor exactly. The Spanish, when they arrived in the 1530s, tore down parts of these walls to build their own cathedrals and governor's houses on the foundations, which is why colonial Cusco today sits on top of Inca masonry that nobody could really improve on.

indian-numerals-zero-decimal-system.context_blurb: The number system almost the entire world uses today — ten digits counting from a shape for nothing up through a shape for nine, with place-value notation that lets you write any number by stringing those digits together — is often called in Europe the Arabic numerals, but Arab mathematicians themselves called the system the Indian numerals, because they knew exactly where it had come from. Indian mathematicians during the Gupta era and the following centuries worked out the full decimal place-value system, including the crucial innovation of using a specific symbol as a placeholder for an empty position, which represents the number zero in its own right. The mathematician Brahmagupta in the 7th century AD was the first known person to lay out systematic rules of arithmetic for the number zero as a quantity in its own right (not just a placeholder) and for operations with negative numbers. The system traveled west through the Islamic world, especially through the writings of the great Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi in 9th-century Baghdad, and reached medieval Europe through Italian merchants and Latin translations in the 12th and 13th centuries. The modern computerized world runs on this Indian intellectual achievement every single second, usually without a thought about where it came from.

indian-ocean-trade-spread-of-indian-cult.context_blurb: For over two thousand years, the Indian Ocean has been one of the busiest highways of human exchange, with annual monsoon winds driving sailing traffic east and west on a reliable seasonal cycle. South Indian and Sri Lankan merchants knew these winds thousands of years ago, and from early in the first millennium AD, Indian traders, Hindu priests, and Buddhist monks began traveling across the ocean to the coasts and islands of Southeast Asia, carrying with them Sanskrit, Indian religion, Indian script, Indian political ideas, and Indian artistic styles. Over the following centuries, these imports blended with existing Southeast Asian cultures to produce the famous Indianized kingdoms of early Southeast Asia: Funan, Champa, Srivijaya, the Khmer Empire, the early kingdoms of Java and Sumatra, and others. These kingdoms built Hindu and Buddhist temple complexes — including the great stone cities at Angkor and Borobudur — and used Sanskrit for royal inscriptions and Indian scripts for their own writing systems. The spread of Indian civilization east across the ocean was not a conquest but a slow cultural diffusion, carried on the backs of merchants, scholars, and monks who sailed with the winds. Modern Southeast Asian languages and alphabets still carry the deep traces.

indulgences-tetzel.context_blurb: An indulgence, in medieval Catholic teaching, was a formal reduction of the time a soul had to spend in purgatory before entering heaven. The theology behind it had been built up over centuries and had respectable roots, but by the early 16th century the system had drifted a long way from its origins. In the Germany of 1517, the pope was raising money for the ongoing rebuilding of Saint Peter's basilica in Rome, and he had made an arrangement with a very ambitious young German churchman named Albert of Mainz that put the preaching and selling of indulgences across half of Germany in his hands. The friar Albert hired for the hard-sell preaching tour was a Dominican named Johann Tetzel. Tetzel traveled from town to town setting up a booth near the parish church, promising that an indulgence could lift a dead loved one straight out of purgatory in exchange for the right coin, and even coining a short jingle to drive the sales. His preaching so outraged a small-town Augustinian friar in Wittenberg that the friar — one Martin Luther — wrote a public list of ninety-five theses attacking the whole business. The rest, as they say, is Reformation.

indus-valley-civilization-harappa-mohenj.context_blurb: Along the valley of the Indus River and its tributaries, in what is now Pakistan and northwestern India, a sophisticated urban civilization flourished from roughly 2600 to 1900 BC — one of the four earliest river-valley civilizations alongside Mesopotamia, Egypt, and ancient China. The two best-known cities are Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, both of which had carefully laid-out streets on a grid, standardized fired-brick construction, elaborate drainage systems (including private flushing toilets and public sewers that would not be matched in Europe for over three thousand years), granaries, baths, and uniform weights and measures that suggest some kind of centralized administration. The Indus civilization traded over long distances by sea with Mesopotamia and overland with Afghanistan. Its writing system survives on thousands of small clay seals showing animals and short strings of signs, but it has resisted all attempts at decipherment, and we still cannot read what those seals say. The whole urban civilization went into decline between 1900 and 1300 BC for reasons that are still debated, probably involving climate change, drying rivers, and shifts in the monsoon rather than foreign invasion. It is one of the great unsolved mysteries of ancient history.

industrial-revolution-textiles-and-the-f.context_blurb: The Industrial Revolution began in late-eighteenth-century Britain, and the first thing it transformed was the making of cloth. For thousands of years, spinning thread and weaving it into fabric had been slow work done by hand in cottages, usually by women fitting it around farm chores. In the space of about fifty years, a series of English inventors — James Hargreaves, Richard Arkwright, Samuel Crompton, Edmund Cartwright — stacked clever mechanical ideas on top of one another until a single powered machine could do the work of many hand-spinners at once, and a single rural stream, dammed and harnessed, could drive the whole plant. Arkwright in particular grasped that his real contribution was not any one of his machines but the discipline of gathering workers under one roof, by the clock, and keeping the equipment running day and night. His water-powered mills around Cromford became the pattern that would be copied around the world, and later writers gave him a grand honorific that reflected that organising achievement. Cotton flooded out of Lancashire; prices crashed; small weavers who tried to keep working at home were ruined. In the troubled years 1811-13, displaced hand-workers across the English Midlands began smashing the new machines by night under the banner of a mysterious leader whose actual existence historians have been debating ever since; Parliament treated the act very harshly indeed, and the young poet Lord Byron gave a famous speech in the House of Lords on the workers' behalf. The mills themselves ran on cheap, controllable labour of a kind that would appal any modern inspector. Modern factories, modern wages, and modern debates about them all begin here.

interwar-western-breakthroughs-the-expan.context_blurb: The 1920s and 1930s were, quietly, one of the greatest periods of Western scientific discovery, and two of its biggest finds would reshape the modern world. In 1927 the Belgian astronomer and clergyman Georges Lemaitre published the first mathematical model of an expanding universe — the idea that galaxies are rushing apart from each other because space itself is stretching, which meant the whole cosmos must have begun from a single compact beginning in the distant past. Albert Einstein at first refused to believe it, since he had put a 'cosmological constant' into his own equations to prevent exactly that conclusion, and he told Lemaitre so in person at a conference. But in 1929 the American astronomer Edwin Hubble, working with the 100-inch telescope on Mount Wilson, measured the recession of distant galaxies and showed that Lemaitre was right. Meanwhile at St. Mary's Hospital in London, the Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation in 1928 to find a mould had killed the bacteria on a petri dish he had left out, and the active substance he isolated from that mould would, in time, save tens of millions of lives from infection. The expanding universe and the age of antibiotics both grew out of patient laboratory work by a few people who kept paying attention.

invasion-of-poland-and-blitzkrieg.context_blurb: On September 1, 1939, Nazi Germany invaded Poland from the west, launching the Second World War in Europe. Two days later, Britain and France, honoring their guarantee of Polish independence, declared war on Germany, though neither did much to help Poland militarily. On September 17 the Soviet Union, having secretly agreed in the Nazi-Soviet Pact to divide Poland with Germany, invaded Poland from the east. The Polish army, numerically substantial but outclassed in air power, armor, and radio communications, was overwhelmed within five weeks. The German tactics, which combined fast armored columns, close air support from the Luftwaffe, and radio-coordinated maneuver, became famous as blitzkrieg (lightning war) and shocked military observers around the world. Warsaw fell in late September after a punishing siege. Hundreds of thousands of Poles were killed, and the country was partitioned between the German and Soviet occupation zones. The Polish government went into exile in London and ran a government-in-exile throughout the war, while a Polish underground state (including the Polish Home Army) operated secretly inside occupied Poland for the next six years. Poland would not be free again until 1989, half a century later, after Soviet-era communist rule finally collapsed.

investiture-controversy-canossa-1077.context_blurb: In the late 11th century, a reforming pope and a hot-tempered German emperor collided over a question that sounds narrow but was actually enormous: who gets to appoint the bishops of Christendom, the Church or the king? Bishops ran huge estates and held real worldly power, and both sides needed them loyal. The pope insisted the appointment had to be the Church's; the emperor insisted it had to be his. The emperor's own nobles threatened to desert him unless he made peace with the pope, and he ended up making the long winter journey to a mountain castle in northern Italy where the pope was staying, and was forced to wait outside as a penitent before he could be forgiven. The scene burned itself into European memory as the moment a secular ruler bowed to the Church, and it has been invoked by rulers and reformers ever since, often as a line they refuse to cross again. The pope himself was eventually driven from Rome by the same emperor years later and died in bitter exile. The real question underneath the quarrel, how to divide spiritual and worldly authority, outlasted both of them, and in one form or another has never stopped being asked in the West.

iron-curtain-churchill-s-fulton-speech.context_blurb: In March 1946, Winston Churchill, who had been Britain's wartime prime minister until his party lost the postwar election, gave a speech at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, with American President Harry Truman seated behind him on the platform. The speech was formally titled The Sinews of Peace, but it has been known ever since by its most famous phrase: Churchill described a long political barrier dropping across the continent of Europe from the Baltic Sea in the north to the Adriatic Sea in the south, cutting off the capitals of a line of European states that had passed into the Soviet sphere, where ancient civilizations found themselves subject to an increasingly total form of political control from Moscow. The speech was controversial at the time; the Second World War had ended less than a year earlier with the Soviet Union as a victorious ally, and much Western public opinion was not yet ready to see the Soviets as an adversary. Within two years, however, the Soviet consolidation of Eastern Europe through rigged elections, political purges, and the February 1948 coup in Czechoslovakia had made Churchill's warning look prescient. The phrase that passed into the English language from this speech — iron curtain — became one of the defining images of the entire Cold War.

iron-working-in-sub-saharan-africa-nok.context_blurb: The Nok culture of what is now central Nigeria is one of the earliest known iron-working cultures in sub-Saharan Africa, flourishing from roughly 1500 BC to AD 500 on the Jos Plateau and surrounding areas. The Nok are known today mostly from the extraordinary terracotta figurines they left behind — stylized hollow clay heads and figures, up to life size, of men and women with elaborately dressed hair, pierced eyes, and carefully modeled features, found by the hundreds in and around their village sites. Alongside these figurines, archaeologists have found furnaces, iron slag, forged iron tools, and the remnants of a well-developed metalworking tradition. Where exactly Nok iron-working came from — whether it was invented independently in sub-Saharan Africa, or diffused south across the Sahara from the Mediterranean — is a question archaeologists still argue about. What is clear is that iron tools were being produced in sub-Saharan Africa thousands of years ago, allowing more productive farming and the growth of the complex societies that would eventually include the kingdoms of Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Benin, and Great Zimbabwe. The Nok terracottas themselves are now treasured museum pieces, and some have unfortunately been looted into the illegal international antiquities trade.

isaac-newton-and-universal-gravitation.context_blurb: Isaac Newton was an English mathematician and natural philosopher born on Christmas Day 1642, the same year Galileo died, who became arguably the greatest scientist who ever lived. He was raised by his grandmother on a Lincolnshire farm, nearly stayed a farm boy, and only ended up at Cambridge because an uncle noticed he was a prodigy. When plague closed the university he spent a year or two at his family home working out, by himself, the mathematics of motion, the law that holds the heavens together, and the fact that white light is made of colors. He later wrote his masterpiece, the Principia Mathematica, which turned those ideas into a system that explained everything from a falling object to the orbit of the Moon with the same handful of equations. Newton was also a serious alchemist, a secret theologian, and a bitter rival to other scientists; the gentle genius of the schoolbook picture is a myth. He ran the Royal Mint, hunted counterfeiters to the gallows, and ruled British science for decades as president of the Royal Society. He died in 1727 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, the first scientist ever to be given that honor.

isaac-newton-gravity-and-motion.context_blurb: Isaac Newton was an English mathematician and natural philosopher born in Lincolnshire in 1642, the posthumous son of a farmer who had never learned to write. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, as a poor sizar — a servant to richer students — and when the plague closed the university in 1665 he went home to the family farm. In the eighteen months he spent there alone as a young man he laid the groundwork for three enormous things at once: a new mathematics for handling continuous change, a sweeping theory of light and colour, and a hunch about the force that would, in time, link falling objects on Earth to the regular motions of the night sky. He kept most of this to himself for twenty years. Only the patient prodding of the astronomer Edmond Halley, who even paid for the printing out of his own pocket, got Newton to work his physics up into the enormous Latin book he finally finished in 1687 — the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica. In it he stated the laws of motion that still carry his name and used them, together with a single law of universal attraction between masses, to derive the orbits of the planets, the ocean tides, and the paths of comets. He also later feuded bitterly with the German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz over which of the two of them had invented the new calculus first. Newton eventually became Warden and then Master of the Royal Mint, an irascible defender of his own priority, and President of the Royal Society. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.

islamic-art-and-architecture-alhambra-do.context_blurb: Islamic art and architecture developed in the centuries after the 7th-century rise of Islam into one of the richest and most distinctive artistic traditions in human history. Because mainstream Sunni Islam discouraged pictorial representation of God or of living beings in a religious context, Islamic artists poured enormous creative energy into non-representational decoration: elaborate geometric patterns, flowing arabesque vegetal designs, and the artistic calligraphy of Arabic script, which itself became the central visual expression of Qur'anic text on the walls of mosques, palaces, and manuscripts. Islamic architects developed distinctive forms like the pointed horseshoe arch, the muqarnas honeycomb vaults that look like stalactites, the colorful tile mosaics of the Persian and Turkish traditions, and gardens laid out as four-part reflections of paradise. Several specific monuments stand as peaks of the tradition: the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (built in the 690s on the Temple Mount, one of the oldest surviving Islamic buildings), the Alhambra palace in Granada (a 14th-century jewel-box of Nasrid-era interiors in Moorish Spain), the Great Mosque of Cordoba, Isfahan's blue-tiled Safavid mosques, the Taj Mahal in Mughal India, and the Suleymaniye Mosque in Ottoman Istanbul. Each represents a different regional flowering of a shared tradition that spanned three continents.

islamic-art-calligraphy-and-geometric-pa.context_blurb: Islamic sacred art developed under the strong influence of a prophetic tradition warning against making images of living beings, especially in places of worship — the fear was that pictures of prophets or holy figures would become idols. Instead, Muslim artists turned to two extraordinary visual traditions: beautifully stylized writing, and intricate geometric patterns that cover walls, domes, and tilework. The writing — called Arabic calligraphy — most often set the verses of the Qur'an into art themselves, since the Qur'an in Arabic is understood by Muslims to be the actual, uncreated speech of God. The geometric patterns were built from compass-and-straightedge constructions and ratios that modern mathematicians have found startlingly sophisticated, and some of them anticipate symmetries that European mathematics would only name much later. The result is a sacred art that invites the eye to wander forever without resting on any single face or figure, which treats mathematics itself as a kind of worship — proportion, symmetry, and endless subdivision as a way of pointing to the one God who cannot be depicted at all — while secular Islamic art could and did include people and animals, especially in miniature painting and in the private palaces of Persian and Mughal rulers.

islamic-golden-age-algebra-optics-medici.context_blurb: Between roughly the eighth and the thirteenth centuries, a vast swath of the Islamic world — stretching from Spain through North Africa to Persia and Central Asia — hosted an extraordinary burst of learning that historians now call the Islamic Golden Age. In cities like Baghdad, Cairo, Cordoba, and Bukhara, caliphs and princes paid handsomely for Greek, Persian, and Indian manuscripts to be hunted down, translated into Arabic, and corrected. Great libraries like the House of Wisdom in Baghdad gathered thousands of scholars, Muslim and Christian and Jewish, to copy, argue over, and build on the works of the ancients. Out of this common workshop came Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician whose two most famous short books gave their names to things every modern schoolchild and every modern programmer encounters. The Persian polymath Ibn Sina — known to Europe as Avicenna — wrote vast philosophical and medical textbooks that would still be used in European universities for centuries after his death. In Cairo, the physicist Ibn al-Haytham spent years in a darkened room overturning the old Greek account of how human sight actually works and laying the real foundations of the science of optics. Ibn al-Nafis in thirteenth-century Damascus correctly described the circulation of the blood through the lungs three centuries before any European. When Latin Europe eventually started to catch up, it did so largely by reading them.

islamic-golden-age-science-and-math.context_blurb: Between about the eighth and thirteenth centuries, the Islamic world ran what historians now call the Golden Age — a span of about five hundred years when it was the most advanced scientific civilization on earth. The caliphs of Baghdad gathered Greek, Persian, Indian, and Syriac texts into their great translation academy, paid translators extravagantly, and set scholars loose on every branch of knowledge from medicine and chemistry to astronomy, optics, and mathematics. The Muslim scholars treated respectful skepticism of great authorities as a duty, and the astronomer Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham) overturned a thousand years of Greek thought by giving the modern explanation of how we see. The same civilization gave Europe several words it still uses for stepwise mathematical procedures and whole branches of math, and it put a working astrolabe in the hands of every well-equipped navigator and astronomer from Spain to Samarkand. When the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 the Golden Age effectively ended, though many of its gifts to the wider world had already crossed into Christian Europe through the great translation schools of Toledo and Palermo — the Islamic civilization's lasting bequest to a West that would, within a few centuries, pass it back again with its own additions through the Scientific Revolution.

island-hopping-strategy.context_blurb: After the American victories at Coral Sea and Midway in 1942 reversed the strategic initiative in the Pacific War, American and Allied forces began a slow, bloody, two-pronged offensive back across the Pacific toward the Japanese home islands. The southern prong, under General Douglas MacArthur, worked up through New Guinea and the Philippines. The central prong, under Admiral Chester Nimitz, worked across the central Pacific through a series of brutal amphibious landings on small Japanese-held islands — Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Guam, Peleliu, Iwo Jima, Okinawa — in a strategy that became known as island-hopping. Instead of trying to capture every Japanese-held island in sequence, the Allies isolated and bypassed many of the stronger Japanese bases and concentrated on seizing the islands they needed as bases for the next step, letting the bypassed Japanese garrisons wither on the vine. The individual island battles were ferocious, with Japanese defenders fighting almost to the last man and American and Allied casualties mounting at each step. By mid-1945, American forces were on Okinawa within easy bombing range of the Japanese home islands. The planned invasion of the home islands never happened, because the atomic bombings in August and the Soviet declaration of war ended the Pacific War before it was needed.

italian-unification-risorgimento-garibal.context_blurb: In 1815 Italy was not a country but a peninsula of small kingdoms, duchies, papal lands, and provinces of the Austrian Empire, each with its own ruler, currency, and dialect. The movement to pull them into a single nation-state is called the Risorgimento, 'the Resurgence,' and it unfolded in fits and starts across the middle of the nineteenth century. Two very different figures became its most famous faces. The flamboyant soldier Giuseppe Garibaldi, a dashing veteran of earlier revolutions overseas, led the dramatic volunteer expeditions in the south, famous for their distinctive uniform. The patient northern statesman Camillo Cavour, prime minister of the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, worked by diplomacy, railways, taxation, and quiet alliances to put Piedmont at the head of the unification movement. The king they fought under was Victor Emmanuel II of the House of Savoy. The questions ahead cover Garibaldi's volunteer troops, his nickname, his famous landing in Sicily and march up the peninsula, the moment he handed over the fruits of his southern conquest to the king, Cavour's dying words, and a famous question about why the new king was called 'the second' when he was the first king of a united Italy. It matters because the Risorgimento is one of the great nineteenth-century national stories — a modern state born out of mountains, barricades, red-shirted volunteers, and patient diplomacy.

jacques-louis-david-and-neoclassicism.context_blurb: Jacques-Louis David (1748 to 1825) was a French painter who became the leading European Neoclassical painter of his age and the official painter of two very different French regimes, the Revolution and the Empire. He trained in Rome in the 1770s under the influence of the ancient Roman ruins and the ongoing scholarly rediscovery of classical antiquity, and he brought back a severe, hard-edged, sculptural style of painting focused on Roman and Greek subjects — oath-takings, heroic deaths, Spartan mothers watching their sons go to war. His pre-Revolution paintings became visual propaganda for a particular Roman-republican vision of civic virtue, and when the French Revolution broke out he adopted its cause with the same severe moral enthusiasm. He served in the revolutionary government, voted for the execution of the king, and produced several of the Revolution's most iconic paintings, including the martyrdom of a particular revolutionary leader lying dead in his bathtub. When Napoleon rose to power, David served Napoleon as official painter and produced massive canvases of the Napoleonic imperial court. After Napoleon's final defeat, David was exiled to Brussels and died there. His enormous technical talent and his willingness to put his art at the service of successive regimes make him one of the great unresolved cases in Western art.

jainism-mahavira.context_blurb: Jainism is one of the ancient Indian religious traditions, roughly contemporary with early Buddhism, that has endured as a distinct minority tradition in India for over two thousand five hundred years. Its central figure is Mahavira, a 6th-century BC teacher regarded by Jains as the twenty-fourth and last tirthankara, or ford-maker, of the current age — a human being who achieved full spiritual liberation and taught the way to other souls. Jain teaching centers on a strict ethical principle of ahimsa, non-violence toward all living beings, which is taken more seriously in daily practice than in almost any other religious tradition. Devout Jain monks and nuns refuse to eat anything that required killing (not just meat but root vegetables, which involve killing the plant), sweep the ground in front of them to avoid stepping on insects, filter their water to avoid swallowing microscopic life, and in some cases cover their mouths to avoid inhaling tiny creatures. Jain lay followers aim at the same ideals in more moderate forms. The Jains have been merchants, scholars, and bankers across the Indian subcontinent for millennia, and their famously strict ethics gave Mahatma Gandhi, who grew up in a region of heavy Jain influence, the core idea of non-violence that he brought into modern politics.

james-madison-father-of-the-constitution.context_blurb: James Madison was a small, scholarly Virginia planter who became the single most important intellectual architect of the United States Constitution. He arrived at the Constitutional Convention of 1787 in Philadelphia with a plan already in his pocket — the Virginia Plan — that framed the convention's agenda from day one. He kept the detailed notes of the convention that are now our main window into its debates, co-authored the Federalist Papers under the pen name Publius during the ratification fight, and then wrote and shepherded the Bill of Rights through the First Congress. He later served as Thomas Jefferson's secretary of state for eight years and as fourth president of the United States from 1809 to 1817, including throughout the War of 1812 — a war during which the British briefly captured and burned Washington, and during which his wife Dolley became famous for saving the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington from the executive mansion as the British were coming. Madison was physically small, often quiet in company, and devoted to constitutional government in a way that outlasted every political upheaval of his lifetime. He died in 1836, the last of the founding generation to pass away, having lived long enough to see the republic he had designed survive its first half-century.

james-watt-and-the-steam-engine.context_blurb: James Watt was a Scottish instrument-maker who, in the 1760s and 1770s, redesigned the steam engine so radically that his name is now attached to the whole age that followed. Earlier atmospheric engines, built in the previous century, had been used to pump water out of coal mines; they worked but they wasted most of their fuel heating and then cooling the same giant cylinder over and over again. One Sunday afternoon on the Glasgow common, while on a university repair job, Watt saw how to fix the waste — a single idea that would eventually drive mills, factories, locomotives, and steamships. He partnered with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton, who had the capital and the workshop to turn Watt's drawings into working engines, and together they built the engines that powered the first phase of the Industrial Revolution.
