The questions ahead cover the piece of lab equipment Watt was handed to fix in that famous story, a childhood legend about young James watching something on his family's hearth, the first great application he aimed his engines at, his central mental fix for the waste problem, where he said he first saw it, the famous unit of power he invented so customers could compare his engines with the horses they were replacing, the heat concept of his scientist friend Joseph Black that lies behind his insight, one of his later machine inventions that let a steam engine regulate its own speed, and one odd story about an angry visitor he met at his door. It matters because Watt's engines are the central technology that pulled the Western economy out of a muscle-and-wind world and into the long industrial boom.

jamestown-the-first-english-colonies.context_blurb: England arrived late to the colonization race. Its first permanent North American settlement was planted in 1607 on a swampy island in a tidal Virginia river by about a hundred men sent by a London joint-stock company looking for gold, a passage to Asia, or anything else that could turn a profit. There was no gold, the water was foul, half the men were gentlemen who refused to dig, and most of the first colonists starved or died of disease. A tough ex-soldier named Captain John Smith, who had already lived one of the strangest lives on the Atlantic — enslaved, escaped, and roundabout traveled across half of Europe — imposed a strict discipline that kept the colony alive through its worst years. A settler eventually married Pocahontas, the chief's daughter, and bred a new strain of a profitable crop that finally gave Virginia something to sell to England. The year 1619 brought two more firsts to the colony that would shape all of American history: a new kind of political institution the colonists had hungered for from the start, and the first shipload of enslaved Africans. Both legacies, self-government and slavery, started on the same muddy riverbank, and their long collision shaped nearly every great American political argument that would follow.

jan-van-eyck-and-the-northern-renaissanc.context_blurb: Jan van Eyck (around 1390 to 1441) was a Flemish painter who became court painter to the Duke of Burgundy and worked mainly in the city of Bruges in what is now Belgium. He is traditionally and probably wrongly credited with inventing oil painting; he did not invent the technique but he transformed it, pioneering the use of thin translucent oil-based glazes layered over a careful underpainting to produce a kind of luminous realism that stunned every artist who saw it. His surfaces glow like gemstones. His religious altarpieces — especially the gigantic multi-panel Ghent Altarpiece in St. Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent, done jointly with his brother Hubert — and his individual portraits of merchants, their wives, their rooms, their fur-trimmed sleeves, their brass chandeliers, their lap dogs, and the convex mirrors on their walls set a new standard for observational realism in European painting a full generation before the Italian Renaissance really hit its stride. His double portrait of a Flemish merchant couple in a bedroom is one of the most studied paintings in Western art history. He signed his paintings with his own name and the proud phrase "Jan van Eyck was here," an unusual act of self-assertion by a painter in that age.

japanese-american-internment.context_blurb: After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the United States government forcibly removed roughly 120,000 Japanese Americans and legal residents of Japanese ancestry from their homes along the Pacific coast and interned them in a chain of hastily built relocation camps across the interior American West for the duration of the war. The order was signed by President Franklin Roosevelt as Executive Order 9066 in February 1942, under pressure from military commanders and West Coast politicians who claimed that American citizens of Japanese ancestry were a security threat. Over two thirds of the interned people were American citizens by birth. There was no comparable mass internment of German Americans or Italian Americans despite the fact that the United States was also at war with Germany and Italy. The internment was challenged in the courts; the Supreme Court initially upheld it in the 1944 Korematsu decision. The internees lost their homes, their businesses, and much of their life savings. Decades later, in 1988, the United States Congress formally apologized for the internment and voted a reparations payment of $20,000 to each surviving internee. The internment is now treated as one of the darkest American civil-liberties failures of the twentieth century.

japanese-art-hokusai-s-great-wave-and-wo.context_blurb: Japan developed one of the great visual-art traditions of the world, from the Buddhist religious painting of the Nara and Heian periods, through medieval ink paintings influenced by Chinese models, to the great woodblock printing of the Edo period. From the 17th century through the mid-19th century, Edo (modern Tokyo) supported a vibrant popular culture of theaters, pleasure districts, and public amusements, and a dedicated school of popular artists produced colored woodblock prints — ukiyo-e, or pictures of the floating world — depicting kabuki actors, famous courtesans, scenes of theatrical life, and famous landscapes. Several ukiyo-e masters reached worldwide fame. Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849), who worked under dozens of pseudonyms over his very long and prolific career, produced a famous series of views of Mount Fuji whose most famous print, showing an enormous curling wave about to break over small fishing boats with the mountain in the distance, has become one of the most-reproduced images in the world. Utagawa Hiroshige produced parallel landscape series. When Japan reopened to international trade in the mid-19th century, Japanese prints flooded into Europe and had an enormous influence on Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, and later European modernism, from Monet to van Gogh to Mary Cassatt.

joan-of-arc.context_blurb: In the early 15th century, during a long and grinding war between England and France, a teenage peasant girl from a tiny village in eastern France walked out of her father's house and insisted that God had sent her to drive the English out of her country and crown the rightful heir. Against every reason not to listen, she talked her way to the French court, convinced the uncrowned prince she was for real, and in a few astonishing months led the French army to a string of victories that cracked a long and famous siege and put her prince on his throne. Then she was captured, sold to her enemies, put through a long and sickening Church trial as a heretic, and burned alive at a few months past her nineteenth birthday. Decades later a different trial cleared her name, and centuries after that the Church made her a saint. The young girl who went into battle in boys' clothes, carrying a banner heavier than her own body, has never stopped being one of the Western world's most startling human beings, and the record of her trial, where a frightened girl without a lawyer answered theologians with astonishing poise, is still one of the great documents of medieval history.

john-adams-second-president-xyz-affair.context_blurb: John Adams was a Massachusetts country lawyer who defended the Boston Massacre soldiers because he believed every accused man deserved a fair trial, then became one of the fiercest early advocates of American independence, served on the committee that drafted the Declaration of Independence, worked as the American minister to the Netherlands and later to Britain, served as George Washington's vice president for eight long years during which he was mostly ignored, and finally served one term as the second president of the United States, from 1797 to 1801. His presidency was dominated by a crisis in relations with revolutionary France, in which French foreign-ministry agents demanded bribes before they would even open negotiations with American envoys — an incident later known as the XYZ Affair. The scandal pushed the United States to the edge of open war with France. Adams refused to be stampeded, built up the United States Navy quickly, negotiated a resolution, and avoided a full war that many of his own Federalist Party had wanted. His political reward for the restraint was to lose the next election to Thomas Jefferson. He retired to his farm in Quincy, Massachusetts, and lived another twenty-five years. He and Jefferson, old friends-and-rivals, both died on the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1826.

john-cabot-the-northwest-passage-search.context_blurb: John Cabot was a Venetian captain working out of Bristol in England who, in 1497, sailed west under a patent from King Henry VII and bumped into the coast of Newfoundland. He was almost certainly hunting for Asia; what he found instead were the Grand Banks, where fish gathered in such extraordinary numbers that English and Portuguese fishing fleets would cross the Atlantic every summer for the next three hundred years to haul them in by the ton. Cabot sailed home with no gold and no silk, but his report launched an English dream of a shortcut over the top of the New World to China. Later captains tried to make the dream real — Martin Frobisher, John Davis, Henry Hudson, William Baffin — and finally, in the 1840s, Sir John Franklin, whose entire two-ship Arctic expedition disappeared in the ice. Franklin's lost wrecks were found only in the twenty-first century, when careful sonar searches finally pinned them to the sea floor near where Inuit testimony had placed them all along. A workable Northwest Passage really did open at last, but only after the Arctic ice sheet began to retreat under modern climate change, well over four centuries after Cabot had first imagined it.

john-calvin-calvinism.context_blurb: John Calvin was a 16th-century French theologian whose careful, systematic version of Protestant Christianity would reshape Scotland, the Netherlands, and much of English-speaking North America. He was born in Noyon in 1509, the son of a cathedral administrator, and his early training steered him toward a learned profession at the universities of Paris and Orleans. In his twenties he underwent a sudden personal religious conversion, had to flee France, and spent his first exile years quietly writing a long book — the Institutes of the Christian Religion — meant to lay out the Protestant faith in orderly form. Passing through the small city of Geneva, he was pressed into service there by a fiery older reformer named Guillaume Farel, and apart from one brief banishment he spent the rest of his life running the religious life of that city as a kind of model Protestant commonwealth. His Geneva was austere and intensely disciplined. He also presided over one of the ugliest episodes of early Protestant history, when the city tried, convicted, and executed a Spanish anti-Trinitarian doctor named Michael Servetus for heresy — a death that Protestants and Catholics alike approved of at the time but that modern readers have mostly held against Calvin. He died in 1564. His followers would systematize his thought into a famous five-point summary that we still call Calvinism today.

john-locke-and-natural-rights.context_blurb: John Locke was a 17th-century English philosopher and physician whose political writing became the most important single influence on the American Declaration of Independence a hundred years after his death. Locke was born in 1632 to a Puritan family, studied at Oxford, and spent much of his career as personal physician and adviser to a leading English nobleman, which pulled him into the dangerous politics of his age. He spent years in exile in the Dutch Republic, returned to England after the Glorious Revolution of 1688, and lived long enough to see constitutional government take root in his own country. His great works argue that human beings are born free and equal, that they possess natural rights which no king or government creates, and that government is justified only when it protects those rights with the consent of the governed. If it does not, Locke argued, the people have the right to replace it. These ideas sound obvious today, which is itself a measure of how completely they won. Locke died in 1704 at the Essex country house of friends, reading aloud from the Psalms. He was still writing new chapters of philosophy almost to the end.

john-paul-ii-s-warsaw-homily-be-not-afra.context_blurb: The Polish cardinal Karol Wojtyla was elected pope in October 1978 and took the name John Paul II, becoming the first non-Italian pope in over four hundred years. He was also the first pope from a communist-ruled country. In June 1979, less than a year after his election, he returned to his Polish homeland for a long pilgrimage during which he celebrated open-air Masses attended by millions of Poles — a huge fraction of the entire Polish population came out to see him, in a country where the officially atheist Communist government controlled the press, the police, and the schools. The scale of the turnout astonished everyone, including the Polish Communist government and the Soviets, who had tried to discourage the visit. The pope's repeated public message, drawn from the Gospel, was that Christians should not be afraid of the regimes that threatened them. The crowds listening took the message directly. Within a year a shipyard electrician named Lech Walesa in Gdansk had helped found Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, which within a decade had helped bring down the entire communist system in Poland. John Paul II's 1979 visit to Poland is one of the clearest cases in recent history of a religious speech setting off a political earthquake.

joseph-lister-and-antiseptic-surgery.context_blurb: Joseph Lister was a Quaker-educated English surgeon who in the 1860s was running a surgical ward at the Royal Infirmary in Glasgow. In those days hospital surgery was itself a death sentence as often as not: perhaps half of all patients operated on for compound fractures or amputations died afterwards of what doctors glumly called 'hospitalism' — raging wound infections that spread through wards and killed in a few days. Surgeons wore their blood-stiffened coats as badges of experience and operated without washing their hands or their instruments. Lister read the new work of the French chemist Louis Pasteur, which blamed souring and spoiling on invisible microbes drifting in the air, and he made an inspired leap: perhaps the same microbes were what killed his patients, and perhaps a particular common industrial chemical could be used to kill them before they got into the wound. He began bathing the operating field, the dressings, and his own hands in it. His death rates fell dramatically. Most of his colleagues were slow to believe him, and some of the sharpest hospital nurses and surgeons of the day made cutting jokes at the strange new idea's expense, but Lister kept publishing, kept travelling, and kept speaking at medical congresses, and within twenty years his antiseptic methods, soon refined into sterile technique, had conquered surgical practice. Modern operating theatres are the direct descendants of his bloody Glasgow ward.

julius-caesar-crossing-the-rubicon.context_blurb: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and politician whose decision in the winter of 49 BC to march his army across a small river into Italy proper lit the fuse of a civil war that destroyed the Roman Republic. The river in question marked the boundary beyond which a Roman general was not allowed to bring his troops under arms, and by crossing it Caesar committed open treason against the state. He did it anyway, famously speaking a short Greek phrase as he gave the order. Within a few years he had defeated the senatorial forces led by his old friend and rival Pompey, made himself dictator of Rome, and was assassinated on the Senate floor by former allies. His adopted heir would eventually finish the civil wars and become Augustus. Caesar's crossing has given English the idiom to "cross the Rubicon" for any irreversible step, and the river's name is used two thousand years later to describe any point of no return — which is why Rubicon is also the name of a space mission and a brand of soft drink, among other things.

justinian-and-the-surviving-eastern-byza.context_blurb: Justinian the Great was a Byzantine emperor who ruled from AD 527 to 565 from the city his predecessor Constantine had built on the Bosphorus. He is often called the last Roman emperor because he tried, more seriously than anyone else after the fall of the western half, to put the old Roman world back together. His armies, led by the brilliant general Belisarius, re-conquered large parts of the lost West including North Africa and much of Italy, though the gains were partly undone within a generation of his death. He married Theodora, a former actress with a formidable will, and the two of them ruled as partners through a famous riot that nearly cost them their throne. Justinian ordered the codification of all Roman law into one systematic collection, which has stayed the foundation of civil law in most of continental Europe ever since. He commissioned one of the greatest churches ever built, a huge domed cathedral in his capital whose scale and construction techniques astonished every age that followed. He died an old man in his bed, and his vast building projects and his law books outlasted every emperor who came after him.

justinian-and-theodora.context_blurb: Justinian I ruled Byzantium from 527 to 565 and tried to put the whole Roman Empire back together before anyone else could. He is often remembered with his empress Theodora, a former actress whose rise to the throne was so irregular that a special law was passed to allow the marriage. The pair survived a terrifying week in 532 called the Nika riots, when a factional feud exploded into a full insurrection and Justinian was ready to flee until Theodora reportedly refused to run and shamed the men around her into holding the city. Justinian sent his brilliant general Belisarius to recover Italy from the Ostrogoths and North Africa from the Vandals, rebuilt Hagia Sophia from the ashes left by the riots on a scale no earlier Christian church had ever attempted, and most importantly commissioned a complete overhaul of Roman law called the Corpus Juris Civilis. His reign was also hit by one of the worst natural catastrophes of ancient history, which struck in his twentieth year on the throne and killed perhaps a quarter of the Mediterranean population — ending any serious chance of restoring the old western Roman provinces, breaking the empire's finances, and leaving a long memory of unfinished grandeur that shaped Byzantine politics for the next two centuries.

justinian-s-code-corpus-juris-civilis.context_blurb: The emperor Justinian came to the throne in 527 to find Roman law in a mess — a thousand years of statutes, imperial decrees, and the writings of famous jurists had piled up without any serious effort to clean them up and make them consistent. He appointed a brilliant lawyer named Tribonian to lead a commission of about ten jurists to sort through the whole accumulated inheritance, keep what still mattered, cut what contradicted itself, and set the whole thing out in a comprehensive series of books. The resulting Corpus Juris Civilis — the Body of Civil Law — was finished in just a few years in the early 530s, in four parts: the Code (collected imperial statutes), the Digest (excerpts from the great classical jurists), the Institutes (a textbook for students), and later the Novellae (new laws Justinian issued afterward). The Digest alone preserves nearly all we know of the Roman legal tradition's greatest writers, since most of their original works have been lost. When medieval scholars at the University of Bologna rediscovered the Digest in the eleventh century, it became the basis of a legal revival that shaped the civil-law tradition still in force across most of continental Europe and much of the world today.

kamikaze-pilots.context_blurb: In the final year of the Pacific War, as Japan's military fortunes declined sharply and the United States Navy and Marine Corps closed in on the Japanese home islands, the Imperial Japanese Navy and Army deliberately organized units of pilots whose mission was to deliberately crash their aircraft, loaded with bombs or extra fuel, into American ships. The pilots were called kamikaze, from a Japanese phrase meaning divine wind that recalled the storms that had destroyed Mongol invasion fleets in the thirteenth century. The first large organized kamikaze attacks took place during the American landings in the Philippines in October 1944 and continued through the end of the war. The great majority of kamikaze attacks were concentrated at the Battle of Okinawa in the spring of 1945, where thousands of kamikaze sorties sank or damaged a long list of American and British warships off the island. Over three thousand kamikaze pilots were killed. The attacks sank roughly fifty Allied warships and damaged hundreds more, which was significant but did not come close to stopping the Allied advance. The willingness of young Japanese men to die in this way, combined with Japan's refusal to surrender even after Okinawa, deeply shaped American calculations about what invading the Japanese home islands would cost.

katyn-and-the-soviet-invasion-of-poland-.context_blurb: On September 17, 1939, barely two weeks after Nazi Germany invaded Poland from the west, the Soviet Union invaded from the east under the terms of a secret deal Hitler and Stalin had signed the month before. The Red Army swallowed the eastern half of Poland and took hundreds of thousands of Polish soldiers prisoner, including the officer corps — the professional military leadership of the Polish state, together with lawyers, doctors, scholars, and reserve officers who had been called up for service. In the spring of 1940, on direct orders signed by Stalin himself and the Soviet Politburo, the NKVD took roughly 22,000 of these men out into the forests at Katyn and other sites, shot each of them in the back of the head, and bulldozed the bodies into mass pits. The Soviet Union denied having done it for decades, blaming the massacre on the Germans, and the Western Allies went along in silence through World War II because they needed Moscow against Hitler. Only after the Soviet Union itself was gone did Mikhail Gorbachev and later Boris Yeltsin finally hand over the signed order and admit Soviet guilt. Katyn remains the clearest single piece of forensic evidence historians have of what Stalin's regime did to its political enemies, and it still sits uneasily in Russian-Polish relations today.

kepler-s-laws-of-planetary-motion.context_blurb: Johannes Kepler was a 17th-century German mathematician and astronomer who inherited one of the greatest piles of raw astronomical data ever assembled and, after years of wrestling with it, produced three mathematical laws that describe how planets actually move in the sky. Kepler was a devout Lutheran who believed the heavens must display God's mathematical mind, and he thought it was his duty to find the pattern. He worked under the Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe, who had spent his life measuring the positions of the planets to a previously unheard-of precision, and after Tycho's death Kepler was left with the records and the task. The results overturned a 2000-year-old assumption that the orbits of the heavens must be perfect circles and replaced it with something stranger and more useful. Kepler's own life was marked by hardship: his mother was tried for witchcraft and he had to defend her in court, his first wife and favorite son died young, and his patron and his home town were caught up in the religious wars that tore 17th-century Europe apart. He died in 1630. His work later gave Isaac Newton the clue he needed to formulate universal gravitation.

king-arthur-the-round-table-chivalric-le.context_blurb: Somewhere in the mists of post-Roman Britain, a war-leader may once have held back the invading Saxons for a generation. Over the centuries that followed, that memory grew into something far larger: the greatest story the Middle Ages ever told itself about what a king and his knights were supposed to be. In the Arthurian legend, a boy of unknown parentage pulls a magical sword from a stone, is crowned king, gathers the finest knights in the world around a famous table built so that no seat is higher than any other, and sends them out looking for a sacred relic that only the pure of heart can touch. There is a wizard who manipulates history from the shadows, a mysterious woman from a body of water who gives him a second blade, a traitor nephew, and a love triangle that will destroy them all. By the time these stories were being written down, in the works of a Welsh cleric, a French court poet, and an English prisoner, no one really believed the legend was straight history any more. But the ideal of the knight who serves God, protects the weak, and keeps his word was being built from these tales for a thousand years, and still shapes what we mean today by the word honor.

kingdom-bronzes-of-benin.context_blurb: The Kingdom of Benin, in the forested country of what is now southwestern Nigeria, was a long-lived and powerful West African state from at least the 11th century AD until a British punitive expedition sacked its capital in 1897. For centuries it was ruled by hereditary monarchs called obas, and its royal court sat behind huge walled earthworks that modern archaeology has shown were among the largest earthworks constructed anywhere in the pre-industrial world. The kingdom is best known today for the extraordinary metalwork its royal craftsmen produced: lifelike cast-brass human heads of past obas, long cast-brass plaques that once covered the pillars of the royal palace, and sculpted figures of warriors, hunters, leopards, and courtiers, all made by the lost-wax casting technique at a level of technical skill that stunned European observers when the pieces first reached Europe. The British expedition in 1897 looted thousands of these pieces, and they are now scattered among museums across Europe and the United States, where ongoing demands for their return have become one of the most-watched cases in the global debate about colonial-era museum collections. Benin's own descendants — the kingdom and the obaship still exist in modern Nigeria — are the main voices calling for the Bronzes to come home.

kingdom-of-aksum-axum.context_blurb: The Kingdom of Aksum rose in the Ethiopian highlands and the Red Sea coast of what is now Eritrea during the 1st century AD, controlled a hinge of the Indian Ocean trade network between the Roman Mediterranean and the Indian subcontinent, and remained a serious regional power through the 7th century. At its height Aksum traded in ivory, gold, incense, and slaves, minted its own coinage (in gold, silver, and bronze — one of the few African kingdoms to issue its own gold coinage in antiquity), spoke an early form of Ge'ez, and built a tradition of enormous carved stone obelisks called stelae to mark royal tombs. The tallest of these stelae originally stood over thirty meters high and is one of the largest single monolithic stone monuments anywhere in the ancient world. Aksum is also the kingdom where King Ezana adopted Christianity in the 4th century, which founded the Ethiopian Christian tradition that continues today. The old capital still stands, with its stele field, its ancient Christian churches, and a treasury chapel that modern Ethiopian Orthodox tradition claims houses the original Ark of the Covenant. Aksum declined over the 7th and 8th centuries as Islamic expansion along the Red Sea trade routes cut off its access to the sea, and the Ethiopian state's political center eventually moved south.

kingdom-of-kongo.context_blurb: The Kingdom of Kongo, which arose in the late 14th century in the lower Congo River basin near the Atlantic coast of what is now Angola and Democratic Republic of Congo, was one of the great centralized African kingdoms encountered by the earliest Portuguese explorers in the 1480s. The king of Kongo, called the Manikongo, ruled from a capital called Mbanza Kongo over a confederation of provinces, with a complicated royal court and well-organized tribute system. The king, Nzinga a Nkuwu, converted to Christianity shortly after Portuguese contact and took the Christian name Joao I. His son and successor, Afonso I, became a devout Catholic ruler, learned to write Portuguese, corresponded directly with the kings of Portugal and the pope, built Christian churches, and tried to run Kongo as a Christian kingdom aligned with the Portuguese crown. The relationship with Portugal was deeply damaged over the following century by the Portuguese demand for slaves, which fueled the early Atlantic slave trade and eventually destabilized the kingdom. Kongo struggled on in various forms through the colonial period, and its Christian culture — a West African Catholic tradition with its own saints and local practices — has had a long afterlife.

kingdom-of-kush-nubia-mero.context_blurb: South of ancient Egypt, up the Nile beyond the first cataract into what is now northern Sudan, lay the long-lived African kingdoms the Egyptians called Kush — a civilization that interacted with Egypt for over two thousand years as an occasional vassal, an occasional conqueror, and a close cultural neighbor. Nubian kings from the city of Napata actually ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty for most of the 8th and 7th centuries BC, filling the whole lower Nile with their own pyramid-building tradition. After an Assyrian invasion forced them back south, the Nubian capital eventually shifted upriver to Meroe, which flourished as a wealthy kingdom from the 3rd century BC until the 4th century AD. The Meroitic kingdom developed its own alphabetic script (still only partly deciphered), smelted iron on a large scale, built its own distinctive steep-sided pyramids (small compared to Egyptian ones but far more numerous — there are more pyramids in Sudan than in Egypt), and traded gold and ivory into the wider Mediterranean world through Egypt. Meroe fell to the rising kingdom of Aksum in the 4th century AD and over the following centuries was gradually absorbed into the emerging Christian kingdoms of Nubia, which lasted until Islamic conquest in the medieval period.

knights-chivalry-the-code.context_blurb: For much of the Middle Ages, the fighting elite of Christian Europe were armored horsemen trained from boyhood, first as pages running small errands for ladies, then as teenage attendants to a working knight, learning to ride, to serve, and to fight, and finally sworn as full warriors in a long ceremony that mixed prayer, bathing, and a ceremonial blow across the shoulder. Their job was to fight; their expensive horse and armor meant someone had to feed and arm them; and the code they were supposed to live by, loosely called chivalry, laid duties on them toward their lord, their faith, and ordinary people without the means to defend themselves. In peacetime they tested themselves at tournaments, which were both sport and training, and which also sometimes killed them. The reality was often uglier than the code, and famous knights broke the code as often as they kept it, massacring prisoners or looting ordinary villages when they thought no one was watching. The story covers both sides, the training and the gear, the tournaments and the warhorses, and the famous moments, some of them generous and some of them bloody, when chivalry worked or memorably failed. The modern English word 'chivalry' still carries both halves of this inheritance, the beautiful ideal and the real difficulty of ever actually living up to it.

korea-three-kingdoms-goryeo-joseon.context_blurb: Korean history runs through a sequence of major dynasties that together cover nearly two thousand years. The Three Kingdoms period from the 1st century BC to the 7th century AD saw three rival states — Goguryeo in the north and across much of modern Manchuria, Baekje in the southwest, and Silla in the southeast — vying for control of the peninsula. The Silla kingdom, in alliance with Tang-dynasty China, eventually unified most of Korea under its rule in the late 7th century. Silla was followed by the Goryeo dynasty (918 to 1392), from which the English word Korea derives, which produced extraordinary celadon ceramics, early movable-type printing with metal type centuries before Gutenberg, and the entire woodblock-printed Buddhist Tripitaka. The following Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1910), the longest-ruling royal house in East Asian history, consolidated Korea as a thoroughly Confucian state, developed the ingenious hangul alphabet under King Sejong the Great in the 15th century, and fought off two major Japanese invasions in the 1590s. Joseon ended at Japanese annexation in 1910 and the Korean Peninsula was divided in half after World War II in a tragedy that is still being lived out today.

korean-berlin-spy-drama-espionage.context_blurb: The Cold War, running from the late 1940s to 1991, was in large part a quiet war of intelligence agencies. The main antagonists — the American Central Intelligence Agency and the Soviet KGB, with the British MI6 and the East German Stasi as major supporting characters — ran enormous worldwide operations recruiting agents, running defectors, conducting signals intelligence, waging propaganda, and (in some cases) running covert paramilitary operations. The divided city of Berlin was the most intense espionage theater of the Cold War, with four occupation sectors, hundreds of intelligence officers from both sides operating within walking distance of each other, and the Berlin Wall after 1961 running right through what had been the city center. The Korean War of 1950 to 1953 and its tense aftermath along the 38th parallel became another front for intelligence work. Famous spies on both sides — the Cambridge Five (Burgess, Maclean, Philby, Blunt, Cairncross) who passed British secrets to the Soviets, the American diplomat Alger Hiss, the physicist Klaus Fuchs who passed atomic secrets, the pilot Francis Gary Powers of the U-2 shot down over the Soviet Union — became household names at various points. Much of the espionage history is still only partly declassified, and new documents continue to appear from Western and ex-Soviet archives.

korean-war-the-38th-parallel.context_blurb: After the Second World War, the Korean peninsula was divided along the 38th parallel of latitude into a Soviet-occupied northern half and an American-occupied southern half. The two occupation zones eventually produced two separate governments in 1948 — a communist People's Democratic Republic in the north under Kim Il-sung and a non-communist Republic of Korea in the south under Syngman Rhee — and in June 1950 the North Korean army crossed the parallel and invaded the south, apparently with Soviet and Chinese approval. American and United Nations forces, under the overall command of General Douglas MacArthur, intervened on behalf of South Korea and pushed the North Koreans back to the Chinese border. China then entered the war on the North Korean side, sending enormous numbers of troops across the Yalu River and pushing the UN forces back south. The front line eventually stabilized near where it had started, around the 38th parallel. An armistice signed in July 1953 ended active hostilities, but no formal peace treaty was ever signed, and the heavily militarized Demilitarized Zone between the two Koreas is still one of the most dangerous borders in the world. The war killed roughly three million people, mostly Korean civilians, and left the peninsula divided.

kristallnacht.context_blurb: On the night of November 9 to 10, 1938, a coordinated wave of attacks against Jewish-owned businesses, synagogues, and homes swept across Nazi Germany and the recently annexed Austria. Nazi Party stormtroopers and ordinary civilian mobs, acting under the direction of propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, burned over a thousand synagogues, smashed the windows of over seven thousand Jewish-owned shops, destroyed thousands of Jewish homes and places of worship, beat Jewish Germans in the streets, killed over a hundred, and arrested some thirty thousand Jewish men who were sent to the Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen concentration camps. The whole event was triggered by the Nazis as a supposedly spontaneous public reaction to the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris by a young Polish Jew. The German term that became attached to the night — the broken-glass night — referred to the glass of thousands of smashed shop windows glittering in the streets the next morning. Kristallnacht marked a sharp escalation of the Nazi persecution of German Jews. From that night forward the Nazi state moved from legal discrimination into open violence. The international response was muted. Several hundred thousand German Jews fled over the following months, but many were refused entry by every country they applied to.

kublai-khan-the-yuan-dynasty.context_blurb: Kublai Khan, the grandson of Genghis Khan, was the Mongol ruler who completed the conquest of China that his grandfather had begun. In 1271 he formally declared himself the first emperor of a new dynasty, the Yuan, with a Chinese dynastic name and his capital at Dadu, on the site of modern Beijing. Under Yuan rule, China was for the first time governed by a non-Chinese dynasty. Kublai imported Persian, Central Asian, Tibetan, and even European administrators into the Mongol service, treating ethnic Han Chinese as the lowest of four tiered social classes, which did not endear his dynasty to the people it ruled. He failed in two attempted maritime invasions of Japan, where typhoons remembered in Japanese as the kamikaze (divine wind) destroyed his fleets. His court was famously opulent, with foreign ambassadors arriving from every corner of the Old World, and it was there that a Venetian merchant named Marco Polo claimed to have served for years in the 1270s and 1280s. The Yuan dynasty survived Kublai himself by less than a century. By the mid-14th century, popular revolts, famine, inflation, and factional fighting at court brought the dynasty down, and the ethnic Chinese Ming dynasty replaced it in 1368.

kublai-khan-the-yuan-marco-polo.context_blurb: Kublai Khan was the grandson of Genghis Khan and the Mongol ruler who completed the conquest of China that his grandfather had begun. In 1271 he formally established the Yuan dynasty with himself as emperor and his capital at Dadu, on the site of modern Beijing. Under Yuan rule China was for the first time governed by a non-Chinese dynasty, and the Mongols imported Persian, Turkic, Tibetan, and European experts into their administration while treating ethnic Han Chinese as a lower caste. Kublai's court was famously opulent, with foreign ambassadors arriving from every quarter of the Old World. One such foreign visitor, a Venetian merchant named Marco Polo, claimed to have served Kublai for years in the 1270s and 1280s and to have traveled all over the empire on imperial business, and after his return to Italy he dictated a book that gave medieval Europe its first detailed secondhand picture of Chinese wealth, cities, and government. Modern historians still argue about how much of Marco Polo's account is firsthand and how much was embellished or borrowed, but the book was wildly influential in Europe. Kublai Khan himself died in 1294, and the Yuan dynasty collapsed into civil war and local revolt within another seventy years, giving way to the native Chinese Ming.

labor-unions-and-the-early-reform-moveme.context_blurb: In the first half of the nineteenth century, working people in Britain and the United States began forming the first modern labor unions, cooperative societies, and mass political movements for the vote. The British Industrial Revolution had thrown together huge new working populations in cities like Manchester, Leeds, and Glasgow, people who did not own the machines they worked on, who could be fired at will, and who had no vote. Early union organizing was illegal or barely tolerated: judges applied old laws against conspiracies to break up any sworn society of workers; employers blacklisted organizers; magistrates sentenced strikers to transportation on penal colony ships. Out of that struggle came a string of foundational stories. The questions ahead cover the tree in a Dorset village under which a group of farm laborers were said to have met, the pay cut that pushed them to organize, the technicality on which the government condemned them, the brutal convict punishment one of them described, the great working-class political movement for parliamentary reform called Chartism and one of its central demands, the way opponents mocked its mass petitions, a factory-reform pamphlet with a shocking name, and an economist's quieter explanation for why real wages across the century rose in the end. It matters because this is the moment when a mass democratic politics of wages, hours, and the vote first took shape — the beginning of the labor movement that would reshape every industrial country.

lalibela-s-rock-hewn-churches.context_blurb: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia in the 12th and 13th centuries AD, under the Zagwe king Gebre Mesqel Lalibela, workers carved an extraordinary cluster of Christian churches directly down into the solid rock of a volcanic plateau. The churches were not built on top of the ground; they were hewn out of the ground, sunk below the surface in deep rectangular trenches, with their doorways and roofs cut at the original ground level and the whole buildings — complete with columns, arched windows, interior naves, and cross-shaped floor plans — chiseled out of the surrounding rock like enormous sculptures. The complex contains eleven monolithic churches, connected to each other by rock-cut tunnels and courtyards, and all of them are still in active use today for Ethiopian Orthodox worship. Lalibela was intended to be a kind of New Jerusalem in Ethiopia, built to give Ethiopian Christians their own place of pilgrimage at a time when Muslim conquest had made travel to the actual Jerusalem difficult. The churches are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the great marvels of medieval Christian architecture, and they are especially impressive given that they were quietly produced by African Christians in the Zagwe dynasty's generation, roughly the same time that the Gothic cathedrals were rising in France.

las-casas-the-salamanca-school-and-the-d.context_blurb: Bartolome de Las Casas was a 16th-century Spanish priest who had come to the New World as a landowning encomendero — a holder of grants of Indigenous forced labor — but experienced a moral conversion in middle age and spent the rest of his long life as the fiercest critic of Spanish treatment of Indigenous Americans. He wrote and lobbied and petitioned the Spanish crown until he won laws limiting Indigenous enslavement, and he debated other theologians in person on whether the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were full human beings with souls and natural rights, a position he passionately argued they were. Working around the same question, a group of Spanish Dominican theologians at the University of Salamanca, led by Francisco de Vitoria, developed the first serious systematic theory of natural rights that applied universally to all human beings, regardless of race or religion. Their arguments laid the intellectual groundwork that would eventually feed into modern international law and human-rights theory, and they stand as a Western — and specifically Christian — moral tradition that pushed back against the worst behavior of Western conquerors. The record of the Spanish conquest is dark; the record of Las Casas and the Salamanca School is one of the few bright threads inside it.

lascaux-altamira-cave-paintings.context_blurb: During the last Ice Age, from around 40,000 to 10,000 years ago, prehistoric human beings in Europe produced astonishing painted art deep inside limestone caves across what is now southwestern France and northern Spain. The paintings are of large animals — horses, bulls, aurochs, bison, deer, mammoths, lions, rhinos — rendered in sure dark outlines filled with ochre browns and reds, charcoal blacks, and sometimes elaborate shading suggesting the muscular bulk of the animal. The paintings are often located in deep, cramped, hard-to-reach parts of the cave systems, far from any living area, which suggests that they had a ritual rather than a decorative purpose. The two best-known sites are Lascaux Cave in the Dordogne region of France (discovered in 1940 by four local teenagers and their dog) and Altamira Cave in northern Spain (discovered in the 1870s by a girl exploring with her father, whose claim about the paintings' extreme age was dismissed by professional archaeologists for years). Both caves had to be closed to ordinary visitors in the 20th century because the breath of tourists was damaging the paint; carefully built replica caves are now open nearby. The paintings are the oldest major art most Europeans still think of as their inheritance.

later-crusades-the-sack-of-constantinopl.context_blurb: By the early 13th century, Europe's crusading movement had already lost control of its own holy war. One large expedition, meant to retake Jerusalem by way of Egypt, ran out of money owed to its Venetian shippers and ended up detouring to a different target instead. The target was the greatest Christian city in the world, the capital of the eastern Roman Empire, which the crusaders sacked, carving up its lands between western lords and shipping its treasures home as plunder. Priceless relics, famous works of ancient bronze and gold, and whole libraries of Greek learning were looted or destroyed, and the eastern empire never fully recovered. The split between western and eastern Christians, which had been bitter already, became a wound that would never heal in the Middle Ages, and that eastern Christians still remember today. Later crusades drifted even further from the ideal that had launched the movement in the first place, becoming a tool for whichever ruler could persuade a pope to bless his own private war. The memory of what Christians did to other Christians in the year of this sack haunted the whole enterprise ever after. The story covers the sack itself, the Christian treasures that ended up in western Europe as a result, and the mood of a crusading movement that had quietly started to lose its own soul.

latin-american-independence-bolivar-and-.context_blurb: Between roughly 1810 and 1825, nearly all of Spain's vast empire in the Americas broke away from Madrid and declared itself into existence as a cluster of new independent republics. Two generals became the great symbols of the movement. From the north, the Venezuelan-born Simon Bolivar, from a wealthy Creole family and educated in Europe, raised armies that marched out of Venezuela, over the Andes, and down through what would become Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and the mountainous country later named Bolivia in his honor. From the south, the Argentine general Jose de San Martin trained a disciplined army at the foot of the Andes, led it over the mountain passes, liberated Chile with the help of local patriots, and sailed north to Peru. In 1822 the two commanders met at Guayaquil in a famously secret conversation; soon afterward San Martin quietly left the stage, leaving Bolivar to finish the war. The questions ahead cover Bolivar's great nickname, his most famous feat of mountain warfare, the pack animals he leaned on in the Andes, a decisive battle on his northern campaign, San Martin's dreamed-of future for the liberated republics, and Bolivar's bitter dying words. It matters because this was the moment the modern map of Latin America took shape — a dozen new republics, enormous promise, and bitter arguments about how to govern them that would echo through the next two centuries.

lavoisier-and-modern-chemistry.context_blurb: Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier was an 18th-century French nobleman, tax official, and the founder of modern chemistry. Working mostly in a private laboratory in Paris, he brought the scales and the balance into chemistry and demanded that every experiment be weighed before and after, which turned chemistry from an alchemical craft into a real quantitative science. He proved what burning actually is, named oxygen and hydrogen, and co-authored the first systematic textbook of chemistry that still looks like chemistry today. He also discovered that in any chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed — the law of the conservation of mass. All of that would be enough to make him famous. Instead he is also remembered as a tragedy: because his official job as a tax collector made him an enemy of the French Revolution, he was arrested during the Reign of Terror and executed by guillotine in May 1794, aged fifty. The mathematician Lagrange said bitterly that it would take a century to produce another head like his. The French Revolution's willingness to kill one of its greatest minds became the defining image of what happens when ideology runs ahead of common sense.

lawrence-of-arabia-and-the-arab-revolt.context_blurb: The Arab Revolt against Ottoman rule began in June 1916, when the Sharif of Mecca, Hussein bin Ali, declared his family's war against the Turks in exchange for a promise of British support for an independent Arab kingdom after the war. Lawrence of Arabia — Thomas Edward Lawrence, a shy young Oxford archaeologist who had worked in Ottoman Syria on an archaeological dig before the war — joined the revolt as a British liaison officer and became its Western face. He fought alongside Hussein's son Faisal, learned the tribal politics of the Hejaz, dressed in Arab robes, and helped plan a long and clever campaign of raids on the Hejaz Railway that ran down the spine of Arabia. The revolt's great military surprise was the capture of the Red Sea port of Aqaba, taken in an operation that caught the Ottoman garrison completely off-guard. But what Lawrence and the Arabs did not know was that the British and French had already struck a secret deal of their own — the Sykes-Picot Agreement — about what to do with the Ottoman Arab lands after the war, one that would not include the independent Arab kingdom Hussein had been promised. The betrayal would shape the modern Middle East for the next hundred years.

lemaitre-the-priest-who-proposed-the-big.context_blurb: Georges Lemaitre was a Belgian Catholic priest, a decorated artillery officer from the First World War, and a trained astrophysicist with doctorates from Louvain and MIT. In 1927, working from Einstein's equations of general relativity, he published a paper arguing that the universe is not an eternal static thing but is actually expanding, with distant galaxies flying away from us faster the farther off they are. Two years later the American astronomer Edwin Hubble reported the same expansion from his telescope observations at Mount Wilson, confirming Lemaitre's math. Lemaitre then took the logic to its startling conclusion: if everything is flying apart now, in the distant past everything must have been packed together, so the universe had a beginning. He called this starting state the 'primeval atom' — the deeply misleading nickname 'the Big Bang' was coined decades later as a sneer by a rival astronomer who disliked the whole idea. Einstein himself at first rejected Lemaitre's expanding universe, telling the young priest to his face that his mathematics was fine but his physics was objectionable; years later Einstein publicly retracted and praised him instead. Lemaitre spent the rest of his life as a professor at Louvain and later as president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences. He thought carefully about how the physics he had helped invent should and should not be talked about in public, and he gave both his scientific colleagues and his fellow Catholics firm advice on the matter whenever he was asked.

lenin-s-red-terror-and-the-founding-of-t.context_blurb: When the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917 they immediately began a program of terror against their enemies, both real and imagined. Vladimir Lenin set up a political police force called the Cheka within six weeks of the Revolution, under the command of a cold Polish aristocrat-turned-revolutionary named Felix Dzerzhinsky, and the Cheka was built from the start as a political enforcement arm. After a would-be assassin shot and wounded Lenin in August 1918, the Red Terror was formally declared, and in a matter of months the Cheka executed tens of thousands of nobles, priests, officers, factory owners, kulak peasants, and anyone the regime chose to treat as a class enemy. Lenin personally pushed for new institutions of mass imprisonment to be built from scratch, and the Soviet forced-labor camp system was born in 1923 in the old monastery buildings on the Solovetsky islands up near the Arctic Circle, where the system's violence operated under its own rules. Across the 1920s and 1930s the system swelled into a vast archipelago of camps and prisons across Siberia and the north; by Stalin's time it would hold millions. The scale and cruelty of what Lenin had set in motion were not fully documented in the West until the writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn smuggled out his book 'The Gulag Archipelago' in the 1970s.

leonardo-da-vinci.context_blurb: Leonardo da Vinci was a Florentine painter, sculptor, military engineer, anatomist, inventor, hydraulic engineer, and natural historian, and he was first-rate at every one of these — a combination that even his contemporaries did not know what to do with. He was born in 1452 in a hill town outside Florence, trained as a teenage apprentice in the workshop of the painter Verrocchio, and spent the next decades moving between the courts of Milan, Rome, and finally the French king Francis I, who adored him and settled him in a country manor in the Loire Valley at the end of his life. He painted only a small number of finished pictures, including one portrait of a young Florentine wife that would eventually become the most famous image in the world, and a huge wall painting of the Last Supper in a Milan monastery. But he filled thousands of notebook pages with sketches, observations, and designs for machines that would not actually be built for centuries after his death. He is remembered as the model of what a 'Renaissance man' was — endlessly curious, equally at home with brush and chisel and pen and dissection knife, drawn to anything that moved or lived or worked, and often leaving great projects unfinished because another more interesting project had already caught his eye. He died in France in 1519.

leonardo-da-vinci-michelangelo.context_blurb: Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo Buonarroti were the two giants of the Italian Renaissance and, by all accounts, could not stand each other. Leonardo was the older man, a painter who filled thousands of notebook pages with sketches of flying machines, dissected cadavers, river engineering, musical instruments, and anatomical studies no one would equal for centuries, and he kept his private notebooks in a peculiar hand that, as a famous and much-copied quirk, used an unusual trick to make casual reading harder. Michelangelo was a generation younger, sharp-tongued, deeply religious, and insisted on a particular identity as a craftsman, one that put stone and chisel ahead of brush and panel in his own imagination. He spent four backbreaking years painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel from a scaffold he had designed himself and then, decades later, carved a colossal statue of the biblical king David from an abandoned block of marble. The city of Florence once hired the two of them to paint competing battle murals on opposite walls of the same great council hall; the project became almost as famous for the rivalry as for the images themselves, and what the two artists actually produced is known today mostly from preparatory sketches and from the memories of contemporaries who saw the drafts in progress.

leonardo-da-vinci-mona-lisa-and-last-sup.context_blurb: Leonardo da Vinci (1452 to 1519) was an Italian Renaissance polymath — painter, sculptor, architect, engineer, anatomist, inventor, and tireless notebook-keeper. He was born out of wedlock in the Tuscan town of Vinci, trained in the workshop of the Florentine artist Verrocchio, and spent most of his adult life moving between Florence, Milan, Rome, and finally France, where he died at the court of King Francis I. He completed only a small number of paintings and left many of them unfinished, but the ones he did finish include some of the most famous paintings in Western art, including a mural of the Last Supper on the wall of a convent dining hall in Milan and a portrait of a young Florentine merchant's wife now hanging behind bulletproof glass in the Louvre in Paris. Leonardo was also a serious scientist by the standards of his age — his anatomical dissections and drawings are extraordinary, and his notebooks are full of mechanical inventions, flying machines, and curious observations about water, birds, and the formation of mountains. Most of his work was never published in his lifetime. His influence on Western painting through pupils and imitators was large; his influence through his unpublished notebooks had to wait several centuries for a proper audience.

lewis-and-clark-sacagawea.context_blurb: In 1804, less than two years after Thomas Jefferson had bought the vast Louisiana Territory from Napoleon's France, Jefferson sent his personal secretary Meriwether Lewis and Lewis's old army friend William Clark west with a small expedition to explore the new territory, find a water route to the Pacific if one existed, map the land, catalog its plants and animals, and establish American contact with its Indigenous peoples. The expedition — called the Corps of Discovery — set out from St. Louis up the Missouri River in the spring of 1804, wintered among the Mandan villages in what is now North Dakota, picked up during that winter a French-Canadian interpreter named Toussaint Charbonneau and his young Shoshone wife Sacagawea with their newborn son, crossed the Rocky Mountains with Shoshone help, reached the Pacific Ocean in the autumn of 1805, overwintered on the Oregon coast, and returned to St. Louis in 1806 with astonishing journals full of new species, new maps, and new information. Sacagawea's presence with the party is often credited as one of the reasons it survived; a young woman carrying an infant was a visible signal that the party came in peace rather than as a war band. She is now one of the most-honored Indigenous figures in American history.

liberation-of-paris.context_blurb: On August 25, 1944, after four years of Nazi occupation, the city of Paris was liberated by a combined force of Free French soldiers under General Jacques Leclerc and American soldiers of the United States Fourth Infantry Division, supported by a popular uprising of the French Resistance that had seized key points across the city in the preceding week. The Allied high command had originally planned to bypass Paris and keep driving east, judging that fighting through the city would consume resources needed for the pursuit into Germany, but General Dwight Eisenhower was persuaded to divert Leclerc's armored division into the capital. The German military governor of Paris, General Dietrich von Choltitz, had been ordered by Hitler to destroy the city rather than let it fall intact into Allied hands, and had explosives placed on the great landmarks of Paris including the Eiffel Tower, Notre-Dame, and the bridges over the Seine. He disobeyed the order and surrendered the city intact. General Charles de Gaulle entered Paris the next day in a huge triumphal walk down the Champs-Elysees. The liberation became one of the most emotionally charged moments of the war in Western Europe. Four years of German occupation ended in a single day of jubilation in the streets of the French capital.

liberation-of-the-camps.context_blurb: In the last months of the war in Europe, as the Soviet Red Army advanced from the east and American, British, Canadian, and other Western Allied forces advanced from the west, Allied soldiers began liberating the Nazi concentration camps and death camps scattered across occupied Europe. The Red Army liberated Majdanek, in occupied Poland, in July 1944, encountering the first intact extermination facility most Allied officials had ever seen; Western journalists were initially skeptical of the reports. Auschwitz-Birkenau fell to Soviet forces on January 27, 1945, with thousands of surviving prisoners still inside, though the Germans had evacuated most prisoners on brutal forced marches west in the preceding weeks. Over the following months Western Allied forces entered Bergen-Belsen (where Anne Frank had died only weeks earlier), Dachau, Buchenwald, and dozens of other camps. The Allied soldiers who liberated the camps saw conditions that permanently changed how they thought about the enemy they had been fighting. Allied commanders required local German civilians to be marched through the camps and shown what their own government had been doing. Photographic and film documentation from the liberations became central evidence at the Nuremberg Trials. The January anniversary of Auschwitz's liberation is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

lincoln-s-assassination.context_blurb: On the evening of April 14, 1865 — Good Friday, five days after Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox — President Abraham Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C., while watching a comedy called Our American Cousin from the presidential box. He died early the next morning in a boarding-house across the street without regaining consciousness. The killer was John Wilkes Booth, a well-known actor from a famous theatrical family and a bitter Confederate sympathizer who had been plotting against Lincoln for months. Booth had organized a small conspiracy that aimed to behead the federal government in a single night by striking at several leaders at once; some of his co-conspirators attacked their targets, some lost their nerve, and in the end only Booth's own attack succeeded. Booth escaped on horseback into Virginia and was tracked down and shot in a tobacco barn twelve days later. The questions ahead cover the Latin phrase Booth shouted on stage, the small firearm he used, who he was before the shooting, the major Civil War event that pushed the plot forward, the full shape of the plot, a notable historical first among the convicted conspirators, the moment in the play Booth timed his shot to, a chance object that saved one of his other targets, a strange earlier incident in which one of Booth's older brothers saved a prominent young man from being killed on a train platform, Booth's last words, the reason the president's box was unguarded that night, and the famous eulogy spoken over Lincoln's body in the little bedroom where he died. It matters because the assassination deepened the national trauma of the Civil War and ripped the reunited country out of the hands of the one leader most committed to a merciful peace.

linear-perspective-in-art.context_blurb: Linear perspective is the geometric trick that lets a painter draw a three-dimensional scene onto a flat panel so that it looks like a real space the viewer could step into. It was figured out by Florentine artists and architects in the early 15th century, with the architect Filippo Brunelleschi usually credited with the first clear demonstration, and the method was quickly written up in treatises for other painters. The method depends on a single technical idea that any Renaissance apprentice would learn before mixing paint — a way of pinning the scene to the position of a viewer standing at one specific place. Within a generation the new technique spread across Italy, and by 1500 painters as different as Masaccio, Piero della Francesca, Mantegna, Raphael, and Leonardo had absorbed it so thoroughly that it became invisible — the normal way a Western picture was built. Later baroque painters played brilliantly with the same math, pushing illusion to new extremes, and the arrival of linear perspective is often marked as the moment Western painting shook loose from medieval conventions and set out on a path that would run until the invention of the camera. Scholars have argued ever since over how much of the credit should go to the mathematicians, how much to the artists themselves, and how much to the strange workshop demonstrations the first Florentines are said to have staged in the open street for curious passers-by.

linnaeus-and-biological-classification.context_blurb: Carl Linnaeus was an 18th-century Swedish botanist and physician who gave the natural world its filing system. Before him, naturalists described plants and animals in long, inconsistent Latin phrases that nobody could agree on. Linnaeus proposed a simple scheme: every living thing gets exactly two names, a genus and a species, both in Latin, and every species belongs to a tidy nested hierarchy of kingdom, class, order, genus, and species. He published the system in his huge book Systema Naturae and kept expanding it through many editions over his life. Within a generation almost every working naturalist on Earth was using his method, and over 250 years later we still are. Linnaeus had a bit of mischief in him; when a critic attacked his work, he quietly named an ugly weed after the man, which is a joke that lived forever in the botanical literature. He also classified humans within his system, placing us among the primates, which was controversial. He died in 1778 in Uppsala, a famous man and still Sweden's most celebrated scientist.

lise-meitner-and-the-discovery-of-nuclea.context_blurb: Lise Meitner was an Austrian-Jewish physicist who in the 1920s and 1930s was one of the leading nuclear researchers in Europe, working for decades in Berlin as the scientific partner of the chemist Otto Hahn. Together they bombarded the heaviest known elements with neutrons, trying to understand what was happening when the nuclei absorbed them. In 1938 the Nazi annexation of Austria stripped Meitner of her citizenship and left her, as a Jewish scientist, in mortal danger inside Germany. She fled across the border with almost nothing and ended up in Sweden. Hahn kept the lab running and in late 1938 wrote to her urgently with a strange result: when he and his assistant Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons they appeared to be making an element about half uranium's size. Meitner, on a Christmas walk in the snow with her nephew Otto Frisch, worked out what had happened. The uranium nucleus had actually split in two, releasing an enormous bolt of energy that Einstein's famous equation predicted exactly. They coined a short new name for the process and published their explanation in early 1939. Within six years the discovery had become bombs over Hiroshima and Nagasaki and reactors generating electrical power. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded in 1944 for the discovery is a decision many physicists have been quietly furious about ever since, because of who was and was not on the award.

locke-natural-rights-and-the-philosophic.context_blurb: The men who wrote the American Declaration of Independence and the Constitution did not invent their political ideas out of nothing. They drew heavily on the political philosophy of the English Enlightenment, especially on the writings of John Locke, whose Second Treatise of Government (published anonymously in 1689) had provided the clearest systematic statement of natural rights theory in the English language. Locke argued that human beings are born free and equal, that they possess by nature certain rights that no government creates and no government may legitimately take away, that governments are instituted to secure those rights and derive their just authority from the consent of the governed, and that when governments turn against those rights the people have the right to replace them. The famous opening paragraphs of the American Declaration of Independence are almost a condensed paraphrase of Locke. The founders also drew on Montesquieu's analysis of mixed government, on the classical Roman historians, on the English common law tradition, and on their own Christian — mostly Protestant — moral inheritance. Locke's natural-rights framework was the single most important philosophical thread binding the whole American founding together, and it is still the basic ethical vocabulary of American constitutional argument today.

louis-pasteur-germ-theory-and-vaccines.context_blurb: Louis Pasteur was a nineteenth-century French scientist who began his career studying the strange two-handedness of crystals and ended it as the most famous man of science in France. His work ran down a single thread: that invisible living things, microbes, were behind an astonishing range of problems people had always blamed on the air itself. He showed that microbes were what caused certain French drinks to spoil, and he invented a gentle heat-treatment to kill the microbes without ruining the taste — a process that still carries his name on milk cartons today. He proved, in a famously beautiful flask experiment with a specially shaped glass neck, that life does not simply bubble up out of nothing in a sealed broth. He went on to vaccines, extending the century-old idea of smallpox inoculation into a genuine laboratory science. His first great livestock triumph was a public demonstration on a field full of sheep whose details are still cited in textbooks. His greatest and most dangerous gamble was a treatment for one of the oldest terrors of the countryside — a disease that follows the bite of certain mad animals — which he tried in 1885 on a nine-year-old boy who would otherwise certainly have died. The boy lived. Donations poured in from around the world to found the Pasteur Institute in Paris, which still exists. Pasteur himself was not a trained physician and could not legally treat human patients, which made every one of his medical gambles a legal as well as a scientific risk.

louisiana-purchase-1803.context_blurb: In 1803 the United States, under President Thomas Jefferson, bought the Louisiana Territory from France for roughly fifteen million dollars, approximately doubling the territorial size of the country overnight. The purchase stretched from the mouth of the Mississippi River northwest to the Canadian border and west to the Rocky Mountains, and it was eventually broken up into fifteen current American states or parts of them. The sale happened mostly for reasons on the French side. Napoleon Bonaparte had briefly tried to reassemble a French American empire with Louisiana as its agricultural supply center for the sugar colony of Saint-Domingue, but a successful slave revolt on Saint-Domingue (which would become Haiti) wrecked that plan, and a renewed war with Britain required Napoleon to concentrate his resources at home. He offered to sell the whole territory to the American envoys, who had only been authorized to buy the port of New Orleans and surrounding Spanish Florida. Jefferson had serious constitutional qualms about whether the federal government even had the authority to buy foreign territory, but he swallowed them. The Senate ratified the purchase, and the Lewis and Clark expedition set out the following year to begin to see what Jefferson had just bought.

luther-s-bible-vernacular-scripture.context_blurb: In the early 1520s Martin Luther produced the first great German translation of the Bible — not the first translation into German, but the first one that caught on, read eagerly by anyone who could get hold of a copy. Luther had been declared an outlaw at the Diet of Worms in 1521 for refusing to recant his teachings, which meant that any imperial subject could kill him on sight without legal penalty. His powerful protector, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, staged a mock kidnapping on Luther's way home and hid him safely in a mountain fortress called the Wartburg, where Luther spent nearly a year in disguise, growing a beard, pretending to be a nobleman, and translating the New Testament into German at an astonishing pace. The complete Bible, Old Testament and New, took him longer and involved help from a small team of Hebrew and Greek specialists. The finished translation put the full Christian Scriptures into the hands of ordinary German-speaking people — including the farmer behind his plow — and had an enormous shaping effect on German life, religion, and culture that scholars still trace today. Later it was imitated in English, Dutch, Czech, and a dozen other tongues, and the whole Reformation movement would from then on be a movement of ordinary Christians reading Scripture in their own kitchens.

machiavelli-the-prince.context_blurb: Niccolo Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, political writer, and sometime playwright who lost his career in a single bad year and spent the rest of his life trying to get it back. He was born in 1469 to an old and respectable Florentine family that was not rich, and he rose through the Florentine republic's civil service to run its foreign correspondence and organize a citizen militia. Then in 1512 the Medici family returned to Florence by force of arms, and Machiavelli, as a committed republican, was out. He was accused of plotting against the new regime, arrested, tortured, and finally banished to the small farm his family still owned outside the city. There, in a letter to a friend that is one of the great documents in European literature, he described how he passed his evenings on his small farm, surrounded by his family and his books. On the farm he wrote the short, sharp little book of political advice that would eventually make his name a curse word — The Prince, a handbook on how a ruler keeps power, dedicated to the very Medici who had broken him in the hope of winning his way back into their service. The hope did not come to anything in his lifetime. He died in 1527.

machu-picchu.context_blurb: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca royal estate perched on a steep ridge high in the Andes above the Urubamba River valley in modern Peru. It was built around AD 1450 for the great Inca ruler Pachacuti, who had led the explosive expansion of the Inca Empire out of Cusco, and it probably functioned as a seasonal retreat for the Inca court rather than as an everyday town. It contains terraced farmland, a sacred central plaza, residential buildings, temples, elaborate stone fountains fed by mountain springs, and some of the finest Inca stonework anywhere. After the Spanish conquest, the Inca kept the location to themselves; it was never discovered or sacked by the Spanish, which is why Machu Picchu is in better shape than almost any other Inca site. By the 1600s it had been abandoned, and local people kept farming the terraces on and off for centuries while the main buildings slowly went to vine and jungle. In 1911 the American historian Hiram Bingham, guided by local farmers, publicized its existence to the outside world. It is now one of the most-visited archaeological sites on Earth and is often used as the single iconic image of the Inca past.

magellan-s-circumnavigation.context_blurb: Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese captain sailing in Spanish service who, in 1519, set out with five ships and about 240 men to find a westward route to the Spice Islands by sailing all the way around South America. He found and threaded the narrow, storm-ridden strait at the continent's southern tip that now bears his name, crossed the enormous ocean beyond it, and found it to be vastly, murderously larger than any European had guessed. His men starved and sickened on open water for months, driven to desperate measures just to survive. Magellan himself never finished the voyage; he was killed in a shoreline skirmish in the Philippines after wading in with a small party against overwhelming odds. One of his junior officers, a Basque pilot, eventually brought one battered ship home to Spain three years after they had set out, with only a tiny band of surviving crew aboard, becoming the first expedition in human history to circle the globe. The chroniclers of the voyage, especially the Italian scholar Antonio Pigafetta, left behind one of the most unforgettable travelers' tales ever written in European literature, filled with sea monsters, strange birds, bewildered islanders, and bewildered Spaniards in equal measure.

magna-carta-1215.context_blurb: In the early 13th century, an unpopular English king had lost his French lands, picked a public fight with the Church, and squeezed his barons for every penny he could find to pay his wars. The barons eventually rose, took the capital, and cornered him at a famous spot outside London, where he was forced to attach his royal mark to a long charter listing the limits of his power. He broke the charter almost at once; a sympathetic pope obligingly declared it void; the king died within a year, and the charter might have died with him except that his boy heir's regents reissued it to shore up a shaky throne, and later kings kept reissuing it when they needed money. From that series of accidents, a mostly feudal document packed with narrow baronial grievances became, over the centuries, a kind of charter of English liberty, read and reread by generations who kept finding new rights in its old Latin. Most of its clauses have long since been repealed, but a handful still stand, and modern constitutional law in the English-speaking world still looks back to this early 13th-century agreement as one of its founding stones. The story covers the quarrel, the charter, the lives that made it, and the long afterlife it has had.

mahabharata-ramayana-epics.context_blurb: The two great Sanskrit epics of ancient India, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, were composed in versions reaching their current forms in the first few centuries AD but drawing on much older oral material that stretches back into the early first millennium BC. The Mahabharata is one of the longest poems in world literature, several times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined. It tells the story of a long dynastic feud between two sets of royal cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, culminating in an enormous war fought on the field of Kurukshetra. The Bhagavad Gita, one of the central religious texts of Hinduism, is a conversation that takes place on the eve of that war between the warrior Arjuna and his charioteer, who turns out to be the god Krishna. The Ramayana tells the story of Prince Rama, his wife Sita, his loyal brother Lakshmana, and the monkey-king Hanuman, as Rama rescues Sita from the demon king Ravana of Lanka.
