Scholars came from across North Africa, the Middle East, and the Sahel to study at Timbuktu's three great mosque-schools — Djinguereber, Sankore, and Sidi Yahya — and over the centuries the city accumulated a staggering library of Arabic manuscripts on jurisprudence, grammar, mathematics, astronomy, music, poetry, logic, pharmacology, and theology. By some estimates, hundreds of thousands of manuscripts still survive in private family libraries in and around Timbuktu, many of them in fragile condition and only recently catalogued. When Islamist militants briefly took the city in 2012, local librarians and families organized a secret evacuation of tens of thousands of manuscripts to Bamako to save them from destruction, a story that drew worldwide attention. Timbuktu stands as the clearest counterexample to the old lie that West Africa produced no written tradition before the Europeans arrived, and the manuscripts themselves are still being studied by scholars today.

timur-tamerlane-samarkand.context_blurb: Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane (from the Persian Timur the Lame — he had been crippled in a youthful fight), was a 14th-century Turko-Mongol conqueror from Central Asia who built the last great nomad-born empire of the pre-modern period. Based in his capital at Samarkand in what is now Uzbekistan, Timur conquered a huge territory from his home region east into northern India, west into Persia and Anatolia, and south into the Levant and Mesopotamia, between 1370 and his death in 1405. His campaigns were spectacularly destructive, with many cities razed and their inhabitants killed; he was estimated by some modern historians to have killed in the tens of millions, which would make his conquests one of the deadliest campaigns in human history relative to the population of his age. At the same time, Timur was a serious patron of Islamic art and architecture, and he transformed Samarkand into one of the great cities of the medieval Muslim world, with its tall turquoise-domed madrasas on the central Registan square, built by craftsmen he had deported from the places he had destroyed. The Timurid dynasty he founded would produce the Mughal line that eventually conquered northern India and built the Taj Mahal. He died planning an invasion of China.

trajan-and-the-empire-at-its-greatest-ex.context_blurb: Trajan was a Roman emperor who ruled from AD 98 to 117 and under whom the Roman Empire reached its greatest territorial extent. Born in Spain, he was the first emperor from the provinces rather than from Italy itself. He fought successful wars north of the Danube against the Dacians in what is now Romania, bringing home enormous amounts of gold and funding a major building program in Rome including a huge new forum and a tall commemorative column that still stands near the ruins of his forum. He also pushed east against the Parthian Empire in modern Iran and Iraq, briefly bringing Mesopotamia under Roman rule before his successor pulled back. His reign is remembered as one of the happy periods of Roman history, with a well-run administration and relative peace at home. A famous late ritual of Roman politics was that when a new emperor was proclaimed, the Senate would wish him to be "luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan," a measure of how high this provincial-born general had set the bar for his successors. He died on campaign in the East and was deified by a grateful Senate.

trans-saharan-trade-the-salt-gold-carava.context_blurb: For over a thousand years, from roughly the 8th century AD through the 16th, long camel caravans crossed the Sahara Desert in both directions, linking the Mediterranean coast of North Africa with the Sahel and savanna regions south of the desert. The economic engine of this trade was a near-even exchange between two commodities, each one abundant on one side and desperately needed on the other. Gold mined in the Bambuk, Bure, and Akan goldfields south of the desert was traded north to the Mediterranean economies. Salt cut from Saharan oases like Taghaza and Taoudenni was traded south to peoples who had no local sources and desperately needed it for food preservation and health. The trade also moved copper, textiles, horses, enslaved people, books, and ideas, including Islam itself, which gradually spread south across the desert from the 11th century onward. The great West African empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai all built their wealth on controlling the southern terminus of this trade, and the cities of Timbuktu, Djenne, Gao, and Kano became famous as its hubs. The trans-Saharan trade declined over the 16th and 17th centuries as European ships sailing down the Atlantic coast of Africa redirected much of the gold trade to coastal ports, cutting out the Saharan middlemen.

treaty-of-paris-1783.context_blurb: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 formally ended the American Revolutionary War between the United States and Great Britain and gave the new country extraordinarily favorable peace terms. The American delegation that negotiated the treaty was composed of Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, John Jay, and Henry Laurens, and they ran rings around the exhausted British government and the incompletely engaged French foreign ministry. The treaty formally recognized American independence, which was the central point. It set the western boundary of the new country at the Mississippi River rather than at the Appalachian crest, which the French and Spanish would have preferred, giving the United States a huge territorial legacy to grow into over the following century. It guaranteed American fishing rights off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. It provided for the repayment of debts owed by Americans to British creditors, and for the restoration of property to loyalists who had sided with Britain, though both of these were only sporadically honored. It did not resolve the question of frontier military posts, Native American alliances, and British impressment of American sailors, all of which would help cause the War of 1812 three decades later. On the whole, however, it was one of the best treaties the new United States ever signed.

treaty-of-tordesillas.context_blurb: Within two years of Columbus's first voyage, Portugal and Spain were on the edge of a war over who got what in the newly discovered Atlantic. Pope Alexander VI, a Spaniard himself, drew a first line down the globe to divide the finds, but Portugal's king thought the line sat too close to his own coast. In 1494 the two Iberian crowns met in the small Spanish town of Tordesillas and negotiated a new line — a meridian running north-south through the Atlantic a few hundred leagues west of the Cape Verde islands, with Portugal getting everything east of it and Spain getting everything west. Nobody else was consulted; the English, French, Dutch, and the inhabitants of the lands being divided had no say at all. The treaty's biggest practical consequence turned up in 1500, when a Portuguese fleet bound for India made landfall on the easternmost bulge of South America and the Portuguese quickly realized they had a technical claim to it under the agreement they had just signed. That is why, uniquely among the large nations of the Americas, one giant modern country still speaks a different Iberian language from all of its neighbors. The Tordesillas line itself turned out to be nearly impossible to draw accurately with the navigation tools of the age, and later generations of mapmakers and diplomats would spend decades arguing about where exactly it should have fallen on the New World coasts.

treaty-of-versailles.context_blurb: The Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919, formally ended World War I between the Allied Powers and Germany after six months of hard negotiation at the Paris Peace Conference. The treaty's most consequential terms included the loss of German territory in Europe and overseas, strict limits on the size and equipment of the German armed forces, heavy financial reparations assessed on Germany as the losing side, and the creation of a new international organization to maintain the peace. The French prime minister Georges Clemenceau wanted the treaty to be harsh enough to prevent Germany from ever threatening France again; British prime minister David Lloyd George, caught between British electoral demands for a punitive peace and his own belief that too hard a settlement would create future trouble, held the middle; and Woodrow Wilson pressed for his Fourteen Points. The signing ceremony itself took place in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles outside Paris, deliberately chosen for its symbolic weight in earlier French history. Germans resented the treaty from the moment it was signed and would spend the next twenty years finding ways around its provisions, and the economist John Maynard Keynes resigned from the British delegation to write his own critique of the terms. French Marshal Ferdinand Foch, who had wanted a harsher deal, left the ceremony openly predicting that this treaty would not keep the peace long.

trench-warfare-and-the-western-front.context_blurb: After the German advance of 1914 ground to a halt at the Marne, the Western Front settled into two parallel systems of trenches stretching 475 miles from the English Channel to the Swiss border, and for nearly four years the war in the west stood still. Soldiers lived under conditions almost impossible to describe later — standing in cold mud, under constant shellfire, in dugouts that leaked, among corpses and lice and vermin — and the simple business of being an infantryman in the trenches was deadly even without an attack. The soldiers' slang for every piece of their new world — their boots, their uniforms, the ground between the lines, the German shells, the diseases of the wet — grew up like a secret language that outlived the war. Every so often a general ordered an attack: the men went forward in the pre-dawn, across the open ground toward the enemy, and died in rows against barbed wire and machine guns. By 1918 roughly 10 million soldiers had been killed, mostly for a few miles of torn-up French and Belgian farmland — and the whole terrible imagery, from the gas-mask to the barbed wire, became fixed in the Western imagination of what modern war is.

truman-doctrine-containment.context_blurb: In March 1947, American President Harry Truman addressed a joint session of Congress on behalf of Greece and Turkey, two countries that Britain had informed Washington it could no longer afford to defend against communist pressure. In the speech, Truman asked Congress for emergency aid and committed the United States to a much broader principle: that the United States would support free peoples anywhere in the world who were resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. The speech is usually remembered as the formal beginning of the American Cold War policy that came to be known as containment — the idea that the United States would systematically oppose the expansion of Soviet and communist influence wherever it threatened to extend. The intellectual framework for containment had been laid out by the American diplomat and historian George Kennan in a famous long telegram from Moscow in 1946 and in a 1947 anonymous Foreign Affairs article. Containment shaped American foreign policy in Korea, in Berlin, in Vietnam, in Cuba, in Latin America, in the Middle East, and in Afghanistan over the following four decades. Its ultimate verdict depended on whether one judged its individual applications well or poorly, but the Soviet Union did eventually collapse largely from internal pressures, which is what Kennan had thought might eventually happen.

tuskegee-airmen.context_blurb: The Tuskegee Airmen were a group of African American military pilots who trained and served in the segregated United States Army Air Forces during the Second World War, flying combat missions in Europe and North Africa despite the entrenched racial prejudice of the American military of the 1940s. The men were trained at Tuskegee Army Air Field in Alabama, where the Tuskegee Institute founded by Booker T. Washington in the 1880s had become the center of African American higher education. Over several thousand African American men trained at Tuskegee during the war, including nearly a thousand pilots. The 332nd Fighter Group of the Tuskegee Airmen flew bomber-escort missions over Nazi-occupied Europe from Italian bases, developing a reputation for exceptional discipline and effectiveness in protecting the bombers under their escort. Many of the pilots won Distinguished Flying Crosses and other decorations. Their wartime record played a significant role in building the political and moral case for racial integration of the United States armed forces, which President Harry S. Truman ordered by executive order in 1948. The surviving Tuskegee Airmen later received the Congressional Gold Medal in 2007 for their collective wartime service and for the broader civil-rights significance of what they had done.

tutankhamun-and-his-tomb.context_blurb: Tutankhamun was a minor Egyptian pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty who ruled briefly in the mid-fourteenth century BC and died young, probably around age nineteen. He was politically unimportant during his lifetime; his main historical achievement was partially reversing the religious revolution of his father (or possibly brother) Akhenaten, who had tried to force a near-monotheistic worship of a single sun-disc god on Egypt in place of the traditional pantheon. Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes was comparatively small — probably hastily converted from a lesser tomb when he died unexpectedly — and in a stroke of unprecedented archaeological luck, it was never thoroughly robbed in antiquity. It was discovered in November 1922 by the British Egyptologist Howard Carter, working for the English nobleman Lord Carnarvon, almost by chance in the course of his final season of excavations. The tomb contained thousands of objects, including the famous solid gold funerary mask, nested gilded coffins, chariots, furniture, jewelry, weapons, and clothing. The discovery became a worldwide sensation and set off the twentieth-century popular craze about ancient Egypt that still has its grip on museum attendance and movie casting today. Tutankhamun himself is now one of the most famous pharaohs, mostly because his tomb survived.

tycho-brahe-and-the-war-on-the-data.context_blurb: Tycho Brahe was a wealthy Danish nobleman astronomer of the second half of the sixteenth century, a towering, red-haired, hard-drinking figure who, after losing part of his face in a student duel over a point of mathematics, wore a prosthetic for the rest of his life. King Frederick II of Denmark gave him an entire island, Hven, in the sound between Denmark and Sweden, on which Tycho built an enormous observatory called Uraniborg, equipped with the biggest and best brass measuring instruments ever constructed in Europe. He hired a staff, trained students, and over about two decades of patient naked-eye observation — the telescope had not yet been invented — he gathered a mountain of positional data on the Sun, the Moon, the planets, and nearly a thousand stars, measurements several times more accurate than anything that had come before. He also offered his own compromise model of the universe in which the Earth stayed still but the other planets revolved around the Sun, which in turn circled the Earth. Falling out with Denmark's new king in 1597, Tycho moved to the court of the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolph II near Prague, where he took on as his assistant a brilliant, half-blind young German mathematician named Johannes Kepler. Tycho died unexpectedly in 1601, and Kepler, inheriting his boss's precious tables, eventually used Tycho's observations of Mars to deliver a knockout blow to one of the most ancient Greek assumptions about how the heavenly bodies had to move, replacing it with a geometric shape of his own.

tycho-brahe-s-observations.context_blurb: Tycho Brahe was a 16th-century Danish nobleman and astronomer who, in an age before telescopes, performed the most accurate observations of the night sky anyone had ever done. The Danish king granted him an entire island in the Baltic to build his great observatory on, and he filled it with huge, carefully constructed instruments that let him measure the positions of stars and planets with unprecedented precision. Tycho was a flamboyant character who lost part of his nose in a duel over a mathematical dispute and wore a metal replacement for the rest of his life, and his observatory was as much a princely court as a research facility. He was not himself a Copernican; he proposed a compromise system in which the planets orbit the Sun, but the Sun orbits a stationary Earth. His real legacy was the data: when he died in 1601 in Prague, his young assistant Johannes Kepler inherited the records, and it was Kepler's work on them that produced the laws of planetary motion that would eventually make the heliocentric picture undeniable.

urbanization-and-the-growth-of-industria.context_blurb: During the nineteenth century the great European and American industrial cities grew faster than any cities had ever grown before. London doubled, then doubled again; Manchester, Birmingham, Chicago, and New York exploded in population; the water supplies, sewers, and streets built for towns of fifty thousand suddenly had to serve millions. The cost was enormous. Dense tenement districts bred overcrowding; private wells and shallow pumps were polluted by neighboring cesspools; and great epidemic diseases — cholera above all — swept the slums with terrifying speed. The questions ahead walk through two of the most famous nineteenth-century urban health stories. The first is the London physician John Snow and his investigation of a cholera outbreak in the Soho neighborhood of London in 1854, in which he used a hand-drawn map of case locations to zero in on a specific contaminated water source. The second is the engineer Joseph Bazalgette, who after a notorious hot summer when the stench of the Thames became a national scandal was authorized to build London's first great modern sewer system. The story covers Snow's famous intervention, a telling observation he made about who in the neighborhood did not get sick, who finally pushed the sewer project through, a later investigation that revisited Snow's outbreak, and the design philosophy Bazalgette brought to his pipe sizes. It matters because out of these decades, modern public health, modern water supply, and the modern engineered city are born.

v-e-day-and-v-j-day.context_blurb: The two end-of-war victory days of the Second World War — Victory in Europe Day and Victory in Japan Day — were celebrated at opposite ends of the summer of 1945. On May 8, 1945, the Western Allies celebrated Victory in Europe Day, marking the formal unconditional surrender of all German military forces and the end of the war in Europe. The formal surrender had been signed the previous day at Reims in northeastern France, with ratification signed in Berlin on May 8. Enormous public celebrations swept across Britain and the United States, with crowds pouring into Trafalgar Square in London, Times Square in New York, and across every town and village in the Allied world. Three months later, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet declaration of war on Japan, the Japanese emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender in a radio broadcast on August 15, 1945, which was celebrated as Victory in Japan Day across the Allied world. The actual formal surrender was signed aboard the American battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945. The two victory days ended the deadliest war in human history after nearly six years of fighting and roughly eighty million dead.

valley-forge-winter-1777-78.context_blurb: In the winter of 1777 to 1778, after a hard year of fighting in which the Continental Army had lost Philadelphia to the British, George Washington chose to winter his army at Valley Forge, a hilly site about twenty miles northwest of Philadelphia. The six-month encampment there became one of the defining experiences of the American Revolution. The weather was brutally cold; the army's supply system had broken down; soldiers were short of food, short of blankets, short of shoes, and sometimes short of all three at once. Hundreds died of exposure and disease, and thousands more deserted. During the same winter, however, the Prussian officer Baron Friedrich von Steuben arrived from France and systematically drilled the ragged Continental Army into disciplined fighting units along European lines. When the army emerged from Valley Forge in the spring of 1778 to fight the British column marching back out of Philadelphia across New Jersey, it was a visibly different army. The winter at Valley Forge is remembered less as a battle than as a test of endurance that the army and its commander barely survived, and that forged the Continental Army into a force capable of the campaigns that would eventually produce the victory at Yorktown three years later.

van-gogh-starry-night-and-the-ear.context_blurb: Vincent van Gogh (1853 to 1890) was a Dutch painter who spent most of his adult life as a failure, sold only one painting while he was alive, suffered from mental illness that was never properly diagnosed, and in a famous incident late in 1888 cut off part of his own left ear during an argument with the French painter Paul Gauguin in Arles. He voluntarily committed himself afterward to an asylum in the small town of Saint-Remy-de-Provence, where he painted some of his most famous works, including a swirling moonlit landscape of a Provencal village under a wildly turbulent sky full of stars, which is now one of the most-reproduced paintings in the world and hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. He produced around 2,100 artworks across his roughly ten-year career, including over 860 oil paintings, most of them in the final two years of his life. His younger brother Theo supported him emotionally and financially throughout his life, and the correspondence between the two of them has become one of the most quoted artists' letter collections in Western literature. He died in southern France at thirty-seven of a gunshot wound traditionally called self-inflicted. His art has gone from almost unsold to among the most valuable in the world.

vasco-da-gama-and-the-sea-route-to-india.context_blurb: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese nobleman and ship captain in the service of King Manuel I. He was given command, in 1497, of a four-ship expedition tasked with finishing a project the Portuguese crown had been working on for most of a century: finding an all-sea route around Africa to the spice markets of India. Portuguese captains before him had crept southward along the African coast one headland at a time, Bartolomeu Dias had rounded the southern tip in 1488, and the arithmetic suggested the Indian Ocean lay just beyond. Da Gama's fleet sailed from Lisbon in July 1497. In an audacious piece of navigation he swung far out into the open South Atlantic to catch favourable winds instead of hugging the African coast, and spent some three months out of sight of land before touching Africa again below the Cape. From the East African ports of Mozambique, Mombasa, and Malindi — where he found a competent local pilot who knew the Indian Ocean well — he caught a favourable wind across to the Malabar coast of southern India. He landed at Calicut in May 1498. The spice cargo he struggled home with the following year sold in Lisbon for roughly sixty times what the whole voyage had cost, and the long and tightly controlled grip that older trading networks had held on the East-West spice trade had been quietly broken. Da Gama made two more voyages to India and died there in 1524 as viceroy.

vasco-da-gama-reaches-india.context_blurb: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese captain who finally completed the plan Prince Henry the Navigator had set in motion seventy years earlier. In 1497 he sailed from Lisbon with four ships, rounded the southern tip of Africa, caught a seasonal wind straight across the Indian Ocean with the help of a local Indian Ocean navigator he picked up along the East African coast, and in May 1498 anchored off a bustling Hindu-ruled spice port on India's Malabar Coast. Portugal was now the first European kingdom with a direct sea route to the spice markets. His diplomacy was clumsy — the gifts he had brought along were out of their depth in a court used to the trading world of the western Indian Ocean, and the local ruler and his courtiers took the measure of what Portugal had on offer and were not impressed. Da Gama still fought his way home with a cargo of pepper so valuable it paid for the whole expedition many times over. His later voyages back to the same coast were much more violent, and included at least one act whose cruelty against unarmed civilians shocked contemporaries even by the hard standards of the age.

vasco-n-ez-de-balboa-sights-the-pacific.context_blurb: Vasco Nunez de Balboa was a Spanish adventurer who had stowed away in a barrel to escape his debts in Hispaniola and ended up leading a small settlement on the mainland of what is now Panama. In September 1513, acting on native tales of a great sea on the far side of the isthmus, he led about 190 Spaniards and a thousand native allies on a brutal march through the jungle. When his guides told him the next hilltop would show it, Balboa carefully arranged the moment so that he, personally, would see the water before anyone else in his party did. Days later, in full armor, he waded out into the surf and formally claimed the entire ocean for the king of Spain. The name he gave the sea was tied to the particulars of his own expedition — specifically to how he had traveled from the Caribbean to reach it — and so felt natural to him and his men, though it did not describe the ocean's actual shape very well. A few years later Magellan, finding the same water calm after his storm-ridden strait, gave it the gentler and more lasting name we still use today. Balboa himself was later framed on a treason charge by a jealous rival governor and beheaded in his own town square.

velazquez-las-meninas.context_blurb: Diego Velazquez (1599 to 1660) was a Spanish painter who became the court painter to King Philip IV of Spain and spent most of his adult life at the Spanish royal court in Madrid producing portraits, mythological scenes, and the occasional religious work for the Habsburg king and his family. His portraits of the royal family — the king, the queen, the royal children, the court dwarfs and fools, and the royal dogs — are among the most psychologically alive portraits in the history of Western painting. His greatest single painting, done in 1656 and still hanging in the Prado Museum in Madrid, is a complicated composition showing the young Infanta Margarita surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting and dwarfs, with Velazquez himself at an easel on the left side of the scene, a dim reflection of the king and queen in a mirror on the back wall, and a courtier climbing a flight of stairs through a doorway in the back — a painting that has been pored over by art historians and philosophers for over three centuries, including by Michel Foucault, who used it as the opening pages of his book The Order of Things. Velazquez had the usual court politics to navigate but seems to have been personally admired by the king throughout his career.

vermeer-girl-with-a-pearl-earring.context_blurb: Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675) was a Dutch painter from the small city of Delft who spent his entire short career there, produced only around three dozen paintings, sold most of them to a small circle of local collectors, and died in debt in his early forties. He was essentially forgotten for the next two hundred years. In the 19th century his work was rediscovered and his reputation grew steadily; today he is treated as one of the handful of greatest painters of the Dutch Golden Age and arguably one of the greatest painters, full stop. His paintings are mostly quiet interior scenes of middle-class Dutch women reading letters, pouring milk, playing music, weighing pearls, or looking up at the viewer. His use of a particular quality of light coming in from a window on the left side of the scene, his careful handling of textiles, pearls, and ceramic, and his almost meditative stillness are instantly recognizable. His most famous single painting shows a young woman turning toward the viewer in a plain dark background, with a blue-and-yellow headscarf and a single luminous pearl earring. The painting now hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague and became the subject of a bestselling 1999 novel and a 2003 film. Most Vermeers hang in the world's great art museums today.

vesalius-and-human-anatomy.context_blurb: Andreas Vesalius was a 16th-century Flemish physician whose book De Humani Corporis Fabrica, published in 1543, overturned a thousand years of medical teaching about the human body. Before Vesalius, European doctors learned anatomy almost entirely from the writings of the ancient Greek physician Galen, who had worked under restrictions that meant he had never actually dissected a human corpse. Vesalius demanded that doctors do their own cutting, and his book was the first great European anatomical atlas based on direct observation of real human bodies, with gorgeous illustrations drawn by artists from Titian's workshop. The book was a scandal in medical circles because it showed, politely but unmistakably, how often Galen had been wrong. Vesalius taught at Padua, served as personal physician to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and then to his son King Philip II of Spain, and died in 1564 on his way back from a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. His book is the moment when European medicine stopped reciting the ancients and started doing its own research, and modern anatomy begins with him.

vietnam-war.context_blurb: The Vietnam War was a long armed conflict in Southeast Asia between the communist government of North Vietnam (backed by the Soviet Union and China) and the non-communist government of South Vietnam (backed by the United States and its allies). The war grew out of the French colonial war in Indochina from 1946 to 1954, during which the Vietnamese communist leader Ho Chi Minh and his general Vo Nguyen Giap drove the French out, after which the country was divided along the 17th parallel pending planned elections that were never held. American military advisers arrived in South Vietnam in the late 1950s, and American combat troops began arriving in large numbers in 1965. At the peak of American involvement in 1968 and 1969, over five hundred thousand American soldiers were in Vietnam. The war featured conventional battles, a brutal counterinsurgency against the Viet Cong guerrilla movement in the South Vietnamese countryside, massive American aerial bombing of North Vietnam, extensive casualties among civilians, and over fifty-eight thousand American military deaths. Deep domestic American opposition to the war grew through the late 1960s. American ground forces were withdrawn in 1973, South Vietnam fell to the North in 1975, and the surviving unified Vietnam was ruled by its Communist Party. The war remains one of the most-argued American military experiences in modern history.

viking-raids-lindisfarne-793.context_blurb: At the end of the 8th century, longships out of Scandinavia appeared off the Northumbrian coast of England and sacked a famous monastery on a tidal island, slaughtering monks and taking treasures and captives. Christian Europe had never seen anything like it, and chroniclers reported that uncanny signs in the sky had warned of the attack. For the next several hundred years, Viking raiders, traders, and settlers reshaped the map of northern Europe, moving captives across the Mediterranean, founding kingdoms in Ireland and in what became Russia, settling the North Atlantic islands and briefly a corner of North America, and eventually, in a famous treaty with an English king, agreeing to settle down inside Christendom on new terms the king and the archbishop could live with. Their shallow, flexible ships could cross oceans and perform landings that no other ships of the age could manage, which made them the most dangerous raiders of their time. Their myths, their sagas, and their clever navigational tools are still remembered, and some of their descendants went on to rewrite English history all over again from the saddle of a different conquest in a different century. The story covers the first great raid, the ships and weapons the raiders used, the explorers who followed, their long-ranging exploration and settlement, and the slow process by which these once-feared raiders became Christian kings and settled neighbors inside the European order they had once terrorized.

virgil-s-aeneid-and-roman-literature.context_blurb: The Aeneid is a Latin epic poem by Virgil, written in the final years of the first century BC under the patronage of the emperor Augustus and considered the greatest work of Roman literature. It tells the story of a Trojan prince named Aeneas, a minor character in Homer's Iliad, who escapes the burning city of Troy with his father on his shoulders and his small son by his hand, wanders the Mediterranean for years guided by the gods, has a doomed love affair with a Phoenician queen, descends into the underworld, and finally lands in Italy to found the line that would become the Roman people. The poem knits together a long Trojan backstory for Rome, a flattering mythological ancestry for Augustus's family, and a serious meditation on the costs of empire and duty. Virgil spent over a decade writing it, was never satisfied, and asked on his deathbed in 19 BC that it be burned, which Augustus refused to allow. The Aeneid became the central school text of the Latin-speaking world for the next fifteen hundred years, and Dante later cast Virgil himself as his personal guide through Hell in the greatest poem of medieval Christendom.

voltaire-and-freedom-of-speech.context_blurb: Voltaire was the pen name of Francois-Marie Arouet, an 18th-century French playwright, essayist, poet, historian, and all-purpose troublemaker who became the most famous writer in Europe during his lifetime. He wrote plays, bestselling novels like Candide, serious histories, and endless streams of satirical verse and letters attacking what he considered the two great tyrannies of his age: religious persecution and arbitrary government. He was imprisoned, exiled, and sued more times than he could count, and he kept writing. His short, sharp phrases could end careers, and his most famous late act was to use his fame to re-open the case of a Protestant named Jean Calas, who had been tortured and executed in Toulouse on almost no evidence of a crime at all. Voltaire's long campaign cleared Calas's name and shamed the French judicial system into reforms. He died in Paris in 1778 at the age of 83, honored and feared. He is remembered now mostly for defending the right of other people to say what he himself disagreed with, which was his bedrock principle whether or not he ever used exactly those words.

wall-street-crash-of-1929.context_blurb: The great New York stock market boom of the late 1920s came apart in the last week of October 1929. Share prices on the New York Stock Exchange had been climbing to dizzying heights all through 1928 and 1929, driven in part by ordinary Americans borrowing from their brokers at ten-to-one leverage ('on margin') to buy more stock. On a Thursday in late October the market broke; the next week it broke again, and again, until a single day on which roughly 16 million shares changed hands and the leading industrial stock prices collapsed. Behind the panic lay a decade's worth of easy credit from the Federal Reserve, which had been holding interest rates below their market level since the 1920 recovery; critics in the Austrian school of economics — Ludwig von Mises in Vienna and Friedrich Hayek in London — would soon argue that the Fed's low interest rates had set up the crisis in the first place. The crash did not cause the Depression that followed on its own; it was the collapse of the banking system over the next three years that did that. But October 1929 was the moment the Roaring Twenties ended, and from the long perspective of history it was the signal that something very big had gone wrong in the American financial order.

war-of-1812-burning-of-washington.context_blurb: The War of 1812 was a strange, inconclusive war fought between the United States and Great Britain from 1812 to 1815, during a brief gap in Britain's long war against Napoleon Bonaparte in Europe. The American grievances were real: British warships had been boarding American merchant ships and seizing sailors they claimed were British deserters, British trade restrictions were throttling American commerce, and British agents were suspected of supplying Native American resistance in the Northwest Territory. President James Madison asked Congress for a declaration of war in June 1812. The war itself went badly for the United States for most of its length. American invasions of Canada mostly failed; the United States Navy fought with distinction but could not stop the Royal Navy. In the summer of 1814 a British raid landed in the Chesapeake Bay, marched on Washington, D.C., defeated a hastily assembled American force at the Battle of Bladensburg, and burned most of the public buildings in the capital city, including the Capitol and the White House. The war finally ended with the Treaty of Ghent on Christmas Eve 1814, which essentially restored the pre-war boundaries. The post-war wave of national confidence it produced, after the lopsided American victory at New Orleans, launched the so-called Era of Good Feelings.

washington-crossing-the-delaware-trenton.context_blurb: On the night of December 25, 1776, after a disastrous autumn in which the Continental Army had been chased out of New York, across New Jersey, and across the Delaware River into Pennsylvania, George Washington staged one of the most audacious operations of the Revolutionary War. He loaded about twenty-four hundred men, their horses, and their artillery into boats and ferried them across the ice-choked Delaware River in a snowstorm during the night. By early morning on December 26, the Continentals surprised a garrison of Hessian mercenaries at Trenton on the New Jersey side of the river, caught them half-asleep after their Christmas Day celebrations, and captured over nine hundred of them with almost no American losses. Washington then evaded a much larger British force sent against him and won a second small battle at Princeton a few days later before retiring to winter quarters at Morristown. The two victories came at a dark moment in the war when American morale was at its lowest. Thomas Paine was writing The American Crisis to urge the country to hold on. Washington's twin strikes revived the Revolution. The crossing was later immortalized by Emanuel Leutze's famous 1851 painting, which hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

washington-resigns-his-commission-the-am.context_blurb: At the end of the American Revolutionary War, after the final peace treaty with Britain had been signed in September 1783, George Washington took the most important single political step of his career. Instead of attempting to turn his victorious army into the base of a permanent political career for himself, he traveled to Annapolis, Maryland, where the Continental Congress was then sitting, and on December 23, 1783, formally surrendered his military commission as commander in chief of the Continental Army. He gave a short, moving speech, laid down his papers, and went home to his farm at Mount Vernon. King George III of Britain, upon being told by the American painter Benjamin West that Washington planned to resign his command and return to his farm, is said to have replied that if he actually did so, he would be the greatest man in the world. The act was deliberately modeled on the ancient Roman story of Cincinnatus, who gave up power to return to his plow. It set the precedent — and the deep moral example — that American military commanders would always submit themselves to civilian political authority. Washington repeated the lesson a decade later by declining a third term as president, which has shaped the whole American political tradition ever since.

washington-s-farewell-address-precedents.context_blurb: In September 1796, as he was preparing to retire from the presidency rather than seek a third term, George Washington published his Farewell Address to the American people in a Philadelphia newspaper. He never actually delivered it as a speech. The address, drafted with the help of Alexander Hamilton and James Madison, was Washington's long parting letter to the country he had led, and it is one of the most important political documents of the founding generation. It warned Americans against three particular dangers he saw ahead. First, he warned against the growth of political parties and factions, which he feared would eventually tear the country apart. Second, he warned against entangling alliances with the quarrels of European powers, urging the United States to maintain commercial relations but keep political and military distance from Europe's wars. Third, he warned against sectional loyalty to any one region of the United States over the union as a whole. Washington's refusal to seek a third term also quietly set the two-term precedent that every subsequent president would follow (with one wartime exception) until the twenty-second amendment made the limit formal law in 1951. The address is still read aloud in the United States Senate every year on Washington's birthday.

watson-crick-franklin-and-the-dna-double.context_blurb: By the late 1940s most biologists had come to accept that the long thin molecule called deoxyribonucleic acid — DNA, which sits inside the chromosomes — was somehow the carrier of hereditary information in living cells. What nobody yet knew was its shape, and the shape mattered because so much of how the molecule actually behaves inside a cell was going to depend on it. In the early 1950s the race to work out the structure brought together an unlikely cast at two British institutions and one American one. At King's College London the brilliant and prickly physical chemist Rosalind Franklin was taking stunning X-ray diffraction photographs of pure fibres of the molecule, from which the structure could in principle be read, while uneasily sharing the project with her colleague Maurice Wilkins. At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, a brash young American visitor named James Watson and the more mathematically trained Englishman Francis Crick were building large physical models in Watson's cramped shared office, trying to guess the structure instead of measuring it. Across the Atlantic the great American chemist Linus Pauling was chasing the same prize. Early in 1953 a crucial X-ray image taken in Franklin's lab came, by a route that is still disputed today, into the hands of the Cambridge pair, and they quickly assembled a model that fit it and all the other known chemical facts in an elegant way. Their one-page paper appeared in the journal Nature in April 1953. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at thirty-seven; the Nobel Prize for the discovery was awarded four years later.

weimar-republic-and-hyperinflation.context_blurb: The German republic that emerged out of the November 1918 revolution — commonly called the Weimar Republic after the small city where its new constitution was drafted — was born in defeat, debt, and civil violence. German governments through 1922 and 1923 financed war reparations and daily expenses mostly by printing money, and by late 1923 the German mark had collapsed in one of history's most famous hyperinflations: prices doubled every few days, workers were paid twice a day and ran to spend their wages before they lost value, and foreign visitors could buy mansions for pocket change in American dollars. The economic ruin wiped out the German middle class's savings and permanently poisoned Weimar democracy's political legitimacy. The government finally stabilized the currency in late 1923, and the mid-1920s became a relative period of calm and cultural brilliance — Berlin cabaret, Bauhaus design, Thomas Mann and Hermann Hesse — before the 1929 crash hit Germany harder than any other country in the industrialized world and sent voters sprinting toward political extremes. The hyperinflation of 1923 was also the moment of Adolf Hitler's first attempt at power, the failed Munich beer-hall coup he staged while the Reichsmark was still cratering.

westward-expansion-and-the-plains-indian.context_blurb: In the three decades after the American Civil War, the United States completed the conquest of the Great Plains. Transcontinental railroads laid steel across the buffalo country; professional buffalo hunters shot the enormous herds down to near-extinction; the U.S. Army fought a long series of campaigns against the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Kiowa, Nez Perce, and other Plains peoples; and treaty after treaty was broken as settlers, miners, and railroads moved onto reservation land. The two most famous episodes of this struggle are the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, in which a combined force under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse destroyed a column of the U.S. Seventh Cavalry under George Armstrong Custer, and the massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890, in which the same cavalry regiment opened fire on a Lakota camp during the suppression of a religious movement known as the Ghost Dance. The questions ahead cover the one living thing that walked off the Custer side of the Little Bighorn, a religious promise the Ghost Dance made to its wearers of a special shirt, a vision of victory experienced by one of the great Lakota leaders before the battle, a famous refusal of Crazy Horse, the specific resource whose discovery in the sacred Black Hills triggered the war, and who most of the dead were at Wounded Knee. It matters because this period marks the end of the Plains peoples' free life — and the moment the United States truly became a continental power from ocean to ocean.

whiskey-rebellion-1794.context_blurb: The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 was an uprising of farmers in western Pennsylvania against a federal tax on distilled spirits that Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton had pushed through Congress in 1791 as part of his broader financial program. Western Pennsylvania farmers, who converted their surplus grain into whiskey because it was easier to ship over the mountains to eastern markets than the raw grain, bitterly resented the tax, and over the next three years their resistance escalated from petition and non-compliance into open intimidation of tax collectors, armed assembly, and the tarring and feathering of federal officers. In the summer of 1794, after thousands of armed Pennsylvanians assembled at an organized muster outside Pittsburgh, President George Washington took the extraordinary step of personally leading a federalized militia force of nearly thirteen thousand men over the Alleghenies into western Pennsylvania to suppress the rebellion. The rebellion melted away without a serious fight; a handful of leaders were arrested and later pardoned. The episode demonstrated, four years into the life of the new federal government, that the Constitution's authority was not optional in the backcountry, and it set an early precedent for the federal government's willingness to enforce federal law with federal arms. It also fed early American political divisions over how aggressively the federal government should act.

why-roman-concrete-still-stands-the-self.context_blurb: Many of the great Roman concrete structures — the Pantheon's dome, harbor works that have sat in salt water for over two thousand years, aqueduct arches, tomb interiors, bath complexes — are still standing in nearly original condition, while twentieth-century concrete bridges, parking garages, and highway overpasses are crumbling after only a few decades. For a long time nobody fully understood why. Recent chemistry research on samples taken from Roman concrete has shown that the Roman mix was fundamentally different from the Portland cement used in modern concrete. The Roman mix included a particular volcanic ash from near Mount Vesuvius, mixed hot, and the result is a material that reacts chemically with water over long time scales and actually heals its own cracks when seawater or rainwater seeps into them. Modern engineers are now trying to reverse-engineer the trick to produce longer-lasting concrete for the 21st century. This is one of several places in history where an ancient technology turns out to be subtler than the modern mass-produced replacement, and where the ruins are still teaching us things their builders knew but never wrote down in a chemistry book.

william-harvey-and-blood-circulation.context_blurb: William Harvey was a 17th-century English physician who served as the court doctor to two kings and who, almost single-handedly, overturned the ancient Galenic picture of how blood moves through the human body. Harvey trained at the University of Padua in Italy, where Vesalius's revolution in anatomy was still fresh, and he returned to England convinced that medicine should rest on direct observation and experiment. Over many years of careful work on live animals, cadavers, and tied-off arteries, he worked out what blood actually does inside the body. He published his findings in a slim Latin book in 1628, and it was ridiculed at first; many doctors preferred the old picture because the old picture was what their patients were paying them to use. Harvey rode out the controversy, kept practicing medicine during the English Civil War, and lived to see his ideas accepted by younger physicians. He died in 1657. His work is remembered as one of the moments when experimental science first forced medicine to tell the truth about the human body, no matter how much tradition it offended.

winston-churchill-s-wartime-leadership.context_blurb: Winston Churchill was a British politician, soldier, writer, and painter who had spent most of the 1930s out of government warning in increasingly isolated speeches that Nazi Germany was rearming and that British appeasement would end in disaster. When the Second World War broke out in September 1939 he was brought back into the Chamberlain cabinet as First Lord of the Admiralty, and in May 1940, as German forces broke through into France and the Chamberlain government collapsed, Churchill was invited to form a new coalition government as prime minister. He led Britain for the following five years through its darkest and finest hours. His speeches to the House of Commons and to the British public — on the fall of France, on the Battle of Britain, on the Blitz, on D-Day, on victory — are among the greatest political oratory in the English language. He traveled constantly to meet Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin and to coordinate Allied strategy. He was defeated in the general election of July 1945 just as the Potsdam Conference was still in session, replaced as prime minister by Clement Attlee. Churchill returned as prime minister from 1951 to 1955. He wrote his own six-volume history of the Second World War and in 1953 was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

woodrow-wilson-s-fourteen-points.context_blurb: In January 1918, with America fully in the war, President Woodrow Wilson stood before Congress and laid out his vision for the postwar world in a speech of fourteen numbered proposals. The speech argued for a new kind of transparent diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free international trade, drastic arms reductions, impartial resolution of colonial claims, national self-determination for peoples under foreign rule, and — most important to Wilson personally — the creation of a new world institution to safeguard the independence and territorial integrity of great and small states alike. The speech transformed Wilson into a moral hero in Europe; crowds in Rome, Paris, and Vienna hung his portrait next to religious icons. At the Paris Peace Conference the following year, however, the French prime minister Georges Clemenceau and the British prime minister David Lloyd George watered down his more idealistic proposals, keeping only the general international body he most cared about. Even that triumph soured when Wilson came home: his own Senate refused to ratify the treaty, and he fell gravely ill during a cross-country speaking tour trying to save it. For the last year and a half of his presidency, those around him quietly ran much of the executive branch while a stricken Wilson lay recovering in the White House.

wwi-poetry-and-remembrance.context_blurb: World War I produced a body of English-language poetry still read in schools everywhere a century later. The best known of these poets served in the trenches themselves — Rupert Brooke, who died early of septicaemia on his way to Gallipoli; John McCrae, a Canadian army doctor whose short poem written at a battlefield burial of a friend made a small roadside wildflower of Flanders fields the universal emblem of military remembrance; Siegfried Sassoon, who threw his medals away in protest; and Wilfred Owen, who returned to the front and was killed in action a week before the Armistice. Owen's most famous poem is built around a Latin line of Horace about how sweet and fitting it is to die for one's country, and it ends by denouncing Horace's sentiment with bitter contempt. McCrae's little poem turned its wildflower into the lasting symbol of remembrance, especially across Britain and the Commonwealth, where paper versions are still sold on street-corners every November to raise money for veterans and to mark the day the war ended. The whole literature of the war — poems, memoirs like Robert Graves's 'Goodbye to All That,' and Erich Maria Remarque's novel 'All Quiet on the Western Front' — fixed a particular kind of weary disillusionment in the Western imagination of what modern wars cost.

xerxes-invasion-and-the-greco-persian-wa.context_blurb: The Greco-Persian Wars were a series of conflicts, between about 500 and 449 BC, between the Greek city-states and the Persian Empire, which had become the greatest and most organized empire the Mediterranean world had yet seen. The wars began when Greek cities along the coast of Asia Minor revolted against Persian rule and Athens helped them. The Persian king Darius sent a punitive expedition that was defeated on a coastal plain in Attica. A decade later his son Xerxes launched a much larger invasion by both land and sea, broke through the famous mountain pass of Thermopylae, burned Athens, and was then defeated at a sea battle in a narrow strait and a land battle in central Greece. The remnants of the Persian force withdrew; subsequent Greek operations in the Aegean turned the tide completely. The Greek victory is remembered as the moment that free city-states defeated a vast centralized autocracy against the odds, and the memory of the wars shaped Greek identity afterward. The historian Herodotus wrote his famous book about these events, which is why we know their story in such extraordinary detail.

yorktown-1781-cornwallis-surrenders.context_blurb: The Battle of Yorktown in October 1781 was the final major military engagement of the American Revolutionary War. The British commander in the southern theater, General Charles Cornwallis, had taken his army to a defensive position on the Virginia coast at Yorktown, on the York River, expecting British resupply and reinforcement by sea. Instead, a French fleet under Admiral de Grasse arrived in the Chesapeake Bay from the Caribbean and defeated a British relief fleet in a decisive naval battle. With the Royal Navy driven off, Cornwallis was bottled up on land. George Washington marched the Continental Army and a French expeditionary army under the Comte de Rochambeau rapidly south from the New York area and besieged Yorktown. After several weeks of bombardment and parallel-trench siege warfare, with no relief coming by sea, Cornwallis surrendered his army of over seven thousand British and Hessian troops on October 19, 1781. Legend has it that the British band played a tune called The World Turned Upside Down as the surrender ceremony unfolded. The British government, exhausted by the war, had no stomach for continuing after Yorktown, and formal peace negotiations began the following year. The war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, with the United States as an independent country.

yuri-gagarin-first-human-in-space.context_blurb: Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was a Soviet Air Force pilot, the son of a carpenter and a dairymaid from a village west of Moscow, who had grown up under Nazi occupation during the Second World War. He was selected in 1960, aged twenty-six, out of thousands of young fighter pilots to be one of the first twenty Soviet cosmonauts, and then out of that twenty to be the first to actually fly. On the morning of 12 April 1961 he was strapped into a small spherical capsule called Vostok 1 and lofted into orbit on top of a modified intercontinental ballistic missile by Sergei Korolev's rocket team at a secret launch site in Soviet Kazakhstan. His flight lasted 108 minutes. He made one complete loop around the Earth at an altitude of a little over 300 kilometres, becoming the first human being to leave the planet, and returned safely to a soft touchdown on farmland near the Volga, surprising a startled peasant woman and her granddaughter who had been in the field. The Soviet government then paraded him around the world as a propaganda hero. Gagarin wanted to fly again, but his superiors, afraid of losing a national icon, kept him mostly on the ground. He died in 1968 at the age of 34 in the crash of a MiG-15 jet trainer during what should have been a routine flight; the exact cause of the crash is still debated. The town where he had trained for his historic flight was renamed Star City in his honour.

zheng-he-s-treasure-fleet-voyages.context_blurb: In the first third of the 15th century, the Chinese Ming dynasty under the Yongle Emperor sponsored a series of seven massive overseas voyages commanded by the Muslim court eunuch Zheng He. The fleet he led was by all accounts the most powerful on Earth: hundreds of ships, including some of the largest wooden sailing vessels ever built, carrying tens of thousands of sailors, soldiers, diplomats, translators, and craftsmen. The voyages between 1405 and 1433 touched Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and the east coast of Africa, where Zheng He traded for exotic goods including giraffes, zebras, and ostriches that astonished the Ming court. The voyages were not primarily commercial; they were diplomatic shows of force intended to demonstrate Ming might and to collect tribute from distant kings, and they succeeded on their own terms. After the Yongle Emperor's death and Zheng He's own death on his final voyage, however, a change in court policy ended the voyages abruptly. The Ming turned inward, destroyed many of the records, let the great shipyards decay, and forbade overseas trade for most of the following century. Fifty years later Portuguese caravels began their own, much smaller voyages down the African coast, and the world's long-distance seafaring future shifted west.

ziggurats.context_blurb: A ziggurat is a type of enormous stepped platform-temple built out of mud brick (with fired-brick exterior facings) that was the signature religious architecture of ancient Mesopotamian civilization, from the late third millennium BC through the first half of the first millennium BC. Ziggurats were built by the Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians, and other Mesopotamian peoples, and each major Mesopotamian city had at least one, dedicated to its patron god. The ziggurat consisted of a series of stacked rectangular terraces, each smaller than the one below, climbing up to a shrine on the top which only priests could enter. The best-known surviving example, partially restored, is the ziggurat of Ur in southern Iraq, built around 2100 BC by the Sumerian king Ur-Nammu. The famous ziggurat of Babylon, called in Akkadian Etemenanki, was dedicated to the god Marduk and is almost certainly the structure behind the biblical story of the Tower of Babel. Mesopotamian ziggurats were not pyramids in the Egyptian sense (they were not tombs) and they were not stepped Mesoamerican pyramids (which developed independently much later in the Americas). They were religious platforms — meeting places between earth and the realm of the city's god — and they dominated the skylines of Mesopotamian cities for over two thousand years.

august-coup-and-the-end-of-the-ussr-1991.context_blurb: By the summer of 1991 the Soviet Union, the communist state Lenin's Bolsheviks founded after seizing Russia in 1917, was coming apart. For seven decades the Communist Party had ruled a sixth of the world's land through censorship, the secret police and the Gulag camps, and its command economy could no longer feed or supply its own people. Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader since 1985, had loosened the Party's grip, and the fifteen republics the Kremlin held together, from the Baltic states to Central Asia, were pulling away. In August 1991 eight hardline officials, among them the KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov, Defense Minister Dmitry Yazov and Vice President Gennady Yanayev, moved to seize power and stop a treaty that would have handed real authority to the republics. They struck while Gorbachev was away on holiday in Crimea, declared a state of emergency and sent armored columns into Moscow. Boris Yeltsin, the newly elected president of the Russian republic, refused to obey them, and tens of thousands of unarmed Muscovites gathered around the Russian parliament building to defend it. The plot fell apart within days. The Communist Party never recovered: over the next four months republic after republic declared independence, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus agreed among themselves to end the union, and on December 25, 1991 Gorbachev resigned on live television as president of a country that had ceased to exist. A superpower that had outlasted Hitler's invasion ended without a war, brought down by its own failures and by citizens who stopped obeying.

fall-of-the-berlin-wall-1989.context_blurb: After the Second World War the victorious Allies divided Germany, and Berlin with it. The Soviet zone became East Germany, a communist dictatorship run by the Socialist Unity Party and watched over by its secret police, the Stasi; the western zones became a free and increasingly prosperous West Germany. So many East Germans fled west through Berlin that in August 1961 the East German leader Walter Ulbricht, with Soviet backing, sealed the border overnight and built a wall straight through the city. For twenty-eight years the regime ordered its border guards to shoot anyone who tried to cross, and they killed at least 140 people there. In 1987 the American president Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate and publicly challenged the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev over the wall. By 1989 the system was failing. Gorbachev had made it clear that Soviet tanks would no longer rescue the communist governments of Eastern Europe, Hungary had opened its border with Austria, and East Germans were leaving by the tens of thousands or marching every Monday in Leipzig. The Party forced out its longtime boss Erich Honecker and hurried to draft looser travel rules. On the evening of November 9, 1989, the Party spokesman Günter Schabowski announced those rules at a televised press conference, and within hours huge crowds stood at the Berlin checkpoints, where officers such as Harald Jäger at Bornholmer Strasse had to decide, without orders, what to do. By midnight the border was open. Germany reunified eleven months later, and that night became the lasting image of the end of communist rule in Europe.

gorbachev-glasnost-and-perestroika.context_blurb: Mikhail Gorbachev was the eighth and last leader of the Soviet Union. Born in 1931 to a peasant family in the Stavropol region of southern Russia, he grew up during Stalin's terror and the German invasion, studied law in Moscow, and climbed the ranks of the Communist Party until its ruling Politburo chose him as General Secretary in March 1985, at the age of fifty-four. He inherited a superpower in deep trouble: a state-run economy that produced shortages and falsified reports in place of goods, an unwinnable war in Afghanistan, an arms race it could not afford, and a population that had long since stopped believing the Party's promises. Gorbachev was a convinced communist who meant to save the system, not bury it. He launched two reform programs whose Russian names the whole world soon learned, freed political prisoners such as the physicist Andrei Sakharov, pulled the army out of Afghanistan, and sat down with the American president Ronald Reagan to negotiate real cuts in nuclear weapons. In 1989 he refused to send tanks to prop up the communist governments of Eastern Europe, and they fell one after another; he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990. At home, though, his reforms dissolved the fear that held the Soviet state together faster than they repaired its economy. Hardliners in his own government tried to overthrow him in August 1991, and by the end of that year the country he led had dissolved. Admirers abroad remember him as the man who let the Cold War end without a shot; many Russians remember the empty shelves and the lost empire.
